POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Mon, 09 Nov 2026 19:41:06 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 EU offers cash for Black Sea attack response https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-offers-cash-for-black-sea-attack-response/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Mon, 09 Nov 2026 18:55:24 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9290400 European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced Monday that the EU will help finance some Black Sea security costs after attacks on commercial shipping — blamed on Russia — even as the main diplomatic push to end the crisis unfolds elsewhere.

“Threats, attacks and incursions are rising off the coasts of the Black Sea,” von der Leyen said at the start of her visit to Romania.

In response, she said the bloc will “fast track the work on the Black Sea Maritime Security Hub, with a clear timeline for completion and dedicated funding of €50 million.”

She also announced an additional €10 million in EU cash for Romania’s search-and-rescue operations. The sums are tiny compared to the €16.7 billion Romania is getting under the EU’s SAFE arms loans program.

The hub, announced last year, is a joint control center to be run by Romania and Bulgaria and is expected to be fully operational by the end of the year.

It aims to monitor maritime activity in real time and safeguard vital infrastructure such as undersea power and communication cables. It would offer both countries a unified view of the sea and sky, helping them detect threats before they strike.

Monday’s announcement follows weeks of mounting violence on the Black Sea. Since early October, at least nine ships have been struck in the exclusive economic zones of NATO and EU members Romania and Bulgaria; four were sunk, and 34 sailors are dead or missing.

Other ships have been hit off Russia’s shores.

Both Romania and Bulgaria raised the issue at last month’s meeting of EU leaders and are pressing for more security support. However, while Romania has blamed Russia, Bulgaria has stopped short. Von der Leyen is set to visit Varna, on Bulgaria’s coast, on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, the U.S. is steering talks on a Black Sea ceasefire and an agreement on safe passage, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying Washington is reviewing proposals from Turkey forwarded in late October and is “open” to ideas from India.

An agreement would not end the conflict, Rubio said, but it would “solve a unique aspect” of it by easing the spillover on food security for vulnerable nations.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Oct. 21 that the bloc is working with Turkey, India and food-importing countries in Africa and other regions on a freedom-of-navigation deal. Ukraine has agreed to such an arrangement, she added, but Russia has rejected it.

Von der Leyen said the EU backs Ukraine’s call for a Black Sea ceasefire, referring to “the peace talks taking place in Abu Dhabi tomorrow with European presence.”

Commission chief spokesperson Paula Pinho gave no details on the proposals or the EU’s role. She noted a “common interest” in resolving disruptions, but declined to comment on the intentions of Turkey or the U.S.

Asked whether he foresaw a possible breakthrough this week, Ukraine’s Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi was pessimistic. He said that Kyiv is “preparing to keep our farmers operating without access to the deep-water Black Sea ports for the long term.”

The Black Sea matters to both sides in the war.

The ports of Ukraine’s Greater Odesa region are main channels for its exports, including steel, iron ore and grain, and they bring in billions of dollars. Several ships hit in EU waters were carrying Ukrainian grain.

Most of Russia’s grain exports also leave through Black Sea ports such as Novorossiysk, a major oil export hub, along with Tuapse.

Other countries are deeply invested, too. Near Novorossiysk, the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal, partly owned by U.S. oil giants Chevron and Exxon, handles about 80% of Kazakhstan’s crude exports.

Turkey has suffered the most ship attacks, and tankers headed for Georgia have also come under fire.

Agnes Rønberg contributed reporting.

]]> fr Who’s who for Europe at the Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi https://www.politico.eu/article/whos-who-europe-ukraine-talks-abu-dhabi-russia-war/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Mon, 09 Nov 2026 17:41:56 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9294984 Senior officials from the EU, NATO and key European capitals travel to Abu Dhabi this week to participate in U.S.-brokered talks geared toward ending Russia’s war on Ukraine — allaying fears that Europe risks being completely cut out of the process.

The talks coincide with growing concerns in Europe about potential concessions to Russia after Jared Kushner, son-in law and adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump, said last week that discussions would focus on a “new European security architecture” — a phrase often used by Russian officials to mean reducing NATO’s presence in front-line nations and limits on Ukraine’s armed forces.

Ukraine will be represented by Rustem Umerov, the head of Kyiv’s foreign intelligence service, along with senior officials Kyrylo Budanov and David Arakhamia. Russia’s contingent is to be led by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky. Representing the U.S. side will be Kushner and U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff.

The European contingent includes national security advisers from France, the U.K., Germany and Italy, in addition to senior officials from NATO as well as the European Commission and the European Council. The inclusion of EU figures as well as an Italian representative follows a push by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who warned of fragmentation in a letter to European Council President António Costa last week.

Despite their presence in Abu Dhabi, though, the European team is not expected to be inside the room during the main negotiations, according to two senior officials aware of the format. A German official told POLITICO that the format of talks would be “determined as the discussions progress.” The Kremlin has voiced opposition to Europeans directly participating in the talks, according to the same senior officials.

Here’s a quick look at the key players from Europe in Abu Dhabi.

Günter Sautter (Germany)

Sautter is German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s foreign and security policy adviser and a senior career diplomat who has become a major figure in Europe’s efforts to end Russia’s war — and secure a European seat at the negotiating table.

Besides representing Germany in the E3 format, Sautter is also coordinating the German-led “Berlin Format” — a German-led coalition to bring together Ukraine, the E3 and other European nations such as Italy, Poland or the Scandinavian countries as well as NATO, EU and others including Canada — that seeks to steer Ukraine’s peace talks and coordinate support for Kyiv.

At a press conference with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last week, Merz remarked that Sautter “is now devoting a significant portion of his workforce to diplomatic efforts to end this war.”

Sautter’s main credo in the talks is that there can be no discussion about a future European security architecture before Russia agrees to a ceasefire.

Fabrizio Saggio (Italy)

Fabrizio Saggio, diplomatic adviser to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, will also attend the talks, according to an Italian official.

Saggio, whose surname means “wise” in Italian, has earned the not-particularly-original sobriquet “Mister Wolf” in the Italian press, a reference to his role as Meloni’s go-to troubleshooter on major international issues, resolving problems and providing strategic advice.

Meloni met him during a visit to Tunis, where he was serving as Italian ambassador, to sign a migration deal. “It took her 20 minutes to realize that he was the one” for the job, an Italian diplomat said.

In a letter sent to European Council President António Costa last week and seen by POLITICO, Meloni complained about the proliferation of negotiating formats on Ukraine. She called for this week’s informal gathering of EU leaders in Dublin to also discuss Ukraine and decide “once and for all, who sits at the negotiating table representing the European Union, and with what mandate.” Costa agreed to put the issue on the agenda. 

In the same letter, Meloni also said: “I am not asking for a seat for Italy in this or that format.” But she got one anyway.

Geoffrey van Leeuwen (NATO)

Geoffrey van Leeuwen is NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte’s chief of staff. A career diplomat who has served everywhere from Kabul to Mumbai, van Leeuwen is a longtime Rutte loyalist who was trade minister and national security adviser during the boss’ time as Dutch prime minister.

Known as an affable and sharp operator who largely shuns the public eye, van Leeuwen helped steer NATO through seemingly unending crises mostly prompted by Donald Trump this year, including the U.S. President’s push to annex Greenland and the fallout from the U.S. war in Iran.

NATO doesn’t formally have any role in negotiating a peace deal. But where the talks touch on alliance issues — troop movements, security guarantees or Ukraine’s NATO accession — van Leeuwen will have an interest. His task is primarily “to observe, report back” and make sure “NATO is aware of what’s being said,” said an official familiar with the matter.

Jonathan Powell (United Kingdom)

U.K. National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell is expected to attend on behalf of the U.K.

The former aide to Tony Blair, known for his role in the Northern Ireland peace process, was brought back into government under Keir Starmer and stayed on under Andy Burnham. He has since become one of London’s most reliable links to Washington and is known to have a particularly strong relationship with Witkoff.

His position has come under scrutiny in recent months, however, with reports that he is on his way out of Downing Street.

Bjoern Seibert (European Commission)

Ursula von der Leyen’s chief of Cabinet is her most trusted lieutenant and one of the most influential figures in Brussels. 

A close confidant who helps steer her political and diplomatic work, Seibert is a central player in the EU’s discussions on Ukraine. His presence in Abu Dhabi puts von der Leyen’s office in the mix as Kyiv, Washington and Moscow discuss the war. 

He has joined earlier rounds of Ukraine talks, including meetings in Miami and Oslo with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, where officials discussed security guarantees, territory and Ukraine’s postwar recovery.

Seibert will play a similar role to the national security advisers of the E3 countries and NATO’s van Leeuwen, and will be present at whatever tables they’re sitting at, according to an EU official. But the Europeans are likely to be briefed separately because the Kremlin has repeatedly objected to them being present in the room for the three-way talks, including on Monday.

Anna-Maria Boura (European Council)

As European Council President António Costa’s chief foreign policy adviser, Boura will be the EU’s member countries’ eyes in Abu Dhabi. 

Her place on the ground marks the Council’s return to the Ukraine talks, after Costa’s office was absent from earlier rounds in Miami and Oslo, where Seibert represented the Commission. 

Boura’s profile is rising as Pedro Lourtie, Costa’s chief of Cabinet, is expected to leave for a new diplomatic role in the U.S. (It was Lourtie who opened a channel to the Kremlin this summer, speaking by phone with an official close to Vladimir Putin.) Boura also played a key part in the EU-Canada summit, holding the pen on the bloc’s side of the work on the joint declaration.

Emmanuel Bonne (France)

As Emmanuel Macron’s chief diplomatic adviser, Emmanuel Bonne is the man called upon to jet off to key venues — like Abu Dhabi this week — to lay the groundwork for the French president’s most important geopolitical initiatives.

Bonne, a career diplomat who served in multiple postings in the Middle East, joined Macron’s team in 2019 — a long tenure at the Elysée compared to some of his peers. Bonne was reportedly headed toward the exit in January 2025 due to a major dispute with the president’s chief of military staff, but Macron convinced him to stay on.

Hans von der Burchard, Esther Webber, Zoya Sheftalovich, Jacopo Barigazzi, Nicholas Vinocur, Victor Jack and Joshua Berlinger contributed to this report.

]]> fr France blames Iran for cyberattacks targeting supermarket fridges https://www.politico.eu/article/france-blames-iran-for-cyberattacks-targeting-supermarket-fridges/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Mon, 09 Nov 2026 16:35:43 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9295767 PARIS — French Minister of Foreign Affairs Jean-Noël Barrot said Iran was behind the recent series of “unprecedented” cyberattacks on refrigerators in several major supermarket chains in the country last month.

“Thanks to the outstanding work of the government departments, I am able to confirm that responsibility for this attack lies with the Iranian Revolutionary Guards,” Barrot told reporters Monday at a G7 meeting in Paris. “We will impose sanctions at European level against those responsible.”

Barrot said that 700 food distribution sites in France were impacted in the cyberattack. French prosecutors said shortly after that they were opening an investigation into the hacks.

Though Barrot was only referring to the incidents reported in France, grocery stores across Europe and even French blood banks have been targeted by hackers in recent days. Cyber experts had previously raised concerns that the attacks may have been part of Russia’s ongoing hybrid warfare against Europe, though the Kremlin has denied any involvement.

In a statement, a spokesperson for France’s foreign affairs ministry said the French investigation found that Iran’s cyber unit, Shahid Kaveh, carried out the destructive attacks. Shahid Kaveh, which is linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, carries out offensive cyber operations.

The French investigation will focus on the unit’s head, the Paris prosecutor’s office said in a statement, adding that about 20 fires had been started because of the cyberattack.

“The attackers took remote control of the equipment via web interfaces to trigger abnormal defrost cycles of unlimited duration, while disabling the security alerts on the sensors that were supposed to activate once a certain temperature was exceeded,” it added.

“We just heard now that [the cyberattacks] were attributed to Iran,” European Council President Kaja Kallas said after Barrot’s statement, adding that the matter would be discussed at next week’s European foreign affairs council. If the attribution is confirmed, she said, “[Europe’s] response should be strong.”

The European Commission is also looking into these cyberattacks, which EU Agriculture and Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen described as a “deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain.”

Iran’s foreign affairs ministry and its embassy in Paris did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

]]> en COP31 : comment Emmanuel Macron a perdu le goût du climat https://www.politico.eu/article/cop31-comment-emmanuel-macron-a-perdu-le-gout-du-climat/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Mon, 09 Nov 2026 16:04:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9288027 PARIS — N’est-il plus si chaud pour le climat ?  

Neuf ans après sa fameuse formule “Make our planet great again” , qui lui aura valu des galons de champion du climat à l’international, Emmanuel Macron a choisi de faire l’impasse sur le dernier raout des négociations climatiques de sa décennie élyséenne, la COP31, qui s’ouvre ce lundi à Antalya en Turquie.

Il n’est pas le seul, de nombreux chefs d’Etat ayant également choisi de snober le rendez-vous planétaire cette année. Mais son absence — la quatrième depuis son arrivée au pouvoir — est particulièrement remarquée. 

“Je ne comprends pas, franchement, pourquoi il n’y va pas, pourquoi il n’aide pas l’Union européenne à aller de l’avant”, regrette Laurence Tubiana, ancienne diplomate et architecte de l’Accord de Paris sur le climat. “C’est dommage”, poursuit-elle, relevant les “hésitations” du chef de l’Etat sur les sujets climatiques. 

Officiellement absent pour des raisons d’agenda, comme l’a révélé POLITICO, Emmanuel Macron aurait pourtant aimé en être, lui qui “a pris du plaisir” à participer aux grandes messes du climat, assure ainsi la ministre de la Transition écologique Monique Barbut. “Je pense qu’il regrette [de ne pas pouvoir venir], assure-t-elle. C’est un endroit où il est plutôt très bien accueilli”.

Parmi les soutiens du président, on revendique le choix de manquer certains sommets. 

“La COP n’est pas un rituel incontournable où il faut se montrer. C’est un lieu de négociation pour faire bouger les lignes”, défend quant à elle l’ex-ministre de la Transition écologique Agnès Pannier-Runacher, qui estime qu’il n’y a “pas d’espace de jeu” cette année. 

Reste que parmi ceux qui le connaissent, tous ne sont pas tombés de leur chaise en apprenant la nouvelle, le président n’étant pas, de leur point de vue, un mordu de l’écologie. 

Emmanuel Macron n’est pas “quelqu’un de nativement écolo, ce n’était pas dans son logiciel de base”, reconnaît ainsi sans fard un ex-conseiller de l’exécutif. “Sur la scène internationale, il y voyait une façon de se positionner, d’être un président cool, qui parle aux jeunes”, assure le même.

Les limites du en même temps

Un raisonnement qui illustre bien le rapport du chef de l’Etat à la défense de la planète. 

Côté pile, ses défenseurs louent son activité débordante sur la scène internationale, illustrée par les nombreux sommets sur la biodiversité, la finance climat et la santé environnementale lancés sous son égide, sa défense du Giec, le groupe d’experts dont les travaux constituent la référence scientifique mondiale sur le climat, et du rôle du nucléaire dans la transition verte. Et ce, dans un contexte de durcissement des discussions mondiales sur le climat.  

Sur le plan national, les émissions françaises ont aussi baissé, même si la trajectoire a largement ralenti ces deux dernières années. 

Côté face, il est difficile d’estimer l’effet réel de ces sommets organisés en dehors du cadre onusien.

“Ça fait même plutôt diversion, parce que ça permet à la France de créer ses propres sommets en invitant ses copains, et pas ceux avec qui elle ne s’entend pas”, juge Marine Pouget, responsable de la gouvernance internationale sur le climat au RAC. “Il n’y a rien de concret derrière.”

Au sein des arcanes onusiens, la France a plus de mal à se faire entendre malgré le capital politique que lui a conféré la conclusion de l’Accord de Paris en 2015. 

Les positions françaises sur la finance climat — devenue le principal point de blocage des discussions mondiales sur le climat avec la sortie des énergies fossiles — cristallisent ces difficultés.

Pour des raisons budgétaires et politiques, sous pression de l’extrême droite, l’exécutif tricolore refuse catégoriquement d’augmenter le montant de l’aide climatique versée aux pays en développement. Et reste campé sur l’objectif de 6 milliards d’euros annuels fixé par Emmanuel Macron en décembre 2020, qui fut atteint dès l’année suivante. 

C’est justement cette période qui marque un tournant dans le positionnement du chef de l’Etat sur les enjeux écologiques.

S’il a su tirer parti de la vague verte déclenchée par les manifestations sur le climat au début de son premier mandat, le renoncement à la taxe carbone après le mouvement des Gilets jaunes et la condamnation de l’Etat pour inaction climatique ont laissé des traces, et fini par infuser sur les positions françaises à l’international.

“Pendant quatre, cinq ans, on a surfé sur la vague, il a eu cette image [de champion du climat] et a pu avoir cette ambition, constate un diplomate. A un moment, la fracture est devenue trop grande, et le manque de cohérence trop flagrant.”

L’absence d’une doctrine Macron

C’est au sein de l’Union européenne que ces tensions éclatent au grand jour, à l’automne 2025. Alors que les reculs écologiques se multiplient sur le plan national après la dissolution de l’Assemblée et que les organisations patronales françaises montent au front, Emmanuel Macron semble hésiter, et fait traîner les négociations sur les objectifs climatiques européens.  

Pour la première fois depuis son arrivée au pouvoir, la France sort du camp des ambitieux sur un dossier lié au climat. Le scénario se répète actuellement avec les négociations sur le marché carbone européen, pour lesquelles l’exécutif se retrouve à nouveau écartelé entre les positions des différents ministères.

Ces hésitations reflètent les fractures du monde économique français, entre les entreprises qui ont investi dans la décarbonation et les industriels polluants, comme les chimistes, qui n’ont pas fait la bascule.

Mais elles révèlent aussi les fractures au sein de la coalition centriste qui a conduit Emmanuel Macron au pouvoir. Certains parlementaires du bloc central qui avaient voté la loi Climat et résilience en 2021, principal marqueur écologique du premier quinquennat, étaient ainsi aux abonnés absents au moment de la défendre dans l’hémicycle quatre ans plus tard. 

Des revirements qui nourrissent quelques regrets chez les soutiens les plus écolos du président. L’eurodéputé Pascal Canfin, devenu l’éminence verte du chef de l’Etat sur les sujets européens après son ralliement en 2019, est de ceux-là. 

Emmanuel Macron “n’a jamais conceptualisé d’écologie macroniste” qui aurait “résisté aux modes”, accuse l’ex-directeur général du WWF. 

“Cet aspect pro-climat n’a jamais été identitaire du macronisme, il a été repris, conclut-il. Ça a été une sorte de variable d’ajustement tout au long du quinquennat.”

“‘Referendums’ under occupation are a tool of annexation, not an expression of the people’s will. ]]> en Don’t do the Norway model, Norway tells Britain https://www.politico.eu/article/norway-model-uk-jonas-gahr-store-andy-burnham/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Mon, 09 Nov 2026 14:49:04 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9294816 OSLO — Andy Burnham has been warned by Norway’s leader not to seek to emulate his country’s EU relationship ahead of a summit with European leaders.

In a POLITICO interview, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said he would not recommend the model his country has with the EU to Britain, because the two economies are so different.

Norway, with a population of 5.6 million, is a member of the EU single market through the European Economic Area (EEA) but is not a fully fledged EU member state — and therefore has no voting rights over the bloc’s commercial rules. 

“There’s an obvious democratic deficit in it, but pragmatically, all [Norwegian] Parliaments since 1995 have said this is a reasonable way of doing it,” Støre said. “I don’t see Britain do that. I don’t see Canada do that.” 

The U.K. and Canada are both in the process of seeking closer ties to the bloc of 27 countries, which the U.K. voted to leave a decade ago. 

Burnham has said in the long term he wants to see the U.K. rejoin — and is aiming to scope ideas for better trade terms later this month at a summit with EU leaders. He has said all options should be looked at. 

Støre said in addition to being part of the single market, Norway has had to sign 100 additional agreements with Brussels, covering climate, students, security and other matters. 

“I can tell you after Brexit, British friends called me and said, tell us about the Norwegian way of doing it. And I said, if you left the EU because there was too much Brussels, don’t take the Norwegian version,” he said. 

“Because here, you know, basically we are taking most of their decisions, we implement them. But a country of 5 million people that has been a completely open economy, always adapting to standards, to be part of the global economy, very open economy, we can live with that.” 

He confirmed he would not recommend the Norway model to Britain “because I think it’s very different, you know, and they have to find their solution.” 

Støre added that he could see the U.K., Canada and Norway working strategically together on issues that also matter to the EU, including space cooperation and supply chains for rare earth minerals. 

Støre has been leader of Norway’s Labor Party since 2014 and prime minister since 2021.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Mon, 09 Nov 2026 17:39:03 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 €120m in totally unused border facilities is the latest bill for the monumental waste that was Brexit https://euobserver.com/247911/e120m-in-totally-unused-border-facilities-is-the-latest-bill-for-the-monumental-waste-that-was-brexit/ Mon, 09 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247911 Hundreds of millions have been wasted on Brexit border checks that either don't work or were never used. It's a fitting monument to a failure to plan.]]> As a microcosm for the waste, self-sabotage and basic failure to plan that has been implementing Brexit, it is hard to beat the expensive, endlessly-delayed and ultimately pointless border checks on goods and people imposed by both the UK and EU. 

Data published by the UK’s National Audit Office has revealed that the post-Brexit Conservative governments spent more than £100m (€120m) on border check facilities that were never used. 

Five of the seven “inland border facilities” in England and Wales never got to operational stage because the Tories decided that since food coming from the EU would be the same high standard as it was before Brexit there was no point having extra checks.

In total, the National Audit Office reckons that implementing Brexit cost £4.7bn (€5.6bn).

Much of that taxpayer cash was spent on systems, many of which, if Andy Burnham’s government stays in power for a few years, will soon be obsolete. 

Read more

Whisper it, but the UK’s path back to the EU is beginning to take shape

And the remaining facilities that have been used will now be mothballed in a few months under the new EU-UK agreement on food and drink products that aligns regulation between London and Brussels. 

Elsewhere, freedom of information requests have revealed that Eurotunnel spent €50m on Brexit checks for trucks and €90m on changes for passengers, including an entry and exit system that the French authorities have never used.

]]> MEPs demand Belgium evacuate visa-holders from Gaza as winter flooding makes life catastrophic https://euobserver.com/247914/meps-demand-belgium-evacuate-visa-holders-from-gaza-as-winter-flooding-makes-life-catastrophic/ Mon, 09 Nov 2026 17:26:08 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247914 1,800 people hold Belgian visas for family reunifications or university studies, yet remain stuck in Gaza. And while EU officials and Belgian authorities pass accountability back and forth, devastating floods have displaced even more already displaced people - and a handful of MEPs stand up for the Palestinians that will have to suffer another winter outdoors. ]]> As deadly floods worsen the already catastrophic conditions in Gaza, MEPs have urged the Belgian authorities and EU Commission to evacuate Palestinian families and university students holding Belgian visas after months of worry and unanswered questions.

Many have been rendered homeless once more since heavy rain flooded tens of thousands of tents of displaced families in Gaza at the weekend, reportedly killing four children and leaving another half a million without shelter. 

In a letter sent last Wednesday (4 November), 17 MEPs from the Left, Greens/EFA, liberal group Renew Europe, as well as one non-attached member, implored the Belgian president and foreign minister, as well as Hadja Lahbib, EU commissioner for crisis management, to coordinate the evacuation of Belgian visa holders such as Bardees Abu Kweik , who are still trapped in Gaza. 

“We are still in Gaza, holding valid Belgian visas, yet we have no evacuation appointment and no clear information from the Belgian government,” Abu Kweik told EUobserver from the war-torn strip. 

She and her two children have been waiting to reunite with her husband in Belgium since her visa was accepted in February.

One of her children, a 12-year old, has been in need of medical assistance after being injured in the war: “following the recent rain, my tent flooded, leaving me and my children out on the street. With my child suffering from a severe leg injury—exposed to the cold and rain—our situation has become significantly worse than before.”

Read more

Belgian minister under fire for denying evacuation to 13 Gazan scholarship students

The letter counted 1,800 people in Gaza who currently hold a valid Belgian visa, 10 of whom are students granted places at Belgian universities, holding student visas, and (following highly-divisive parliamentary debates and two months of the semester already gone), are still being denied any assistance in leaving a war zone.

]]> Russia goes quiet on claims of territorial wins, starts bragging about air-strikes on Ukrainian cities instead (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,719) https://euobserver.com/247849/russia-goes-quiet-on-claims-of-territorial-wins-starts-bragging-about-air-strikes-on-ukrainian-cities-instead-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1719/ Mon, 09 Nov 2026 16:14:06 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247849 Russian Z-channels have stopped reporting on movements along the contact lines, instead publishing lists of cities struck by Russian drones and missiles. ]]>
  • Large-scale offensives and widespread casualties are achieving little
  • Ukrainian army may have answer to Russia’s infiltration tactics
  • There are no longer any Russian soldiers in Orikhiv
  • Kyiv facing major logistical problems following attacks on bridges splitting the city
  • Death toll in Komyshuvakha rises to 55; Ukrainians released perpetrator names, and Russians are satisfied with the outcome
  • Maps of the day: Orikhiv
  • Videos of the day: soldiers return from their position after 320 days without rotation; unlike many others, the machine gunner of a Russian mobile team did not flee and paid for his courage

    • On the battlefield, the Ukrainian army has brought Russians to a standstill, but Ukrainian cities face serious problems as a result of Russian air strikes.

    This is also reflected in how Russian Z-channels report on the war.

    Information on movements along the front line has almost completely disappeared, replaced by a daily list of Ukrainian cities struck by Russian drones and missiles.

    This does not mean the Russian army has stopped attacking on the ground.

    Ukrainian soldiers report the exact opposite, but it appears Russian president Vladimir Putin’s strategy is to win the war through bombing and by forcing Ukraine to surrender via making life in cities unbearable.

    Large-scale offensives and widespread casualties are achieving little. “The week at the front was marked by trench warfare and a struggle over logistics. Significantly, the Russian defence ministry’s weekly summary did not report the capture of any populated area,” Russian Telegram channel Two Majors wrote in its weekly summary on Sunday.

    Until recently, the Kremlin had published daily updates of land capture, even when the evidence to support this was lacking.

    Sometimes, such reports were based solely on “flag operations” by individuals who allowed themselves to be filmed by a drone camera, only to be killed or captured shortly afterwards.

    Two Majors speculated that the Kremlin’s silence may be due to cold weather complicating combat operations, but another possible explanation is more interesting.

    The channel said that the Russian army command was secretly reassessing the configuration of the front line because too many false reports of success had come in from the field.

    The explanation is certainly not a halt to the Russian offensive.

    ]]>         Fake bomb warnings are hitting European aviation – but the bigger threat came from Jared Kushner https://euobserver.com/247845/fake-bomb-warnings-are-hitting-european-aviation-but-the-bigger-threat-came-from-jared-kushner/ Mon, 09 Nov 2026 14:15:29 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247845 Every one of the 70-plus warnings sent to airlines, newsrooms and other targets in Europe last week was a hoax. But the harm was real: planes diverted, buildings evacuated, plans disrupted, costs incurred, public confidence eroded, writes Edward Lucas.]]> Every one of the 70-plus warnings sent to airlines, newsrooms and other targets in Europe last week was a hoax.

    But the harm was real: planes diverted, buildings evacuated, plans disrupted, costs incurred, public confidence eroded.

    It was the same story with a much bigger — if metaphorical — recent bomb threat, involving the blowing up of Europe’s security architecture.

    The other threat – from Jared Kushner

    This threat came not by anonymous email, but in a social media post from Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law. It mentioned five goals: “permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.”

    That might sound anodyne on first reading. But given the administration’s record of bullying allies and appeasing adversaries, many interpreted it as signalling a planned east-west stitch-up, probably fuelled by the Trump family’s business interests. 

    Europe does not lack security architecture.

    Everything Kushner cites is in the Paris Charter of 1990, the Budapest Memorandum of 1994, the Nato-Russia Founding Act of 1997 and the Rome Declaration of 2002 (this last one signed by none other than Vladimir Putin). 

    It was Russia, out of pique, paranoia and imperial self-interest, that blew up these agreements. All of them. 

    The starting point for anyone interested in European security should therefore be to get Russia to respect the promises it has already made, along with other countries’ borders and sovereignty.

    But Kushner gave no hint that the US administration will put pressure on the Kremlin on these issues or indeed anything.

    The signs point the other way.

Moldova energy minister Dorin Junghietu on why Chișinău is betting on diversification https://euobserver.com/246837/interview-whenever-we-take-pro-european-political-decisions-russia-cut-or-reduced-gas-supplies-moldova-energy-minister-dorin-junghietu-on-why-chisinau-is-betting-on-diversification/ Mon, 09 Nov 2026 13:43:33 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246837 Moldova suffers from soaring blackout costs and fragile Soviet-era lines. Chisinau, in response, on Monday, inaugurated a new electric grid, linking to Romania and the European grid. The country's energy minister tells EUobserver: 'Russia uses energy as a weapon, and they did it also to Moldova. Whenever we tried to take pro-European political decisions, Russia cut or reduced gas supplies.']]> On Monday (9 November) Moldova inaugurated a new electric grid, the Vulcănești–Chișinău power line, which links the c0untry to Romania and the European grid and is seen as a issue of pressing national independence.

    As winter rolls in, concerns about energy dependence on Russia are once again at the forefront, particularly in countries that have historically relied heavily on Russian supplies. Moldova is one of them.

    In recent years, however, the country has made significant efforts to reduce its dependence on Moscow’s supplies and strengthen its energy security, while accelerating its integration with the EU.

    In an exclusive interview with EUobserver, Moldova’s minister of energy, Dorin Junghietu, discusses the country’s efforts to secure alternative energy supplies, modernise its infrastructure and keep prices affordable, as the country is moving closer to EU integration.

    For many years, Moldova relied heavily on Russia for its energy supplies, both natural gas and electricity. How sustainable was this dependence, and was Moldova ever in a position to realistically reduce or eliminate it?

    Indeed for more than three decades, Moldova depended on a single source of gas, while most of its electricity came from a power plant fuelled by Russian gas.

    We understood how this structural dependence affected our economy and social life. There were several instances when it proved to be a wrong long-term strategy. Russia uses energy as a weapon, and they did it also to Moldova. Whenever we tried to take pro-European political decisions, Russia cut or reduced gas supplies.

    Gas contracts were also renegotiated in the final days of each year, with Moldovan politicians travelling to St Petersburg or Moscow to negotiate conditions.

    These experiences confirmed the need to diversify away from a single supplier. Since 2022 [Russia’s full-invasion of Ukraine], these efforts have accelerated.

    Read more

    Moldova seen as ‘best performer’ on EU-accession reforms, despite onslaught of Russian sabotage

    Transnistria has long been an important part of Moldova’s energy vulnerabilities, particularly because of its dependence on Russian gas and the role of the Cuciurgan power plant in supplying electricity. How does the situation in Transnistria affect Moldova’s overall energy security, and what is your government’s strategy for addressing this vulnerability?

    Until 1 January 2025, approximately 70 percent of Moldova’s electricity needs were supplied by the power plant at Moldavska Kuchurgan in Transnistria.

    When Russian gas transit through Ukraine stopped on that date, the plant could no longer produce electricity. We shifted to imports from Romania and Ukraine.

    This was a decisive moment, making clear the need to completely phase out Russian-linked energy sources. Since then, the right bank of the Dniester has not purchased any commercial electricity from that source. We rely on local generation and imports from Romania and Ukraine when available.

    However, a structural vulnerability remains because our electricity network was configured during Soviet times. Major interconnection and transmission lines were directed towards the power plant in Transnistria. Even the existing Vulcănești–Moldavska–Chișinău line passes through that node.

    The new Vulcănești–Chișinău overhead power line will bypass it and directly connect the Vulcănești and Chișinău electricity nodes.

    How has Moldova’s energy situation changed in recent years, particularly in terms of its dependence on Russian supplies? Why is this change so important for the country’s energy security?

    Our first structural dependence was reduced when the Iași–Ungheni–Chișinău gas pipeline was commissioned, allowing us to import gas from Romania and access European supplies.

    Last year, Energocom, the state-owned company responsible for purchasing gas, had approximately 24 to 26 contracts with different suppliers.

    Electricity diversification also accelerated in 2021 and 2022, when private investors began focusing on renewable energy. In just four to five years, our wind and solar capacities increased 13 to 15 times.

    ]]>         Israel’s anti-Netanyahu bloc needs Europe’s help to stabilise Middle East https://euobserver.com/247694/israels-anti-netanyahu-bloc-needs-europes-help-to-stabilise-middle-east/ Mon, 09 Nov 2026 12:00:35 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247694 The recent elections in Israel and the US create a narrow geopolitical opening for de-escalation in the Middle East, which Europe should seize upon instead of playing wait and see. ]]> The electoral outcomes in Israel and the US, characterised by many as the most consequential of the last 20 years, have the potential for altering the geopolitical landscape of the Middle East.

    The confluence of new power formations in Tel Aviv and Washington might present a new, if fragile, avenue towards stability and de-escalation.

    Yet the tale of these elections contains a harsh lesson for Europe’s leaders: the era of “wait and see” is over.

    The one thing Europe can no longer afford is the luxury of remaining on the sidelines, hoping that political actors in Israel and the US will resolve the region’s crises on their own.

    Continuing to relegate itself to a secondary stakeholder would not only be a diplomatic failing but worse, a strategic error that threatens to leave Europe unable to influence policy decisions in the Middle East that directly impact on its own security and prosperity.

    By maintaining its current posture of inaction, Europe risks bearing the political and economic fallout from developments it had the power to shape but chose to ignore.

    The new reality in Tel Aviv

    The ousting of prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s extremist, right-wing coalition on 27 October marked a shift in Israeli politics.

    The mandate given by president Isaac Herzog to opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a government represents a chance to step away from aggressive annexation and the systematic undermining of democratic norms.

    However, the path ahead is precarious. The potential coalition, while united in its opposition to Netanyahu, is ideologically diverse and faces the immediate and difficult task of securing a solid majority.

    Netanyahu, who remains head of the caretaker government until a new prime minister is sworn in, will most certainly attempt to spoil these efforts.  

    Read more

    Israel’s election may disappoint everyone, as Brussels and Washington face a hard reckoning with a more ‘centrist’ leader

    For a stable anti-Netanyahu government to emerge or to be tolerated, the inclusion of Arab parties is indispensable.

    The centre-right Zionist anti-Netanyahu coalition of Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman, in concert with the 27 seats held by the Arab parties and Yair Golan’s Democrats, possesses the numerical potential to rein in the ideological excesses and extremist policies of the previous years.

    However, Eisenkot’s requirement for all potential coalition partners to confirm Israel’s status as a Jewish State, is a difficult pill to swallow for the Arab parties.

    For the Arab Joint List in particular, this means compromising on fundamental principles to prevent the return of Netanyahu and his racist and supremacist allies, Itamar Ben Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.

    The only other way for Eisenkot to get to 61 seats in the Knesset would require both ultra-orthodox parties to join him in the government.

    This, however, means Lieberman reneging on his electoral pledge not to exempt Haredi men from military service.  

    For the center-right allies led by Eisenkot, most of whom also share an ethno-nationalist world view, the central challenge remains the management of the occupied territory.

    The Zionist anti-Netanyahu bloc will likely pivot from the outgoing government’s policy of open annexation and ethnic cleansing to a policy of managing the conflict under the sole lens of national security.

    Make no mistake, ending the occupation, championing Palestinian self-determination and prioritising a two-state solution, is not on the menu. 

    Read more

    Lead trade MEP Bernd Lange slams EU Commission for ‘hiding’ behind voting rules on banning Israeli settlement imports

    When it comes to Gaza, an Eisenkot-led government might be more open to supporting the implementation of the UN Security Council-approved Gaza peace plan, but it will condition its cooperation and the Israeli Defence Forces’ withdrawal from most of the Strip on full disarmament of [Palestinian militant group] Hamas.

    These caveats notwithstanding, and as a result of external pressure, agreement may eventually be found to reverse the most egregious policies of the Netanyahu era in the West Bank, notably by curbing unscrupulous settlement expansion, halting the ‘E1’ settlement project, dismantling illegal settler outposts in Area C, holding terrorist settlers to account and ending the punitive withholding of clearance revenues from the Palestinian Authority, estimated to be between $4.6bn [€4.1bn] and $6bn. 

    However, it is far from clear whether Eisenkot and his hawkish allies on the center-right will want to pursue a different approach towards Iran and Lebanon.

    While they have criticised Netanyahu for starting the war against Teheran without political exit strategy they full-heartedly support aggressive military action against the Mullah regime [in Iran] and [the Lebanese paramilitary force] Hezbollah.

    Netanyahu knows this as well and might resume military strikes on Iran and its allies in the region while still in power.

    The Washington dynamic

    Predicting the trajectory of US Middle East policy under president Donal Trump, now constrained by a Democrat-dominated Congress, remains complex. While Trump retains broad constitutional prerogatives in foreign policy, the new Congress holds significant leverage through budgetary legislation.

    The announced phase-out of the nearly $4bn in annual US military aid to Israel by Trump is a clear indicator of shifting domestic political winds.

    Given the increasingly negative image of Israel among Democratic voters and politicians, it is improbable that the new Congress will approve further unconditional multi-annual, large-scale military aid.

    The conflict with Tehran introduces a more volatile variable. While the US Constitution demands congressional approval for a declaration of war, Trump might argue that strikes against Iran constitute independent defensive actions necessary to protect American lives and interests, thereby bypassing congressional oversight.

    With no further electoral hurdles until November 2028, Trump faces limited political restraint at home, short of an unlikely impeachment proceeding.

    Read more

    Trump’s mid-term election disaster is not good news for Nato or Ukraine

    Should Trump initiate massive military action the Iranian regime will, in all likelihood, respond by triggering a retaliatory cycle that would inevitably target Gulf states harboring US military assets, including civilian energy infrastructure and desalination plants.

    As witnessed in the past six months, collateral damage reverberates far beyond the region.

    The economic impact is felt globally, hitting US households and European economies alike. Tehran’s strategic calculus remains rooted in the belief that substantial financial and economic costs will compel US partners worldwide to exert pressure on the Trump administration to seek a political, rather than military, solution.

    Furthermore, domestic pressure within the US will likely grow. The non-interventionist MAGA wing, recognising the potential impact on future electoral bids, such as US vice-president JD Vance’s potential 2028 presidential campaign, is increasingly wary of the costs associated with prolonged conflict.

    This also implies revisiting the special relationship with Israel, increasingly seen as a liability for US interests in the region and beyond.

    When combined with the nearly unified opposition from the Democratic party, the political sustainability of massive military intervention in the Gulf is questionable.

    Read more

    G7 releases diesel stocks after Trump pressure, EU denies caving

    Europe’s strategic failure and the path forward

    How can Europe meaningfully impact policy decisions in Tel Aviv, Washington, and the Gulf capitals? The answer requires a twofold, simultaneous approach.

    First, Europe must abandon its muted, reactive diplomacy. It is entirely appropriate to wait until a new government in Tel Aviv is sworn in and congressional races are validated before initiating formal, high-level engagement.

    However, nothing prevents European politicians, parliamentarians and senior officials from pro-actively reaching out to the forces in Israel, the US, and the Gulf that are seeking an end to military conflicts and sustainable political solutions.

    This engagement must emphasize, above all, the imperative of respecting international law as the foundation for any lasting resolution, particularly in the longest-entrenched conflict theatre: occupied Palestine.

    Also, on Iran and the contentious issue of its nuclear programme, the EU has much to offer, having played a critical role in the negotiations that led to the landmark JCPOA agreement with Iran in 2015 on non nuclear non-proliferation.

    Getting there again might probably be the best political outcome one could hope for in view of de-escalation and stability.

    Second, for the EU to regain credibility, it must match its rhetoric with substantive action. It is long overdue for European institutions and member states to fulfill their own obligations under international and European law.

    This requires, inter alia, the immediate banning of trade with Israel’s illegal settlements, in view of the International Court of Justice’s (ICJ’s) advisory opinion of 19 July 2024.

    Read more

    No Israeli bonds on sale in EU for now, in de facto €2.2bn sanction

    Furthermore, the EU must impose sanctions on ministers of the outgoing government, specifically Ben Gvir and Smotrich, for their policies and conduct in Gaza and the West Bank.

    Women in Bosnia and Herzegovina who defended their river from hydropower development have taken their solidarity across the border to support Albanian communities fighting for theirs.

    None of these countries are full European Union members. Brussels generally approaches them as recipients of European democratic standards, not as teachers.

    But what if Europe’s democratic renewal comes not from its political centres, but from its edges?

    Europe faces two connected democratic failures. The first is a failure to listen. The second is a failure of belonging. Looking to Europe’s edges could help address both.

    The peripheries

    First, Brussels has long treated the continent’s peripheries as resources to be used or problems to be managed. Ports move goods. Borderlands police migration. Coastal regions supply energy and tourism. Candidate countries receive instruction on democratic standards. Even when the centre consults local populations, it generally arrives with the questions already written and the solutions largely decided.

    The political traffic generally runs in one direction: ideas flow outward from Brussels, while labour, energy and strategic assets flow inward. Rarely does Europe ask what its margins know that its centres do not.

    Yet borderlands, divided cities, islands and ports confront Europe’s most pressing questions firsthand.

    Who belongs? Who decides what development means? How do people share land, water or public space when their histories and loyalties collide? How does a community act together without agreeing on everything? These are not abstract policy puzzles. They are questions of daily life, answered through negotiation, cooperation, conflict and compromise.

    Read more

    Serbia’s Student List has been inspirational, but the big test will be forming a stable anti-corruption government

    Serbia’s student movement challenged entrenched power through collective mobilisation. Albania’s protesters are asking who gets to decide whether a coastline is a public good or a private opportunity. And Bosnian river defenders have shown that political solidarity can cross a border rather than end at it.

    None offers a blueprint for Europe. All offer practices worth learning from.

    Europe’s second failure runs deeper. Liberal democracy rightly defends rights, constitutional safeguards and equal citizenship. But constitutional patriotism— the hope that shared loyalty to democratic rules can bind diverse societies— has too often proved too thin to satisfy people’s hunger for belonging.

    Institutions can protect freedoms without giving citizens a sense of common purpose. A legal framework is essential. It is not, by itself, a political community.

    Learning from the margins

    Populists have seized this opening. Ethno-nationalist movements offer something that procedural liberalism often struggles to provide: attachment, solidarity, heritage and a story about who “we” are.     Europe cannot answer this threat simply by repeating its commitment to liberal norms. Nor should it concede the desire for rooted, meaningful belonging to those who would turn it into a weapon.

    Here, too, the margins have something to teach. In places where neighbours inherit incompatible memories, where livelihoods depend on contested resources, and where borders cut through relationships, people sometimes build common purpose without first becoming alike. Shared work, obligations, arguments and care for a place can produce attachments stronger than abstract agreement and more generous than ethnic sameness.

    We should not romanticise these practices of course.

    Local solidarities can be exclusionary; informal compromises can entrench injustice. And winning an election is not the same as governing democratically. But refusing to idealise the edges is not a reason to ignore them. It is a reason to examine their political experiments with the seriousness routinely granted to ideas born in European capitals.

    The two failures are connected. When Brussels sees the edges only as territories to administer, it overlooks the democratic practices through which people develop belonging. And when liberal politics neglects belonging, it leaves the field open to the far-right.

    The answer is not another programme dispatched from the centre.

    It is a reversal of the direction of learning. Let communities help define the questions before policy is written. Treat their experiments in shared life, public resources and contested heritage as sources of political insight, not colourful local anecdotes. Bring their ideas into Europe’s democratic debate.

    Serbia’s victory does not prove that the margins have all the answers. It makes an uncomfortable possibility harder to dismiss: Europe should be searching for democratic renewal in the very places it has been taught to overlook.

    This article was written as part of EDGES – [European Democracies, Geographies, Ecologies, and Societies]. Readers interested in joining the network can sign up here.

    In the Nepalese mountains, a woman comes back to her village with jewellry and shining trinkets, giving the appearance of wealth. She promises local kids jobs in Kathmandu.

    “The whole village supports the kids going…. What they didn’t know is she was trafficked,” Lisa Kristine, an American photographer profiling human trafficking victims, told EUobserver.

    The “Slavery: Stories of the Present” exhibition opened on Thursday (5 November) in Géopolis, a city-supported photo-journalism museum in Brussels.

    It features works of two photographers focusing on modern slavery around the world and on women and girls in rural Afghanistan, often forced to marry in their early teens.

    About 50 million people were enslaved as of 2022, with some 27 million in forced labour, and 22 million married against their will, according to the International Labour Organisation data. The number grew by 10 million since 2016.

    Many are sold off to pay for family debts, others are lured with false promises of good job conditions. 

    Read more

    In the EU alone, at least 880,000 people are forced to work, including 270,000 being sex-trafficked.

    Photography, argues Kristine, one of the two photographers whose works make up the exhibition, is a good method of raising awareness on the topic: contrary to statistics or even an eye-to-eye encounter, “a photograph allows for us to really stare.” This way, the viewer can take the time to see the other person and open up to empathy.

    “The issue is rather abstract, full of data… but when you actually see a human being, it speaks more to your heart,” Kristine told EUobserver.

    Pictures by the other photographer, Élise Blanchard, show Afghan girls and women, whose families have often lost their herding grounds or could no longer farm on their land as a result of climate change. Selling their daughters for marriage is a way out of family debts.

    “I’m not trying to frighten somebody or overwhelm somebody with something horrific…” she said, highlighting the human dignity she tries to show through her portraits.

Prime minister Péter Magyar navigates a minefield where each disclosure risks empowering Fidesz loyalists and unsettling Hungary’s neighbours alike. ]]> The series continues as we report on developments following April’s historic election and on the steps taken since then by the Tisza government. This week, we cover the following topics:

    • Secret-police files: familiar names and an embarrassing error.
    • Director of the Institute of International Affairs dismissed – he had also worked for the Fidesz government.
    • Government causes major uproar with cultural budget.
    • Less money may go across the borders.
    • Poll of the week: a majority wants slower, but lawful and effective justice.

    Sándor Lezsák was one of the founders of the Hungarian party called MDF at the time of the country’s regime change from communism; it was in the yard of his house in Lakitelek where the meetings preparing the transition took place, where opposition politicians held discussions in the late 1980s.

    Lezsák later became a Fidesz politician and served as a MEP for the party until the 2026 election. His name also appeared in the state security documents published on Wednesday (4 November), which he immediately and vehemently protested against.

    “Everyone who spreads this vile lie will be held accountable for it in court,” he wrote.

    It soon emerged that his name indeed should not have appeared in the files.

    On Thursday morning the Historical Archives of the State Security Services announced that Lezsák’s name had appeared on the website due to an IT error. In reality he was not a network contact, but a person under surveillance.

    Fidesz politicians immediately seized on the case.

    “Tisza, in truly neo-communist fashion, is lumping perpetrators together with victims,” reacted parliamentary group leader János Bóka, demanding an apology from prime minister Péter Magyar and the resignation of cultural minister Zoltán Tarr.

    Magyar later publicly apologised to Lezsák.

    A belated step

    On 15 September the Hungarian parliament decided to make public, and searchable online, the list of people who cooperated with the communist secret services (the so‑called “network contacts”).

    In the first phase, part of the documents was made accessible on the site nyitottaktak.hu, while the recruitment dossiers – from which the stories of those recruited can be learned in more detail – will be published by 25 February 2027, the Memorial Day for the Victims of the Communist Dictatorship.

    Hungary is thus taking this step 37 years after the regime change, more than 20 years after the Czech Republic and Slovakia did so in 2004.

    Those we already knew about

    It was already known in the case of several well‑known public figures that they had cooperated with the secret services or had come into their sights.

    One such person was Nobel Prize‑winning biologist Katalin Karikó, developer of Pfizer’s vaccines, about whom it emerged in 2021 that state security had recruited her. At the time Karikó said she had been recruited under threat, but had not reported on anyone.

    It had also long been known that other politicians had been recruited: among them József Torgyán, former president of the Independent Smallholders’ Party, who in 1998 was Viktor Orbán’s coalition partner, and István Csurka, who led the far‑right party called MIÉP.

    The files also contain the name of György Nógrádi, one of Fidesz’s best‑known geopolitics experts, who often appears in Slovakia and was previously a guest at MKP (the party of the Hungarians living in Slovakia) campaign events. Nógrádi denies having been an agent.

    New names appear too

    On Wednesday (4 November) the whole of Hungary was feverishly browsing the site nyitottaktak.hu to see which familiar names might surface.

    There were indeed some surprises.

    By Thursday the lists had produced the names of several television personalities, singers, artists and other public figures. One of the best‑known is István Vágó, who for decades hosted popular quiz shows and was regarded as one of the most erudite figures on Hungarian television.

    The list also includes Tibor Dévényi, one of the first Hungarian DJs, who for decades hosted the popular children’s programme Three Wishes on public television. The Fidesz‑adjacent singer Róbert Szikora is likewise among the well‑known names; he has denied having ever reported on anyone.

    Among those on the list there is a sitting Constitutional Court judge (András Patyi), a former ambassador to Washington (András Simonyi), and even a former central bank governor (György Surányi).

L’article De l’idée à la première vente : comment la technologie abaisse les barrières à l’entrepreneuriat est apparu en premier sur Maddyness - Le média pour comprendre l'économie de demain.

]]> Une entreprise peut réussir sans jamais annoncer de levée de fonds. Une affirmation qui résonne plus particulièrement après trois années de correction du capital-risque : de plus de 13 milliards d’euros en 2022, les montants levés par les startups françaises sont revenus à 6,8 milliards en 2025, selon notre recensement MaddyMoney. Avec le retour des exigences de rentabilité, les ventes et la solidité du modèle économique reprennent leur place dans l’appréciation d’un parcours entrepreneurial.

Le commerce en ligne offre précisément un moyen de bâtir une entreprise à partir de ses clients : proposer un produit, trouver des acheteurs et réinvestir les revenus pour développer l’activité. L’ambition peut être de vivre de son savoir-faire, de gagner en autonomie ou de recruter à mesure que les commandes progressent. Les plateformes de e-commerce et l’IA rendent ce parcours plus accessible, en simplifiant la création d’une boutique et une partie de sa gestion.

Tester une idée avant d’élargir son activité

Choisir quelques produits, les présenter, encaisser les paiements et suivre les commandes : les plateformes de e-commerce réunissent des fonctions qu’il fallait auparavant assembler ou faire développer. Selon l’étude The Entrepreneur Effect, 78 % des marchands interrogés par Shopify ont construit eux-mêmes leur boutique sur la plateforme.

Il n’est pas non plus nécessaire de démarrer avec un catalogue étendu. À l’échelle mondiale, 41 % des boutiques Shopify se lancent avec un seul produit, d’après les données de la plateforme. Une offre resserrée permet de confronter une idée aux achats réels avant d’engager davantage de moyens. En 2025, environ 1,2 million de boutiques y ont enregistré leur première vente. Ce chiffre renseigne sur les débuts d’une activité, sans préjuger de sa rentabilité ou de sa pérennité.

L’IA pour avancer avec une petite équipe

L’intelligence artificielle prolonge cette simplification. Pour Julien Tuffery, dirigeant de l’Atelier TUFFERY, enseigne de jeans et vêtements Made in France, « l’IA est d’ores et déjà très présente dans notre quotidien. Nous l’utilisons pour analyser plus rapidement les données, structurer et synthétiser les informations, travailler dans différentes langues, et nous aider dans certaines tâches techniques. Pour une entreprise de notre taille, cela nous donne accès à des capacités qui, auparavant, auraient nécessité beaucoup plus de ressources. »

Sidekick, l’assistant IA de Shopify, joue ce rôle en effectuant de nombreuses tâches, telles que réaliser des calculs, écrire du code, effectuer des recherches sur Internet et mémoriser les informations que lui transmet un marchand. Pour une personne qui lance son activité, l’intérêt est concret : disposer d’une aide pour prendre en main les outils, sans devoir maîtriser chaque fonction dès le départ.

L’IA contribue également à rééquilibrer la concurrence entre petites et grandes marques. En permettant aux consommateurs de rechercher des produits correspondant à des attentes très précises, les assistants IA ouvrent de nouvelles possibilités de visibilité aux enseignes spécialisées, indépendamment de leur notoriété. Selon Shopify, 75 % des ventes attribuées à des recommandations par IA proviennent de boutiques vendant des produits situés hors des 100 catégories les plus courantes. Pour ces entreprises, l’enjeu n’est donc plus seulement d’être connues, mais d’être identifiées comme pertinentes et fiables dans leur domaine. Cela suppose de proposer des informations produits détaillées, des contenus de qualité et une expertise clairement identifiable.

Une évolution que constate Camille Becerra, fondatrice et dirigeante d’Anatae, marque française de thé matcha japonais 100 % biologique et naturel : « Cela a changé notre façon d’envisager le contenu. Les outils d’IA valorisent l’expertise et les informations précises et vérifiables. Nous continuons donc à investir dans des contenus éducatifs sur le thé japonais et veillons à ce que chaque fiche produit indique clairement le cépage, la région, la certification et les analyses en laboratoire. Être la référence dans notre domaine est aujourd’hui plus que jamais une stratégie d’acquisition, et pas seulement une stratégie de marque. »

« Demain, certains de nos clients ne taperont peut-être plus “jeans Made in France” dans un moteur de recherche ; ils demanderont peut-être simplement à une IA quels jeans fabriqués en France ils devraient choisir, complète Julien Tuffery. Cela modifie inévitablement la manière dont une marque doit envisager sa visibilité en ligne. »

Des retombées au-delà de la boutique

Atelier TUFFERY illustre la façon dont le commerce en ligne peut permettre à une entreprise locale de se développer sans quitter son territoire. Depuis Florac, au cœur des Cévennes, la manufacture fondée en 1892 vend désormais ses produits directement en France et dans le monde entier.

« Le web nous a permis de dépasser notre isolement géographique sans jamais avoir à nous déraciner, explique Julien Tuffery. Nous pouvons développer une activité nationale et internationale tout en continuant à fabriquer nos produits là où l’entreprise est née. Aujourd’hui, une commande passée à Paris, Londres, Tokyo ou à l’autre bout du monde peut contribuer directement au développement de notre manufacture et à l’économie d’une région profondément rurale. Le commerce en ligne n’a pas détourné la création de valeur de notre territoire. Au contraire, il nous a donné les moyens de rester ici, d’investir ici et de nous développer ici. »

Cette croissance produit des effets concrets dans les Cévennes. L’entreprise a créé plus de 40 emplois, principalement à Florac et dans les environs. Sa manufacture et sa boutique ont accueilli plus de 40 000 visiteurs au cours des douze derniers mois, tandis que son activité e-commerce génère plus de 20 000 colis par an, contribuant ainsi à l’activité du bureau de poste local.

À l’échelle nationale, Shopify estime que les entreprises qui utilisent sa plateforme ont généré 21,5 milliards d’euros d’activité économique en France et soutenu environ 115 000 emplois entre le 1er juillet 2025 et le 30 juin 2026. Ces estimations reposent sur une modélisation qui tient compte des effets directs, indirects et induits de l’activité des marchands et des partenaires de Shopify.

L’accès à des clients étrangers élargit encore ces retombées. Les ventes transfrontalières des marchands Shopify établis en France ont progressé de 314 % entre 2022 et l’année achevée le 30 juin 2026. Pour les entrepreneurs, vendre à l’étranger demande toujours d’organiser la livraison et le service client. Mais la technologie leur permet désormais de développer une activité internationale tout en restant concentrés sur leur savoir-faire et profondément ancrés dans leur territoire.

« Chaque jour, des entrepreneurs transforment un savoir-faire ou une ambition en une activité concrète, qui crée de l’emploi et participe à la dynamique des territoires, souligne Alexandre Chaumien, responsable des revenus pour l’Europe du Sud chez Shopify. Avec la technologie et l’IA, on leur donne le pouvoir d’aller encore plus loin et de voir encore plus grand. Ces opportunités pour eux le sont aussi pour l’économie française. »

L’article De l’idée à la première vente : comment la technologie abaisse les barrières à l’entrepreneuriat est apparu en premier sur Maddyness - Le média pour comprendre l'économie de demain.

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/nov/09/nvidia-jensen-huang-scandal-investigation-ai-industry-tech-stocks-recovery-slump-latest-news-updates</link>
      <description><p>Shares in world’s most valuable company hit seven-month low after CEO Huang admits to affair, after allegations of relationship with Chinese spy</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/09/nvidia-jensen-huang-affair-trump-musk">Silicon Valley and Trump rally behind Nvidia CEO after his affair with alleged Chinese spy</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/09/who-is-alice-huang-the-woman-linked-to-nvidias-ceo">Who is Alice Huang, the woman linked to Nvidia’s CEO?</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/09/nvidia-affair-huang-trump-national-security">The AI poster boy, the ‘Chinese spy’ and Trump: how an affair may have harmed US security</a></p></li></ul><p><strong>Huang is receiving support from some fellow tech executives, including Elon Musk.</strong></p><p>Musk commented “I agree” on a post by ​Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire that said Huang “did something incredibly dumb” that was “bad for America” but that “Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership”.</p><p>“While Nvidia has sought to reassure us all, ​there are several layers here, beginning with the unfortunate timing.</p><p>“For example: The company is systemically important for tech, markets and the economy; Investors tend to struggle to price in key-person and governance issues; and there are fluid national security and geopolitical dynamics.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/nov/09/nvidia-jensen-huang-scandal-investigation-ai-industry-tech-stocks-recovery-slump-latest-news-updates">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>US job growth exceeds expectations in October despite economic uncertainty</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/06/us-job-growth-october</link>
      <description><p>‘Low-hire, low-fire’ labor market shows sluggish growth but few layoffs, with an interest rate hike expected in December</p><p>The US added 165,000 jobs to the economy in October, a sign of resilience in the labor market amid ongoing war in the Middle East and inflation, according to new data released on Friday.</p><p>Economists had said the labor market has been stuck in a “low-hire, low-fire” state, in which job growth is sluggish but layoffs also remain low, but October’s data surpassed economist expectations. The <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/usemployment">unemployment rate</a> went down slightly to 4.1%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/06/us-job-growth-october">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Rural voters were feeling left behind before the midterms, poll shows</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/05/former-trump-voters-economy</link>
      <description><p>Polling done for the Guardian shows plummeting support from a former key constituency of Donald Trump’s base</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/nov/05/what-happens-after-the-blue-wave-our-reporters-answer-your-midterm-election-results-questions">Q&amp;A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>Polling conducted by the Harris Poll for the Guardian before the election shows just how angry voters were and points to one key reason Republicans lost so badly: plummeting support from rural voters, once a key constituency of Donald Trump’s base.</p><p>Over the summer, 95% of Americans indicated they believed there was an <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/jul/07/cost-of-living-poll-groceries-gas">affordability crisis</a>, particularly because of steep gas and grocery prices. By October, 61% of voters <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/voters-economy-cost-of-living-prices-poll">believed</a> the country was experiencing a recession, even though technically it wasn’t.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/05/former-trump-voters-economy">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>US stocks rise, dollar slides as investors digest Democrats’ midterm victories</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/04/us-dollar-slides-democrats-midterm-election-win-growth-fears</link>
      <description><p>Government bond yields fall while initial fears ease over impact of election results on world’s biggest economy</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/04/midterm-elections-results-senate-house-michigan-maine-mississippi-latest-updates">US midterm elections – live updates</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/04/explainer-midterms-trump-us-global-economy-markets">After US midterms, what will lame-duck Trump mean for global economy?</a></p></li></ul><p>US stocks have surged as investors digest the Democrats’ victories in the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a>, lifted by hopes that <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s turbulent policymaking would be restrained and shaking off initial fears about the impact on growth in the world’s largest economy.</p><p>The Dow Jones rose close to 3%, its best day in over a year, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the benchmark S&amp;P 500 gained about 1.5% each when markets closed on Wednesday afternoon, turning around overnight falls in US stock futures after the news that the Democratic party <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/03/midterm-election-results-live-updates">won control</a> of the Senate and the House of Representatives.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/04/us-dollar-slides-democrats-midterm-election-win-growth-fears">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Trump may have lost but don’t bet Democrats can fix the economy</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/07/democrats-economy-affordability-crisis</link>
      <description><p>There’s not much they can do over the next couple of years to alleviate angry voters’ stress over prices</p><p>It was the economy, again. Although Donald Trump largely ignored it, voters’ acute concerns over the rising cost of living fuelled a political upheaval for the ages that is likely to deliver the biggest swing toward Democrats since Watergate, granting them the largest House majority in nearly four decades alongside their biggest edge in the Senate since 2008.</p><p>Still, having come to power promising to restore affordability, the new crop of Democrats are soon to discover that there is not much they can do over the next couple of years to alleviate angry voters’ stress over pricey gas and groceries, exorbitant mortgages and unaffordable healthcare.</p><p>Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter <a href="https://eduardoelreportero.substack.com/">Being There</a> on Substack</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/07/democrats-economy-affordability-crisis">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Democrats’ success was helped by popular anger over tech, AI and the super rich – life for billionaires could become much more difficult</p><p>The photo of Silicon Valley centibillionaires at Donald Trump’s inauguration – Musk, Bezos and Zuckerberg, front row and side by side – now looks like a hitlist for a blue Congress hellbent on making life difficult for billionaires.</p><p>The picture symbolized at the time the bending of the knee by the richest men in the world to its most powerful, a symbiosis of the ultra-rich. Already unfathomably wealthy, Silicon Valley tycoons believed a Maga-sized public shift to the right would enrich them even more. It did. For several years, while Trump seemed an everlasting kingmaker and AI’s expansion seemed unstoppable, their fortunes ballooned to values beyond comprehension. Elon Musk’s surpassed $1tn.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/05/tech-barons-america-musk-bezos-zuckerberg">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>It is essential not just to fund the public goods the nation needs, it is indispensable to restore a sense of fairness</p><p>Money doesn’t buy happiness, we’re told. Even some economists agree. The Nobel prize-winning economists Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton once <a href="https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1011492107">proposed that</a> rising income increased people’s emotional wellbeing only up to a ceiling of about $115,000 in today’s money.</p><p>They probably hadn’t met many billionaires. The ultra-rich may not pursue happiness in the joyful sense of the word. But they will try every trick in the book to hang on to their stash and woe betide the tax authority that tries to lay a finger on their treasure.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/27/democracy-tax-billionaires">Continue reading...</a></description>
