<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comMon, 09 Nov 2026 20:53:28 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[At Web Summit opener, Palestine gets a brief mention and the loudest cheer]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/at-web-summits-opener-palestine-gets-a-brief-mention-and-the-loudest-cheer/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/at-web-summits-opener-palestine-gets-a-brief-mention-and-the-loudest-cheer/Mon, 09 Nov 2026 20:14:16 +0000Paddy Cosgrave welcomed thousands of Web Summit early arrivals to Lisbon on Monday night, telling them the future of technology was “increasingly Chinese”, with “more than 50 superstars from China’s leading AI labs” attending the technology conference.

“This year’s Web Summit has, without a doubt in my mind, the most important line-up of technology speakers we have ever had,” he said. “They are not from California – they are from China, because Chinese companies are building more for our shared futures than companies from anywhere else. This is just a fact.

“We’re of course grateful to have speakers and partners like Apple, Meta and Google – they are the prominent technology companies of today,” Cosgrave said as he stood alone on stage, with two jumbo-screens of his face bookending the Web Summit logo. “These companies are all, almost without exception, started in California.

“But, increasingly, the superstars of the future are not coming from California, they’re coming from China. They’re the future stars in AI, in robotics, in cars . . . in energy and in so much more.”

Kicking off the opening ceremony was a two-minute dance routine performed by nine humanoid robots created by the Chinese company AgiBot.

Agibot robots swept athletics categories in the first world Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing three months ago.

More than 100 Irish start-ups head to Web Summit alongside largest-ever Chinese delegation

Addressing the crowd gathered in the centre stage of the MEO Arena, Cosgrave wore a speckled moss green Aran jumper. It looked strikingly similar to a jumper that is available to buy for €895 from his wife Faye Dinsmore’s fashion brand.

This one, however, was more bespoke than an off-the-rack knit. It had the phrase “keep the triple lock” stitched across its chest in a not-so-subtle reminder of Cosgrave’s view on the Government’s recent move to reform the traditional pillars of the State’s military neutrality.

Appealing to his techie audience, the triple lock was represented with three padlock emojis.

The mere mention of Palestine would deliver a less predictable gauge of audience views. Three years ago, Cosgrave resigned as chief executive of Web Summit amid controversy caused by him tweeting: “War crimes are war crimes even when committed by allies, and should be called out for what they are.”

Two weeks after Hamas’s attacks of October 7th, 2023, Cosgrave’s condemnation of Israel’s assault on Gaza prompted international companies to withdraw from the high-profile tech conference.

He returned to his post six months later. On Monday, 2½ years on from Cosgrave’s return as chief executive, Casey Lau – host for the first night – decided to roll the dice. Lau shouted out “Palestine” in acknowledgment of one of the countries that has sent start-up delegations to the conference.

“We have people from Paraguay, from Pakistan, from Palestine . . .” he said, trailing off in suspense (or nervousness). But the gamble paid off. It garnered the loudest cheer of the night.

Lau tried to follow up with its flag-bearer – who walked alongside a man carrying the Irish Tricolour in a parade of nationalities represented at the conference – to ask him what his start-up’s purpose is, but to no avail.

]]>Patricia De Melo Moreira<![CDATA[Is the public sector pay offer affordable and fair compared with wages in private firms?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/09/is-the-public-sector-pay-deal-affordable-and-fair-compared-to-private-sector-wage-growth/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/09/is-the-public-sector-pay-deal-affordable-and-fair-compared-to-private-sector-wage-growth/Mon, 09 Nov 2026 14:00:20 +0000Public sector pay talks are on a knife edge. The Government says its latest offer – a 10.5 per cent (11 per cent compounded) pay hike – represents a “substantial” improvement on what had been on the table up to now. Unions are concerned about the duration of the deal and where the backdated elements will kick in.

Specifically, they are concerned that spreading 10.5 per cent over 2.5-3 years (out to 2029) will dilute its annual value and won’t cover cost-of-living increases.

The unions are planning to stage a 24-hour strike on Thursday unless the impasse is resolved. The strike will coincide with a major summit of European leaders taking place in the Convention Centre in Dublin, as part of Ireland’s EU presidency, potentially paralysing the capital.

How much will the Government’s offer cost?

The Government has been repeatedly criticised by the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council and others for failing to adequately budget for things. The €1.2 billion allocation in Budget 2027 for the first year of the public sector pay deal is a case in point. It’s woefully short.

The Government’s latest offer is estimated to cost up to €2 billion next year. One insider said the Coalition had already “blown a hole” through its allocation.

The total cost of the Government’s proposed deal is put at about €4 billion, though, as of now, there are a lot of unknowns on how much will accrue to those on the lower levels of the Civil Service and where backdated element will start from – June or November.

A recent report by the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) noted that the public sector wage bill would account for €31.2 billion (or 27 per cent) of gross spending this year.

On the basis of a public sector pay deal similar to the last one, which was slightly less than the 10.5 per cent currently on the table, the PBO estimated the cost to the exchequer would be between €3.6 billion and €4.7 billion by 2029. This includes projected increases in the public sector headcount (adding new teachers, nurses and gardaí to the payroll).

How will it affect the Government’s fiscal position?

The rule of thumb is that each 1 per cent hike in the public sector pay and pensions bill costs the exchequer roughly €370 million.

On that basis, in 2027 the Government’s proposed deal would cost about €1.3 billion on a recurring basis but about €2 billion in cash terms. The €700 million gap reflects the back pay carried over from the previous deal.

So the Government’s fiscal position would be €800 million worse than forecast in 2027. The additional pay bumps for 2028 and 2029 are also not factored in. That additional money will have to come out of tax resources and will reduce the Government’s budget surpluses over the period.

On the other side of the ledger, the State’s financial position is expected to be boosted by corporate tax receipts, which are predicted to rise to €45 billion by 2030.

Either way, the State will be wrapping more day-to-day spending into potentially risky tax receipts.

How does Government offer compare with what private sector workers are getting?

The Government’s recent economic and fiscal outlook, published alongside last month’s budget, forecast that wages across the economy – which is mainly private sector – would rise by 4.1 per cent in 2027 and by 3.7 per cent in 2028 and 2029.

The Government’s 10.5 per cent deal gives public sector workers a 3-3.5 per cent bump in pay across those years, according to one estimate. On that basis, the hikes are roughly comparable.

Private sector wages have outpaced those in the public sector since 2008. According to the official data, private sector wages are up by between 52-56 per cent over that period versus 25 per cent in the public sector.

Private sector wage growth data is skewed by multinationals that pay their workers significantly more than the average. That said, tech companies in Ireland have been pruning their wage bill.

What is the likelihood of unions accepting the deal?

Workers are in the midst of a nasty cost-of-living shock, compounded by an energy price surge. Meanwhile, the Government is attempting to rein in spending that has been something of a runaway train since the pandemic. Hence the fraught atmosphere around these negotiations.

Minister for Finance Simon Harris said the Coalition’s ability to offer income tax cuts in the recent budget and increases in public sector wages was in stark contrast to many other European governments, who were short on money and facing “extraordinarily difficult” economic decisions.

Trade unions insist, however, that the surge in inflation has severely degraded the purchasing power of their members, particularly those earning €50,000 or less, and must be addressed. They also insist there are acute labour shortages in education and healthcare and argue that a lacklustre deal will worsen the exodus of young nurses and teachers.

With more industrial action looming, a breakthrough needs to come quickly.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Can Jensen Huang survive as Nvidia’s chief executive after spy scandal?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/can-jensen-huang-survive-as-nvidias-chief-executive-after-spy-scandal/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/can-jensen-huang-survive-as-nvidias-chief-executive-after-spy-scandal/Mon, 09 Nov 2026 19:04:55 +0000The investigation of Jensen Huang by Nvidia’s board threatens the future of one of Silicon Valley’s longest-serving executives and a key enabler of the artificial intelligence boom, who has no obvious successor as leader of the world’s second-most-valuable company.

Huang is fighting for survival after admitting to an extramarital affair, believed to be with an executive at a large Nvidia customer whom US officials also allege was working as a Chinese spy.

The prospect that Huang could be forced out as chief executive of the US chipmaker he cofounded more than 30 years ago has alarmed investors and allies in the tech industry. Shares in Nvidia, which late last month ceded its position as the world’s most valuable to Apple amid a broader sell-off in AI stocks, had fallen more than 5 per cent by midday trading on Monday.

“Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” said Shaun Maguire, partner at early Nvidia investor Sequoia Capital, in a social media post.

Nvidia’s chips were instrumental in the creation of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and now sit at the centre of Big Tech’s $1 trillion (€890 billion) AI infrastructure frenzy. Huang has personally stood behind investments and guarantees running into hundreds of billions of dollars for dozens of AI start-ups and data centre providers, as well as lobbying US president Donald Trump for looser AI regulation.

Nvidia investigating reports boss Jensen Huang had affair with Chinese ‘spy’

“Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he IS Nvidia,” analysts at Bernstein said in a note to clients.

With policymakers in Washington pressuring Huang to appear before congressional committees to explain himself, the spotlight is on Nvidia’s board, which said on Sunday it would conduct its own “independent” investigation into the scandal that exploded over the weekend.

The investigation will probably be led by board member and former Cooley LLC chief executive Stephen C Neal, according to people familiar with the inquiry.

“If information was compromised, the implications are a lot bigger than if it was just an affair, which obviously isn’t welcome news,” said a fund manager with a large Nvidia position.

“Nvidia would survive [Huang leaving] but there’s no better person than Jensen to run the company; it would be very different without him.”

In contrast to other leading Big Tech companies, Nvidia’s annual reports and corporate governance paperwork make no specific reference to “succession planning” and set out no details for how it would replace its CEO, even in an emergency, beyond noting that the company “believe[s] in extensive leadership development”.

Huang’s unusually large number of direct reports, numbered at more than 60 according to a 2024 disclosure, present Nvidia’s board with a “pool of excellent candidates for future promotion”, recent filings say.

Huang leads a small core executive team at Nvidia, including chief financial officer Colette Kress, operations chief Debora Shoquist and general counsel Tim Teter. He has become one of Huang’s closest lieutenants since joining in 2017 and has lobbied Washington on export controls.

Jay Puri, a close lieutenant who led Nvidia’s sales operations and deputised for Huang on international visits, stepped down in August and was replaced on the executive team by Microsoft veteran Nick Parker.

Huang, who has cultivated an air of infallibility inside Nvidia, has given no indication he will step down from the role of chief executive.

Recent biographies of Huang and Nvidia, including Tae Kim’s The Nvidia Way and Stephen Witt’s The Thinking Machine, portray him as having a rare combination of technical depth and forward-thinking leadership.

AI bubble? Nvidia is now bigger than Japan, but valuation looks modest

He is known to be able to inspire extraordinary productivity inside a company whose 42,000 employees each generated an average of more than $7 million in annual revenue over the past 12 months, far more than any other Big Tech group.

But Kim also notes that Huang represents the company’s “single point of failure”, functioning as its head of marketing, sales and product development.

His influence in the wider tech industry is also unique. Endorsements by Huang of companies in the AI semiconductor supply chain can supercharge their share prices, while his offhand dismissal early last year of the near-term commercial prospects for quantum computing sent stocks in the sector spiralling.

Despite his imperial stature, Huang owns just 3.6 per cent of Nvidia. That stake makes him Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder and is worth more than $150 billion. However, Huang lacks the special voting rights held by many Silicon Valley founders, including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin, that would allow him to control the board or face down outside investors who might attempt to oust him.

Huang’s total compensation last year of $36.3 million, of which the vast majority came in the form of stock awards, included some $4 million for security paid for by Nvidia, which filings say is “due to the exceptionally high public profile and prominence of our CEO”.

These costs included protection at home and during “personal travel”, as well as using private aircraft for all business trips, according to filings. Huang reimburses Nvidia for personal air travel on private aircraft arranged by the company, according to filings.

Nvidia’s board, whose individual members have until now kept a low profile, confirmed they would appoint a special committee composed of sitting board members assisted by outside counsel to examine the allegations surrounding its chief executive.

Neal joined Nvidia’s board in 2019 and is chair emeritus and senior counsel at Cooley, after serving as the law firm’s chief executive from 2001 to 2008.

Nvidia’s board is unusual among the largest US companies in having no designated chair. A 2025 report by law firm Fenwick found that only one company in the S&P 100 – which would be Nvidia, according to its own filings – had no chair.

In its proxy filings, Nvidia states that this set-up “ensures that each member has an equal voice in the affairs and management of Nvidia”.

The other nine members of Nvidia’s board – excluding Huang, who is himself a director – include four men who have been with the company since the 1990s, a former Taco Bell executive, a professor of aeronautics and a former Goldman Sachs executive who joined only this year.

The board’s public statement on Sunday said it had “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team” and that it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised”.

Nonetheless, his admission of an affair on Sunday shocked employees and former colleagues

Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter who serves as a senior director in Nvidia’s product marketing team and has become an increasingly visible presence at the company’s conferences, cancelled a planned appearance at a company event in South Korea on Monday.

The law in Delaware, where Nvidia is incorporated, says executives have certain fiduciary duties including a duty of care and loyalty to their company.

Nvidia’s code of conduct requires executives to “conduct themselves with the highest degree of integrity, ethics and honesty. Our credibility and reputation depend upon their good judgment, ethical standards and personal integrity.”

Even if Huang is found to have breached those guidelines, his defenders in Silicon Valley argue that he is too big to fire.

“Yes he should have known better,” Sequoia’s Maguire said. “But let’s also not nuke our AI industry because China ran a successful intel op.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>Ritchie B Tongo<![CDATA[European shares climb as banks and defence stocks lead rally]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/european-shares-climb-as-banks-and-defence-stocks-lead-rally/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/european-shares-climb-as-banks-and-defence-stocks-lead-rally/Mon, 09 Nov 2026 18:52:23 +0000European shares climbed more than 1 per cent with gains broadening across sectors, while banks advanced as dealmaking involving Credit ​Agricole and Banco BPM and strong results from Italy’s UniCredit lifted the sector.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 closed 1.26 per cent higher at 656.52 points, with the defence sector leading sectors higher with a 4.2 per cent rise.

New York

Nvidia investigating reports boss Jensen Huang had affair with Chinese ‘spy’

The strong gains allayed concerns about the AI trade, which shook markets following the Democrats’ midterm triumph last week. Ten of 11 large S&P 500 sector indexes were in positive territory, with industrials and consumer discretionary leading gains.

Among the hyperscalers, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon were up between 2 per cent and 5 per cent.

Elon Musk-led Tesla and SpaceX also advanced 5.5 per cent each. – Additional reporting by Reuters

]]>Spencer Platt<![CDATA[ECB contender Klaas Knot ‘will not hesitate’ to act if confronted by debt crisis]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/ecb-contender-klaas-knot-will-not-hesitate-to-act-if-confronted-by-debt-crisis/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/ecb-contender-klaas-knot-will-not-hesitate-to-act-if-confronted-by-debt-crisis/Mon, 09 Nov 2026 17:37:07 +0000Klaas Knot, one of two contenders to become the next president of the European Central Bank (ECB), is open to devising new tools potentially necessary to fight a European debt crisis if he secures the job.

Knot said he was ready to use the ECB’s existing crisis-fighting tools, including bond buying. “If circumstances so dictate, we won’t hesitate [to intervene],” said Knot.

The 59-year-old Dutch man, who led his country’s central bank from 2011 to 2025, was officially nominated on Friday by The Hague to succeed ECB president Christine Lagarde. She will leave the bank in early February, nine months before the end of her eight-year term.

Knot did not rule out creating additional instruments to combat future crises. If the next crisis “is different in nature” from the previous ones that led to the creation of the current tools, “I wouldn’t even exclude the fact that we would design another more tailor-made tool,” he said.

Knot’s main rival is Pablo Hernández de Cos, general manager of the Bank for International Settlements and former Spanish central bank governor, who has been nominated by Madrid.

European leaders might decide on the new ECB president at their next formal summit in late November, but the decision could also be delayed until next month.

ECB grants regulatory approval for Bawag PTSB takeover

The decision requires the consent of at least 16 of the 21 countries that use the euro, representing 65 per cent of its population.

Leaders will also have to agree on a new ECB chief economist and a new board member in charge of the markets portfolio at the central bank. The term of the current chief economist, Irish man Philip Lane, ends in May and European Central Bank governing council member Isabel Schnabel will leave to join the International Monetary Fund in January.

The ECB’s closely watched leadership reshuffle unfolds against the backdrop of a sharp surge in French government borrowing costs since the summer, with yields on its 10-year bonds briefly shooting above 5 per cent last month. The spread, or gap, to German Bunds widened to 1.75 percentage points before it came down slightly, reflecting the premium investors are demanding to hold French debt.

In reference to an infamous remark by Lagarde in early 2020 that the ECB is “not here to close spreads”, which triggered a temporary bond market sell-off, Knot said the ECB should “definitely be there to contain them [spreads] when driven by unwarranted and disorderly market dynamics”.

The Frankfurt-based institution has created “a toolkit to deal with such situations”, he argued.

These include the emergency bond-buying scheme Outright Monetary Transactions, introduced after former European Central Bank president Mario Draghi’s “whatever it takes” speech in 2012 during the euro zone sovereign debt crisis.

In 2022, the central bank also created the transmission protection instrument as it began raising interest rates to fight surging inflation.

Knot stressed that any ECB firefighting needed to be done “in a manner that does not undermine its institutional credibility”, adding that the central bank could not fix unsustainable fiscal policy.

Its current crisis-fighting tools “combine a requirement [for governments] to bring fundamentals in order with a temporary shield against unwarranted or disorderly market dynamics”, said Knot, adding that he has “always been a big proponent” of this approach.

He stressed that there was “no magic single spread level” that would trigger an intervention in bond markets from the ECB and that the central bank was right to stay on the sidelines for now.

Moreover, Knot stressed that rising government debt costs in themselves cannot justify European Central Bank bond buying.

“There is a difference between a repricing from one level to another and disorderly market dynamics with a lot of volatility and a lot of contagion across different markets,” he said, adding that the assessment of what constitutes an unwarranted and disorderly market development always involves “a healthy dose of judgment”.

Knot pushed back against public perceptions of him as a monetary policy hawk who has a preference for high interest rates.

“There are situations in which you have to pursue dovish policy, but there are also situations in which you are expected to conduct hawkish policy,” he said, adding that this was “driven by circumstances, not by personalities or predispositions”.

He noted that “dovish policy” was necessary during the Covid pandemic while the ECB had to pursue a “hawkish” one to fight surging inflation from 2022.

Over the coming months, the European Central Bank’s interest rate policy is likely to be hostage to developments in the Middle East and their impact on energy prices, he said. Policymakers in Frankfurt have increased borrowing costs in two quarter-point steps since June to 2.5 per cent.

He said that if energy prices remained roughly where they were, he saw little need for higher interest rates. “There may be a bit of extra tightening needed, but I don’t think an awful lot of it,” Knot said, adding that any interest rate changes needed to be “very measured”.

Will Christine Lagarde take a shot at the French presidency?

During the early days of the Greek sovereign debt crisis in 2011 and 2012, Knot made headlines by becoming one of the first officials to publicly discuss whether the country might default on its debts or might leave the euro, warning it must not happen involuntarily.

He said his intention was not to argue in favour of such drastic steps but to warn about a “disorderly default or an involuntary Greek exit” as both would have had “devastating effects” on financial stability in Greece and the rest of Europe.

In September 2019, Knot caused a stir by issuing a rare public rebuke of a decision by the ECB’s governing council, when Draghi had pushed through a controversial restart of bond buying and a further reduction in negative interest rates.

“My main concern was about proportionality at a time when the side effects [of quantitative easing] were clearly accumulating,” he said, adding that he preferred to make his point in public rather than have it emerge anonymously through media reports.

“The bar for publishing such a statement again today would clearly be higher,” he acknowledged. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>RuslanDashinsky<![CDATA[AI agents in car dealerships: No time off and they work out how quickly a vehicle will sell]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/ai-agents-in-car-dealerships-they-never-take-time-off-or-get-sick-and-can-work-out-how-quickly-vehicles-will-sell/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/ai-agents-in-car-dealerships-they-never-take-time-off-or-get-sick-and-can-work-out-how-quickly-vehicles-will-sell/Mon, 09 Nov 2026 05:47:00 +0000Car sales, to the buyer at least, haven’t changed all that much since Henry Ford first rolled out the Model T. The sector is long established, with many dealerships in Ireland having decades of heritage.

It’s a human business. One that involves talking to customers, assessing vehicles, deciding what stock to buy and avoid, and, of course, closing sales. On the face of it, this is hardly the poster child for disruption by artificial intelligence (AI).

Yet AI is making an impact, with several Irish companies at the forefront of that movement, with Irish dealers embracing the time benefits that come with deploying AI agents.

“It’s an age-old problem. Leads aren’t responded to quickly enough and they’re not followed up regularly enough,” says Shaun Donnellan, founder of AutoAgent, a company that develops AI agents for dealerships. “Dealerships are too busy, salespeople have huge amounts of paperwork and prep to do along with getting cars from A to B, and much more.

Speed matters in this sector and anywhere in the process where hours or even minutes can be saved is crucial. By the time a buyer is looking at dealerships to engage with, they’ve usually already narrowed down what they want from Google searches.

For the dealership, the goal is to capture and keep the buyer’s attention while their interest is at its peak.

“The customer wants the car. There are probably a few versions of the car available. The first person that responds and captures their time will most likely bring them in and sell them the car,” he says.

Donnellan has already worked with Tony Burke Motors to roll out his AI agents, with the agent having a direct impact on sales.

The long road to building an Irish AI start-up

“Tony has already been a leader for technology in the sector. When I came to him with this, he leaned into it hard. It booked nine appointments for his dealership in July, with five of those turning into sales,” says Donnellan.

AutoAgent deployed Aran, its bespoke agent, with Tony Burke Motors to engage with customers when humans weren’t on hand.

“It’s a response optimisation platform that responds to customers and captures their interest while it’s at its peak. It never takes time off, is never sick, and responds the way your dealership wants with your process,” he says.

What Donnellan is doing is reflecting the wider benefit of AI agents to the auto dealership sector, according to Muireann Heaney, an AI engineer with AI One.

“If you look at a company like AutoAgent, they’ve identified the point in the sales cycle of where issues come up. What they’ve done is realise the information is there and focus on keeping the customer interested for the dealerships,” says Heaney.

“With dealerships, getting the engagement from customers at the start is critical for them. That way the customer knows the dealership is interested and wants to give them information that can help their buying decision.”

Would you trust this AI to sell you a second-hand car?

There is, however, the old adage of more haste, less speed. A classic misuse of AI is getting the fastest answer possible rather than the best one.

“Speed isn’t the major concern because a normal consumer is willing to wait a few seconds. They are focused mostly on accurate and relevant information that they can verify. A fast answer doesn’t always mean it’s a good answer,” says Janet Xiu Shi, an AI quality evaluation adviser.

Of course, trial runs and small roll-outs are one thing. Once AI use goes into full usage within any business, somebody has to be in charge of what it is and isn’t permitted to do. The car dealership sector is no exception.

“From a business perspective, leadership needs to know how to measure AI effectiveness and who takes accountability for it. Operationally, the team needs to know what AI is and isn’t allowed to use as well as being able to evaluate its output,” says Xiu Shi.

That’s why companies like TradeBid have embraced a hybrid approach. The company uses AI to help assess trade-ins but also knows that mistakes can be made. Low-confidence cases automatically get escalated to be looked over by human eyes.

“On the inspection side, because our business relies on the accuracy of AI, we have to make sure the information is as good as possible. Where the confidence is too low on the AI side, we bring in people to take a look,” says Conor O’Boyle, co-founder of TradeBid.

Peter Thiel-backed AI company Cognition establishes Irish presence

The value goes beyond the individual sale to the broader decisions that a dealership wants to make. AI’s value goes beyond customer service work – indeed, quite a lot of it isn’t customer facing at all. It can aid dealerships working out what vehicles to acquire and how quickly they will sell.

“Dealers often complain to us that they don’t have enough time to know what they should be buying. We have so much data that we take retail feeds and analyse it to provide dealers with more discoverability so they can turn over cars faster.”

Time remains at the heart of the problem for dealerships wherever you look. It’s why James Flynn’s Coso.ai is working with them to free that up. His business uses AI to reduce the time spent by businesses on social media.

“Creating content takes a lot of time. Beyond just writing, you’re creating images, graphic design, video editing and more. A week’s worth of content for a business usually takes half a day’s work for them. We cut that down to 15 or 20 minutes on a Friday morning,” says O’Flynn.

That time on a Friday morning, or whatever day, is crucial to a service like Coso.ai working, he says.

“Where you need to watch out is that you don’t necessarily want a full autopilot, because it’s AI, but you want it specific to your brand,” he says.

“Around 90 per cent of businesses don’t have a dedicated social media marketer. We do that element to free up time for people. We’re not putting anyone out of a job, we’re taking a functionality that previously only existed in large companies and putting it into the hands of small and medium businesses across the country.”

The biggest advocates for AI in industry have long cried out that AI will assist workers rather than replace them. A sector as human-centric as car sales might well be the best use-case for those advocates.

Where the disruption is happening is centred around freeing up time for those working in the industry to focus on what they do best, and deliver the most value to the sector.

“AI agents allow the humans in the company to go back to what they are good at. It means they can meet more people in person per day because they have that first step taken care of,” says Heaney.

“The key thing is operational leverage. Nobody wants AI all the time, we like human interaction, but automating the parts of your business that are repeatable operations is where we’ll see the biggest difference.”

Big shortfalls in occupational pension funds against expected liabilities meant employers moved rapidly away from such guarantees, which became promises to pay “where possible”. Don’t make an additional voluntary contribution to your pension – until you read this

On a straight-line basis and assuming no change in fund value, an ARF should last 21 years before being exhausted for someone who retires at 66 and draws down the minimum required.

However, investment is never that simple. Returns fluctuate up and down, leaving you with the risk that you could find your fund has been exhausted before you die.

And, regardless of investment performance, there is always the impact of fund charges to consider. You would be surprised at how these can impact your fund over time.

The whole point of an ARF is that your funds can continue to grow in retirement through investment gains – rather than being set against a moment in time with an annuity – but that does require the ARF holder to keep an eye on the performance of their fund and, if necessary, consult their fund manager or adviser about making changes if required.

Having said that, volumes of investment history confirm that regular chopping and changing of investment strategy is rarely to your advantage. Always remember that investment is a longer-term game, even in an ARF where the risk level for the vast majority of us will be relatively low.

In funding retirement, hopefully your fund is more substantial than the €100,000 used in Aviva’s example, but the figures still show what imputed distribution means for you this year and in the years ahead.

]]><![CDATA[Singapore overtakes Ireland as Apple’s biggest tax shelter]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/08/singapore-overtakes-ireland-as-apples-biggest-tax-shelter/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/08/singapore-overtakes-ireland-as-apples-biggest-tax-shelter/Sun, 08 Nov 2026 15:48:48 +0000Apple shaved $2.7 billion (€2.4 billion) off its tax bill this year by channelling earnings into Singapore, according to new disclosures that reveal how the city-state has become the tech giant’s biggest tax shelter.

The figures, filed together with Apple’s annual report under new US reporting requirements, reveal the company took advantage of Singapore’s tax incentives regime to lower its bill after attributing as much as $50 billion in profits through its Asian hub in 2026.

Its savings in Singapore exceeded the $2.6 billion reduction it achieved via Ireland, Apple’s European headquarters, the disclosures published this week show.

“While Apple’s reliance on Ireland was first revealed more than a decade ago, the enormous tax savings in Singapore are a major revelation,” said Zorka Milin, codirector of the Fact Coalition, a Washington-based tax transparency group.

Apple declined to comment.

The savings show that even after more than a decade of concerted global effort to level the playing field on corporate taxation, large US tech groups continue to reap the rewards of accumulating profits in low-tax jurisdictions.

The filings are part of new US federal accounting rules that require US-listed companies to divulge when their tax on overseas profits differs significantly from the statutory federal rate, which is 21 per cent.

If Apple had been taxed on all of its global profits in 2026 at the US federal rate, it would have incurred a total bill of $33 billion – demonstrating the scale of the $5 billion tax reduction it received from booking profits in Ireland and Singapore. The company incurred corporation taxes totalling $27 billion this year.

Many US multinationals do not pay the 21 per cent federal rate on all their US income because of domestic deductions and tax credits. However, the differential between this rate and the tax incurred elsewhere indicates which overseas jurisdictions a company derives the greatest tax benefit from.

Apple has faced intense scrutiny over its use of offshore hubs to reduce its tax bill. The tech giant was forced to repay more than €13 billion in Irish taxes with interest after a high-profile 2016 EU state aid investigation found it had illegally benefited from tax breaks in the country.

Sales between subsidiaries can allow multinational companies to move profits out of high-tax jurisdictions and into low-tax ones, a strategy known as profit shifting.

The backlash against such manoeuvres led to a landmark deal in 2021, in which countries led by the OECD agreed to introduce a minimum effective corporate tax rate of 15 per cent.

Many low-tax jurisdictions, including Ireland and Singapore, aligned themselves with the OECD effort, with some anticipating an exodus of multinational companies as they raised their tax rates.

But this flight has so far not materialised, allowing the countries to collect windfall tax payments.

Singapore, for example, clawed back $2.5 billion from Apple in 2026 via a top-up tax it implemented last year as it aligned with the OECD initiative.

Mike Lewis, director of investigative think tank TaxWatch, said the global minimum tax set a relatively low floor, meaning that “to some degree, it’s business as usual for some of these companies”.

Others have argued that companies’ decisions to remain for now in these jurisdictions are a sign they are there for reasons aside from low taxes, such as skilled workforces, infrastructure and stable political and legal frameworks.

Apple’s biggest Singaporean subsidiary is a sales and marketing hub, selling products and services to Apple entities overseas and “developing intellectual property”, its accounts show.

Across its two main Singaporean entities, Apple generated about $9 million in pretax profit per employee in 2024, the latest year for which figures can be calculated.

In Ireland last year, Apple’s pretax profit per employee was $6 million. Across the world in 2025, the equivalent figure was less than $1 million.

These vast disparities show the mismatch between the size of Apple’s workforce in these jurisdictions and the substantial profits accrued there.

Singapore rolled out the OECD rules for financial years starting in 2025. Its headline corporate tax rate is 17 per cent, exceeding the global minimum tax, but companies can negotiate incentives that reduce this rate.

The US disclosures indicate Apple benefits from such arrangements, which offer relief and credits for activities deemed by Singapore to be of high economic value.

From 2023 to 2025, Apple’s effective tax rate in Singapore fluctuated about 10 per cent, accounts for its main local entities show.

This year and in the future, the top-up taxes levied as part of the OECD initiative are likely to take the rate closer to 15 per cent.

In 2025 Apple booked pretax profits of nearly $40 billion in its Singaporean subsidiaries, according to their latest published accounts.

This year, the figure could be as high as $50 billion, Financial Times estimates based on the US disclosures suggest.

“We’re starting to get an idea of just how much lost [tax] revenue is being left on the table, billions of dollars just for this one company in a single year,” said Milin, of the Fact Coalition.

Apple has become the magnificent one.

Up over 25 per cent in 2026, the iPhone maker is back on top of the stock market, with a valuation of $5 trillion putting it ahead of Nvidia.

Creative Planning strategist Charlie Bilello recently noted Apple was the only magnificent seven stock to outperform the S&P 500 this year.

The contrast with 2025 is striking. “AI is turning Apple into a market ‘loser’”, headlined Axios in July 2025, a message echoed by Bloomberg (“Apple faces calls to reboot AI strategy with shares slumping”).

Criticised for spending too little on AI, Apple now benefits as investors fret about how much its rivals are spending. Apple generates more free cash flow than any other magnificent seven member, while avoiding the AI spending binge “draining” its peers, says Bilello.

Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta spent a combined $202 billion on capital expenditure in the third quarter alone, more than double the year-earlier figure. Concerns over Alphabet’s cash burn sent its shares down 19 per cent in October, their worst-ever monthly performance.

Apple, which reported earnings on Monday, has essentially become a hedge against the AI trade, outperforming the Nasdaq-100 by almost 20 percentage points over the past six months.

Given its recent run, with shares up 25 per cent since June and $1 trillion added to its market value, Apple has arguably done well simply to hold on to those gains amid the recent market turbulence.

Ironically, the flight to safety has not come cheap. Apple trades at 36 times expected earnings, almost twice the S&P 500 multiple. Apple’s AI issues remain, but its reluctance to spend heavily is looking less foolish as the bills mount up elsewhere.

]]>Frederic J. Brown<![CDATA[Effects of Unite case being quietly felt in courts two years on]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/08/effects-of-unite-case-being-quietly-felt-in-courts-two-years-on/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/08/effects-of-unite-case-being-quietly-felt-in-courts-two-years-on/Sun, 08 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000It’s not only the unions that talk about the waves made by the Supreme Court’s decision in Unite’s case against HA O’Neill a couple of years back. Legal experts are talking about them too.

Last week, at an Irish Congress of Trade Unions event, former chair of the Labour Court Kevin Duffy argued that Chief Justice Donal O’Donnell’s observation in his judgment on the case that “the right to form unions would be of little benefit if the activities of the union and its members were to be regarded as presumptively unlawful” might have the effect of undermining the Government’s claim that it cannot legislate to require employers to engage in collective bargaining in certain circumstances due to constitutional issues.

It is, Duffy suggested, simply a question of political will.

On Friday, Cathy Maguire SC pointed to another of the judgments in the case, that of Judge Brian Murray, as having hinted at the possibility of a right to strike being recognised at some point in the future.

“It is arguably implicit in Article 40.6.1 iii of the Constitution that the right to form trade unions implies in turn at least some – perhaps as yet undefined – zone of freedom for those unions to organise and campaign,” he wrote.

The observation, Maguire made clear, did not do anything to actually recognise such a right but, she said, Murray “raised the question” that it (the constitutional right of freedom of association) “may in the future be held to encompass a right to strike”.

The more immediate benefit to unions already appears to be evidenced in the absence, since the court delivered its decision two years ago, of cases taken by employers seeking injunctions intended to thwart strike action.

The court’s “definitive interpretation” had the effect of “correcting the almost universal approach”, she said, to considering such applications under the existing legislation, sections of which “should be read to give effect to the protection of unions and their members which the Acts were clearly intended to provide,” wrote O’Donnell

With employers having apparently concluded they are less likely to get injunctions, they appear to have more or less abandoned the tactic and, said Maguire, “it appears the court’s intention that these matters be played out on the picket line and not in the Four Courts has been fulfilled”.

]]>Bryan O'Brien

Thousands of soldiers from 11 countries began military exercises in Poland today. They are the first organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing, with the aim of preparing for a role in supporting Ukraine following a potential future peace deal with Russia.

The manoeuvres, which are being jointly led by France and the UK, are taking place in Nowa Dęba, around 100 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, and will last until 22 November.

The development has been condemned by Russia, which says it shows that Western countries are ignoring Moscow’s “legitimate security concerns” and “fueling the spiral of escalation”.​

🇫🇷🇬🇧 KOALICJA: The MNF-U is training to ensure a solid and lasting peace in Ukraine

The Multinational Force-Ukraine (MNF-U), formed from the Coalition of the Willing and under 🇫🇷🇬🇧command, is launching its first major exercise: KOALICJA

📅 November 9–22, 2026
📍In Poland,… pic.twitter.com/Ikcl1uY8N2

— The 🇫🇷 Joint Staff – Military operations (@FrenchForces) November 7, 2026

The plans were first announced in July by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk following a summit of the Coalition of the Willing in Paris. The exercises, taking place on land, in the air, and at sea, are being conducted by the Multinational Force Ukraine (MNF-U), which serves as the military component of the coalition.

“This exercise will show that the Multinational Force-Ukraine is a real, capable, readily deployable force that represents a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine’s long-term stability and security,” said Tom Bateman, the British lieutenant-general commanding MNF-U.

The British Ministry of Defence says that the exercise, which has been named “Koalicja” (meaning “Coalition” in Polish), “will test Allies’ readiness to support Ukraine and rebuild their Armed Forces once the conflict ends”.

France’s armed forces ministry, meanwhile, says that the aim is to ensure that MNF-U is “ready to deploy at the request of the Ukrainian government” in order to help “guarantee a robust and lasting peace in Ukraine”.

 

Around 2,800 troops are being deployed for the manoeuvres, with AFP reporting that this includes 1,100 from France alone. The British defence ministry says it has sent 300 personnel, as well as Typhoon and Voyager aircraft.

In addition, just under 2,000 Polish troops will take part, bringing the total to almost 5,000 personnel, reports Polska Zbrojna, a publication linked to the Polish defence ministry. Other countries taking part are Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and Turkey.

Poland’s defence ministry says the exercises will “demonstrate how quickly participating nations can mobilise and establish forces capable of supporting Ukraine after the end of the war”.

However, although Poland is hosting the manoeuvres, the defence ministry reiterated the country’s position that “it would not send its own soldiers to Ukrainian territory” as part of any postwar settlement. Poland has made clear it intends instead to help provide logistical support.

Nederland doet met enkele honderden militairen mee aan oefening Koalicja in Polen. De Coalition of the Willing traint er met 11 landen op snelle verplaatsing, commandovoering en bevoorrading ter voorbereiding op mogelijke steun aan Oekraïne na beëindiging van de oorlog. pic.twitter.com/JLE6W91HnZ

— Ministerie van Defensie (@Defensie) November 9, 2026

France says that the deployment of forces to Ukraine would include sending instructors to help the country rebuild and strengthen its armed forces, while air missions would enable civlian aircraft to resume flying in Ukrainian airspace.

At sea, MNF-U forces could help clear mines from shipping routes in the Black Sea. The maritime component of the current exercises is being led by Turkey through a simulated operational exercise, without deploying troops to Poland itself.

France, the UK and Poland have emphasised, however, that the MNF-U forces would only be deployed once fighting in Ukraine has ceased and would not carry out peacekeeping or ceasefire-monitoring duties.

Poland will host military exercises later this year with France and the UK to prepare for providing future security guarantees to Ukraine, says PM @donaldtusk.

He also declared Poland's willingness to permanently host more troops from its European allies https://t.co/couian4FrP

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026

On Saturday, the spokeswoman for Russia’s foreign ministry, Maria Zakharova, condemned the exercises, saying that they make “absolutely clear that the West remains unwilling to take Russia’s legitimate security concerns into account and continues to fuel the spiral of escalation”.

She described the deployment of any foreign armed forces to Ukraine as “absolutely unacceptable” and said they would “create additional threats to Russia’s security”.

“Any military units in Ukraine will be regarded by the Russian armed forces as legitimate targets, with all the risks and consequences that entails,” warned Zakharova.

Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova’s answer to a media question in connection with the first military exercises of the so-called Multinational Force – Ukraine under the Coalition of the Willinghttps://t.co/GiouEAmT6J

— Jeff Franzius (@jk55044) November 9, 2026

The exercises come as Ukraine and Russia meet the United States and others for peace talks in Abu Dhabi this week. Ukraine has repeatedly insisted that European security guarantees would be necessary for any peace agreement.

British defence secretary Wes Streeting suggested the exercises forecast precisely such a scenario: “This isn’t a hypothetical plan, it’s a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops.”

Zakharova, however, says that the exercises are “yet another confirmation that the Europeans have no place at the negotiating table”.

]]> Polish government ministers suggest tighter gun controls after deadly terrorist shooting https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/09/polish-government-ministers-suggest-tighter-gun-controls-after-deadly-terrorist-shooting/ Mon, 09 Nov 2026 13:15:28 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106564

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

In the wake of Saturday’s deadly terrorist shooting in Kraków, a deputy defence minister has called for debate on limiting the number and types of weapons people can own. Meanwhile, a deputy interior minister says the tragedy provides an “incentive” to revisit proposals to better register certain guns.

Poland has among the lowest levels of gun ownership in Europe, though the number of firearms licences being issued has risen in recent years and some politicians have called for expanded access to guns. Saturday’s attack was carried out by a man who legally owned firearms.

On Saturday, 24-year-old Michał Oksiński drove through the historic city centre of Kraków, which was packed with tourists and locals, firing at random from his car.

He killed six people and injured over a dozen more. Later in the day, the bodies of the perpetrator’s parents and sister were found in his home, where they had been shot dead.

Oksiński’s rampage was brought to an end in a shootout with two police officers, which left all three with serious injuries. On Monday morning, the police announced that Oksiński had died in hospital. One of the police officers remains in what is described as “serious but stable” condition.

The man who carried out Saturday’s deadly terrorist attack in the Polish city of Kraków has died in hospital from the injuries he sustained during a shootout with police.

One of the two officers who stopped him remains in serious but stable condition https://t.co/rT1YBXhkp7

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 9, 2026

The incident has caused shock in Poland, a country that has never previously experienced this type of mass public shooting.

Speaking to Polsat News on Sunday, deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said that the tragedy “is the best illustration that it makes no sense to talk about expanding access to firearms”.

She added that “it’s already relatively easy” to obtain a gun licence, which can be granted to anyone aged 21 or over who has passed the relevant tests and declared that the firearm is for sporting purposes. Both Oksiński and his father had such licences and legally owned 11 firearms.

“I would like to start a discussion about whether access to such a large number of weapons should actually be so easy,” said Sobkowiak-Czarnecka. “This is also a question of whether someone who uses weapons for sporting purposes should have so many different types of weapons stored at home.”

 

Also speaking to Polsat on Sunday, Czesław Mroczek, a deputy interior minister, said that “weapons are certainly a challenge for us”. He noted that “in Poland we have had many cases of killings using black powder weapons, for which there is not even a register, let alone a permit procedure”.

Such weapons use traditional black powder rather than modern smokeless powder and include firearms manufactured before 1885 and their modern replicas.

According to a recent study by researchers from the Jagiellonian University in Kraków, they make up a considerable proportion of firearm-related fatalities in the country.

While noting that the issue is not directly related to the Kraków attacks, Mroczek said that plans to include these weapons in a register had already been drawn up and “this event [in Kraków] is an incentive for us to reexamine the matter”.

🇵🇱 Poland's interior ministry says black-powder guns, currently exempt from registration, will be entered into the register. The Krakow attack is described as an impulse to review the whole permit system.https://t.co/Nh7dr46MJ7

— Олег Рощин (@oleg_roshchin) November 9, 2026

On Monday morning, the spokesman for the National Prosecutor’s Office, Przemysław Nowak, held a press conference at which he provided further details on their findings so far.

He revealed that Oksiński had been found with two AR-15 rifles and two handguns on his person and in his car, as well as around 500 rounds of ammunition. He had earlier fired “several dozen, possibly several hundred, shots”.

A further seven guns had been found at Oksiński’s home. The total of 11 firearms matched the number of weapons there were permits for, noted Nowak, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska.

“The entire matter related to the weapons and the firearms permits will be reviewed,” added the spokesman. “We know that, since March of this year, he [Oksiński] has held firearms permits for one rifle and one pistol.”

Prosecutors have launched a terror investigation into Saturday’s shooting in Kraków, which left six dead. Three more bodies were later found in the suspect's home.

Further details have also emerged about the heroic actions of police and medical personnel https://t.co/icBJWLRK7c

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 8, 2026

Although gun ownership in Poland is relatively low, it has been rising steadily in recent years, particularly since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with the total number of registered firearms owned by Poles surpassing 1 million, up from around 380,000 in 2014.

Last year, a record 50,709 new gun licences were issued in the country in 2025, up 10.6% compared to a year earlier.

Under Polish law, civilians can apply for licences for sporting, hunting, collecting and personal protection purposes. To obtain one, applicants must undergo medical examinations, pass a test, and join a relevant association, such as the Polish Sports Shooting Association, the Polish Hunting Association, or a collectors’ group.

Licences for sports and collection purposes are the most popular types of permits, together making up 76% of last year’s permits. But the number of licences issued for “personal protection” has grown from just 81 in 2021 to 7,254 last year.

A record 50,709 gun licences were issued in Poland last year and the total number of registered firearms has now surpassed 1 million.

Gun ownership in Poland has risen particularly rapidly since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 https://t.co/axt2YS044Z

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 11, 2026

Access to firearms widened in 2023 under the former government, when parliament passed a law removing “unnecessary administrative and legal barriers.” That allowed members of uniformed services to apply for personal protection permits, a change lawmakers said was intended to “strengthen Poland’s defence potential”.

However, some politicians, especially on the right, have pushed for ownership rules to be further loosened. In September, speaking at the opening of a shooting range, President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, called for “public discussion about responsible access to weapons”.

“Even in the European Union, Poland remains at the bottom of the list in terms of access to firearms,” he said, quoted by Polsat. “Only about 1% of Polish citizens have access to weapons and are skilled at using them. Fortunately, I’m in that 1%.”

In a statement issued on Friday evening, S&P said that its “negative outlook reflects the risk that elevated budgetary deficits and rising government debt could constrain policy flexibility in the face of future shocks”.

A collection of artefacts associated with the Vandals and dating back almost 2,000 years has been handed anonymously to a museum in eastern Poland.

The collection includes a sword, spear and javelin heads, shield components and spurs. Museum staff do not know who originally discovered the burial or exactly where it was located, leaving the circumstances of the find largely a mystery.

The Father Stanisław Staszic Museum in Hrubieszów announced in a Facebook post that the objects had been passed to them anonymously through an intermediary.

The items are in poor condition and will undergo urgent conservation, with the iron components of the weapons particularly vulnerable after centuries in the ground.

They were also exposed to high temperatures during a burial practice in which the deceased was burned along with their personal belongings. The museum says that the nature of the objects indicates that their owner held a high social position.

The most notable object is a sword preserved in three pieces, reflecting the Vandal practice of deliberately breaking or bending weapons and other grave artefacts as part of funeral rituals. The collection also contains two spearheads, both broken.

Other items include a shield boss with a spike, a shield grip, a fragment of a knife, a belt buckle and two spurs. Fragments of a bone comb and a bronze fibula, used to fasten a cloak, were also recovered.

 

The circumstances surrounding the discovery and recovery of the objects remain unknown, but the museum says that, according to the information it has received, the burial site was discovered in an agricultural field several years ago in the municipality of Werbkowice.

“We intend to verify the exact location through archaeological excavations, most likely next summer,” they added. “Based on the information we have gathered, there are strong indications that there may be more similar burials in the area that have been disturbed by agricultural work.”

The opportunity to recover the objects and transfer them to an appropriate institution arose only recently. The museum said that a local metal detectorist played a key role in arranging the transfer, acting as an intermediary in securing the artefacts.

The recovery of the artefacts follows another recent archaeological discovery in the same region. In August, the museum announced that a metal boss from a warrior’s shield dating to the second century was found at a scrap metal yard near Hrubieszów.

The Vandals were an ancient Germanic people believed to have reached the territories of present-day Poland around the 3rd or 2nd century BC.

They lived in the region for several centuries and are generally associated by researchers with the Przeworsk culture, which flourished across parts of present-day Poland during the Iron Age and Roman period.

Around the turn of the 4th and 5th centuries AD, amid the expansion of the Huns, they left Central Europe and moved westwards into the declining Roman Empire. As the Vandals left Central Europe, the Slavic population gradually moved into the region over the following centuries.

The leader of one of the parties in Poland’s ruling coalition has put forward plans for a “constitutional reset” that he hopes can resolve the crisis around the country’s top court.

The proposal, presented on Thursday by deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, head of the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), would remove all current judges on the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) and allow new judges to be chosen only with the approval of 60% of members of parliament and the president.

To take effect, the measure would require amending Poland’s constitution, something that has happened only twice since the document was adopted in 1997 and which also requires a three-fifths majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament.

Apelują o to przedstawiciele organizacji społecznych, Rada Przedsiębiorców, Naczelna Rada Adwokacka, Helsińska Fundacja Praw Człowieka i Episkopat Polski.… pic.twitter.com/3RCsKRlSiM

— Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) November 5, 2026

Kosiniak-Kamysz’s announcement comes amid the fallout from events last Friday, when eight new judges elected to the TK this year by the government’s majority in parliament seized control of the court.

They announced that its chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, had been suspended for failing to fulfil his duties, including by refusing to allow most of those judges to take up their seats on the court.

Święczkowski denounced the takeover as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the tribunal’s remaining six judges, who, like him, were appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, which brought the TK under its political influence when it ruled from 2015 to 2023.

 

As well as pitting judges aligned with the national-conservative PiS, which is now the main opposition party, and the current more liberal government against one another, the dispute also centres around the legitimacy of certain judges.

The government points to the fact that PiS unlawfully appointed three judges to the TK in 2015. As a result, both Polish and European courts have found the tribunal in its current form to be illegitimate.

Meanwhile, Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of the eight judges appointed by the government’s parliamentary majority this year, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications.

The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”

But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026

The standoff has led some NGOs and experts to call for a “constitutional reset”, whereby the TK would be reformed to make the process of selecting judges more consensual and less politicised.

Indeed, the current government even proposed legislation in 2024 that would have required new TK judges to be approved by a three-fifths parliamentary majority. The plans would also have removed unlawfully appointed judges from the PiS era and annulled rulings they were involved in.

That prompted the president at the time, Andrzej Duda, who was also aligned with PiS, to send the bills to the TK, which was still packed with PiS-era judges, for assessment. The tribunal rejected them as unconstitutional the following year.

Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025

Now, Kosiniak-Kamysz has proposed new legislation intended to resolve the issue. His solution would create a mechanism under which parliament, at the request of the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS), could declare the TK “permanently incapable of performing its duties”.

Such a status could only be declared with the support of a three-fifths majority of both houses of parliament – the Sejm and the Senate – combined. It would have to come at the request of the KRS because, says Kosiniak-Kamysz, the terms of judges cannot be shortened without the participation of other judges.

The process of appointing new TK judges would involve the speaker of the Sejm proposing candidates after obtaining the opinions of the heads of the Supreme Court and the Supreme Administrative Court – which are separate from the TK – as well as professional bodies representing legal professions.

The candidates proposed by the speaker would also have to receive the prior consent of the president. For a new TK judge to be approved, they would have to receive the support of three fifths of members of the Sejm and Senate combined.

💬 336 głosów posłów i senatorów. To wykracza poza większość jakąkolwiek koalicyjną dzisiaj sformułowaną – @KosiniakKamysz w Warszawie pic.twitter.com/iLUuM5TSxQ

— 🍀 PSL (@nowePSL) November 5, 2026

Whereas TK judges currently all serve nine-year terms, under Kosiniak-Kamysz’s proposal, five of the judges would serve three-year terms, five of them six-year terms, and the final five would serve for nine years.

Unlike now, the new judges would not have to swear their oath before the president, but before parliament.

Kosiniak-Kamysz emphasised, however, that the measure was intended as a “one-time” emergency tool. “Later, we will return to the method of selecting judges described today in the constitution, or a better one, if there is a majority for it.”

The current method of choosing new TK judges requires only the support of a majority in the Sejm. However, judges must then swear an oath “before the president”, an issue that has become a bone of contention this year.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

Kosiniak-Kamysz’s plans would require changes to Poland’s constitution, which specifies the manner in which TK judges are chosen. A constitutional amendment requires the support of a three-fifths majority in the Sejm and a simple majority in the Senate. It does not need presidential approval.

PSL itself has only 28 members of the 460-seat Sejm and four senators. Kosiniak-Kamysz acknowledged that “it won’t be an easy road” to win the necessary support for his idea.

He appealed not only to his fellow ruling parties, but also to opposition groups that have expressed their backing for a constitutional reset, such as the centre-right Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) and far-right Confederation (Konfederacja).

On Thursday evening, one of Confederation’s leaders, Sławomir Mentzen, shared a photo of himself meeting Kosiniak-Kamysz, with the caption: “It’s going in the right direction”.

However, some voices within the ruling coalition expressed scepticism towards the idea. Borys Budka, a former leader of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) – which is the largest governing party – said it was “hard to imagine changing the constitution alongside someone like PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński”.

Tomasz Trela of The Left (Lewica) likewise said that, “if anyone thinks The Left will change the constitution arm in arm with PiS, they’re mistaken”, reports Polsat News.

On Wednesday, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw announced that it had indicted Braun for four alleged crimes. It was able to do so after the European Parliament, where Braun sits as an MEP, stripped him of immunity earlier this year.

One of the charges, for criminal defamation, stems from Braun’s claim, during a televised presidential debate in April last year, that the yellow paper daffodils distributed each year in Warsaw to mark the anniversary of the 1943 Jewish Ghetto Uprising against German Nazi rule are “symbols of shame”.

Prosecutors say that Braun’s words were “extremely xenophobic, manipulative and aggressive”, and that they defamed the organisers of the daffodil campaign, in particular the POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews in Warsaw.

Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey has warned that AI “may not live up to market expectations” and deliver returns fast enough to investors, risking a sharp fall in valuations.

Bailey said in a speech in Zurich that it may take longer for investors to reap the benefits of heavy AI investment than it is currently assumed. His intervention comes against a backdrop of trillions of dollars being wiped from company valuations in the last week. 

In an address that focused on the threat of AI to financial stability, he warned that there was a “risk” that investors had over-estimated the value of AI, even if “bubble spotting is an imprecise science”. 

“The returns may be good, and they may match expectations, but they take longer to be realised than predicted,” Bailey said. “This has been the case historically with big ‘General Purpose Technology’ innovation – take Edison and electricity for instance. 

“There are good reasons to believe that the world moves faster now, but still the timing may not live up to market expectations.”

He added that financial markets overvalue “uncertain future returns” as it was essential to risk-taking on the part of investors.

Bailey’s latest AI alert

Bailey, who is also chair of the global Financial Stability Board, repeated a previous warning that “everyone is priced to be a winner” in AI stock pricing despite history stating that this was unlikely. He pointed to the dotcom bubble and the ensuing failure of Netscape, the dominant web browser in the 1990s which was superseded by Microsoft and other tech giants. 

A mass sell-off in AI-related stocks following President Trump’s crushing mid-terms election defeat in the US has sparked suggestions that the AI bubble is bursting. 

Last Thursday, more than £2.4 trillion was wiped from the value of the US stock market. On Monday, firms listed on the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq saw stock prices recover slightly from falls last week, with each composite index rising by more than two per cent. 

Shares in Nvidia, one of the largest listed companies in the world, which is essential to wider AI investments, dropped by five per cent following an investigation into chief executive Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. 

Bailey’s intervention on market pricing adds to growing alarm over the high expectations for major tech companies in the US to post bumper profits over the next two years after mass investment in infrastructure. Top American hyperscalers, which are made up of the largest AI companies such as Amazon and Meta, are expected to spend about $900bn (£670bn) in 2026 alone, according to JP Morgan. 

In April this year, Bank deputy governor Sarah Breeden predicted that stock markets would face an “adjustment” and fall due to highly valued AI stocks.

Easyjet has confirmed it is looking at plans to cut head office jobs ahead of its £5.7bn private equity takeover.

The Luton-based carrier is understood to be consulting on proposals that may see 50 head office roles slashed out of a team of over 2,300.

It comes after Easyjet agreed a takeover in July for 715p a share by US firm Apollo, which also owns Wagamama’s parent company, The Restaurant Group.

Shareholders are voting on the deal on Wednesday and, if approved, it is expected to complete in the first quarter of 2027. It is understood the job cuts are not linked to Apollo or its proposed acquisition of Easyjet or any plans it has for the carrier after the takeover closes.

It is also understood Apollo has not been involved in the process nor the proposals.

An Easyjet spokesperson said in a statement: “Our people are integral to Easyjet’s success and as a low-cost airline we always operate efficiently so we can keep fares low for our customers and invest in future growth opportunities.

These proposals affect a very small proportion of head office roles to ensure we are best set up to support the business’ ambitious plans.”

Unions in the UK and Europe have raised concerns over possible job cuts at the carrier after the Apollo deal and debts that would be heaped onto the airline’s balance sheet.

The British Airline Pilots Association (Balpa) trade union has raised concerns, saying recently that “important questions remain regarding the long-term implications of the transaction”.

The trade union added: “Balpa’s principal concern is the extent to which the transaction may affect employees beyond the 12-month period covered by the statements of intention.”

Takeover tussle

Apollo secured the deal in early August after winning in a takeover tussle in the summer with rival US investment firm Castlelake.

Castlelake had previously made a £5.5bn – 690p a share – proposal to buy easyJet, but walked away from the bidding war in August.

City AM revealed in August Easyjet shareholders were at risk of having their stake in the airline seized from them unilaterally and were highly unlikely to be paid a dividend if they opt to retain their stake in the carrier once Apollo’s takeover is complete.

The shares of more than three quarters of FTSE 350 firms have outperformed Nvidia so far this year after the world’s biggest semiconductor firm was blighted by concerns over bloated AI valuations and its billionaire founder was caught in a relationship scandal involving an alleged spy.

Some 68 constituents of the FTSE 100 and 202 members of the FTSE 250 had eclipsed the year-to-date share performance of Nvidia at market close on Monday, according to a City AM analysis. London’s blue-chip index is up 9.3 per cent since the start of the year, on an equal-weight basis.

Nvidia shares, on the other hand, have shed more than seven per cent of their value since the start of the year. That followed a sharp sell-off of the stock in New York on Monday after chief executive Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with an Nvidia customer and alleged Chinese spy, triggering an internal company investigation into the romantic relationship.

“Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together,” Huang said in a statement emailed to staff.

“I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.”

The news wiped as much as $200bn (£150bn) from Nvidia’s market value in a matter of minutes. But the stock had already been under pressure in recent months over growing concern the AI investing boom was running out of steam, tumbling from a peak of around $240 at the start of October to $180 a month later.

“Higher interest rates, worries over how the artificial intelligence spending boom is to be funded and concerns about the Democrats’ plans for regulation and data centres are now being joined by the possibility of a scandal involving the CEO of one of the companies that sits at the very apex of the AI tree, Nvidia,” said AJ Bell investment director Russ Mould.

 “Bulls may be inclined to take President Trump’s lead and shrug off Jensen Huang’s personal problems, in the view the work he does to put Nvidia and the US in the lead in a technological race makes him too valuable to lose, but sceptics will look at past stock market cycles and wonder whether a potential scandal could be yet another reason for more air to leak out of what they see as an AI bubble.”

Mould told City AM the FTSE’s performance “is not something many may have predicted at the start of the year. There has been a worldwide shift toward stodgier sectors in the second half of the year, notably healthcare and consumer staples, and away from tech, so it will be interesting to see if that trend continues, or whether much lower share prices – and thus valuations – in some instances tempt some investors to buy on the dip.”

The Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police has said he wants the government to legislate to ensure football clubs reimburse local forces for the cost of policing matches.

Sir Mark Rowley said the cost of policing London’s six Premier League clubs, and the eight others based in the capital who play lower down the football pyramid, amounts to around £20m annually. 

The latest City Hall stats put a £12.3m cost on policing football matches between August and December last year, with the previous two seasons, between the summers of 2023 and 2025, each seeing around 40,000 officers deployed to keep the peace.

The 2024-25 season stats reveal a recovery rate of just eight per cent, with an outgoing of £23.4m met with a repayment from clubs of just £2.1m.

Policing has its costs

“We’re constantly looking at football matches and it may have some effect on that but we are still looking to government to regulate so that the polluter pays, frankly, and at the moment they don’t pay for most of the resources,” Rowley told City Hall.

“It is a big amount of police resources that are going to police football matches so I would like to see that fully reimbursed.

“I know the government is considering it. I don’t know where they have got with it.”

Football clubs would be expected to fight steps to make them pay more, since any changes could hurt clubs which are near-universally loss making already. Games outside the top flight do not always need Special Police Services re-charging.

It is suggested that total Premier League and club investment in safety and security exceeded £100m last season, while football clubs already pay for Special Police Services if they are required. The cost of this hit north of £8m last season.

Added Mayor of London Sadiq Khan: “I have supported the Commissioner in terms of tweaking that could lead to additional resources for London.

“To be fair, a lot of these football clubs do a lot of great work in the community and the legislation means that inside a stadium there are different rules to outside of the stadium. We’re hopeful we can get further support in relation to this important issue.”

Premier League payments?

Joanne McCartney, London Assembly member for Enfield and Haringey, said: “At a time when the Met is already under pressure to deliver vital services, including counter-terrorism policing, we need to make sure its resources are being used where they are needed most.

“It’s time for clubs to pay a fairer share of the policing costs associated with their matches. That burden should not fall on the public, including fans of rival clubs.

“Premier League clubs generate enormous revenues and benefit from the safe environment that police officers help provide. It gives supporters, including families, greater confidence to attend matches. It is only right that clubs contribute towards the cost of keeping supporters and local communities safe.”

The Home Office was approached for comment.
