]]> 2475535Matt Hardy Matt Hardy HMRC ‘flying blind’ on over 1.2m tax demands after failing to track error rates  https://www.cityam.com/hmrc-flying-blind-on-over-1-2m-tax-demands-after-failing-to-track-error-rates/ Mon, 09 Nov 2026 15:26:57 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2475442

HMRC has been accused of “flying blind” on over 1.2m tax demands after admitting it does not track how many are challenged or cancelled due to errors. The tax authority issued 1,254,201 individual PA302 simple assessment tax calculations in the 2024/25 tax year, according to figures obtained by City AM via a Freedom of Information [...]]]>

HMRC has been accused of “flying blind” on over 1.2m tax demands after admitting it does not track how many are challenged or cancelled due to errors.

The tax authority issued 1,254,201 individual PA302 simple assessment tax calculations in the 2024/25 tax year, according to figures obtained by City AM via a Freedom of Information request.

PA302 forms are sent to taxpayers instead of having them fill out self-assessment tax returns. HMRC uses data it holds from employers, pension providers, banks and government departments to determine how much tax is owed automatically.

Common triggers for a PA302 include a person owing income tax that cannot be automatically collected through the PAYE system, owing HMRC £3,000 or more and having untaxed income, such as high savings interest, which does not require a full self assessment return.

But in response to the FOI, HMRC refused to disclose how many calculations were reduced, cancelled or withdrawn, stating that retrieving the data would exceed cost limits as it does “not hold readily available figures”.

The tax authority admitted the data is not automatically collected and it does not track the total sum of tax incorrectly demanded.

Tracking failure

While the government department does log calls and queries for “operational purposes”, it said it does not distinguish standard enquiries from cases where a taxpayer challenges on grounds that calculations are incorrect.

“This information… does not enable us to identify reliably how many individual PA302 calculations were challenged specifically because the customer considered them to be incorrect,” HMRC wrote in its response.

Steve Webb, the former pensions minister and a partner at pension consultants LCP, said: “It is shocking that HMRC has so little management information about the million-plus tax demands it is sending out every year. 

“If they do not log how often people challenge these assessments and how often they are then withdrawn or revised, HMRC can have little idea of the scale of error or how this is changing over time.”

Outdated systems

The admission has triggered concerns over whether automated errors are quietly penalising Brits who are already feeling the pressure of frozen tax thresholds.

Hundreds of thousands of Brits have been dragged into higher tax bands in the past few years, leaving them exposed to income tax and being issued a PA302 form.

Personal allowance has been fixed at £12,570 since April 2021 and is currently not due to rise until the 2028/29 tax year. The hike in the state pension under the triple lock mechanism has also thrown more people into the income tax net.

One City figure said frozen thresholds and widened margin for error due to more people being issued the forms should be enough reason to begin logging this “kind of information”. Tax advisers estimate HMRC sent 1.8m forms in the 2025/26 tax year and the number will continue to grow.

Webb noted there may be “systematic reasons” why assessments are sent out in error that could “only be picked up if there was proper data on correction rates”.

“HMRC should start recording challenges to simple assessments, otherwise they are ‘flying blind’ when it comes to implementing this part of the tax system,” he said.

This is the latest in a string of accusations from industry figures and advisory boards that HMRC is overly reliant on outdated, legacy IT systems.

In 2025, the Treasury Select Committee criticised the body for still manually handling over 14m postal items, while the Public Accounts Committee has repeatedly targeted its technical shortcomings and rushed transition into using digital systems.

An HMRC spokesperson said: “We do extensive work to ensure people’s Simple Assessment bills are correct. This includes working with third parties to help make sure the information they provide is accurate and carrying out checks on tax calculations before they’re issued.”

How Jensen Huang’s alleged affair echoes past boardroom scandals and could test his future at Nvidia]]>

According to John Updike, “The first breath of adultery is the freest; after it, constraints aping marriage develop.” Today Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, the golden boy behind the world’s first five trillion dollar company, is feeling the pressure of those constraints.

Huang has not only been forced to admit to his affair with former Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (no relation) – he’s also having to come to terms with the fact she might be a spy for the Chinese government. Not a great day for Jensen Huang, then.

Sporting his trademark black leather jacket, it should perhaps not come as too much of a surprise that his midlife crisis also extends to an affair with a younger woman. Their relationship had already raised eyebrows, with Alice posting pictures of the pair enjoying intimate dinners together, which Jensen has previously claimed “have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual”. 

He was being more accurate than he intended: in the heated arena of the corporate boardroom, affairs are surprisingly “normal and not unusual”, although they do tend to cause something of a ruckus when they are inevitably exposed.

Remember the Coldplay kisscam?

Who could forget the infamous Coldplay kisscam footage from last year, when data startup Astronomer boss Andy Byron was caught red-handed – and red-faced – in a clinch with his “chief people officer” Kristin Cabot. Their reaction – attempting to duck from the prying eyes of the camera – caused the footage to go viral and by the next morning, the pair were infamous across the world. Both resigned from the company and they are, rather unfairly, still hounded over it to this day.

In 2023, BP boss Bernard Looney was stripped of a remuneration package worth millions after failing to admit relationships – with an “s” – with various colleagues, with the BP board claiming it had been “knowingly misled”.

The incident recalled Lord Browne’s infamous departure from the same company in 2007, when he was forced to quit after lying under oath about a four-year relationship with Jeff Chevalier.

In an ill-fated attempt to block the Mail on Sunday from publishing the story, Lord Browne went to the High Court, lying under oath about meeting his beau while jogging in a London park, rather than through an escort website. He forfeited a leaving package worth some £15m.

Jensen Huang has joined a large club

Former McDonald’s boss Steve Easterbrook, a rare Brit to reach the summit of corporate America, was fired over an affair in 2019 – it later emerged he, too, had engaged in multiple relationships with people at the fast food company. Easterbrook was subsequently fined by the US financial watchdog for misleading investors: as the saying goes, the cover-up is always worse than the crime.

The same story repeats ad nauseam: in 2005 Boeing CEO Harry Stonecipher was forced out of the firm after admitting to an affair with his vice-president for operations and commercial activities Debra Peabody. In 2006 Walmart’s marketing executive Julie Roehm had an “inappropriate romantic relationship” with Sean Womack, a former marketing VP at the retailer (Walmart claimed the pair had been spotted in a compromising position in a bar).

None of these adulterers survived their indiscretion – but Huang will hope he is simply too big to fail. He is now in full defence mode, publicly apologising to his wife and hanging his grey-haired head in shame. An investigation launched by the company will decide his fate.

Huang should perhaps pay heed to a quote by the American psychologist John M Gottman: “I liken an affair to the shattering of a Waterford crystal vase. You can glue it back together, but it will never be the same again.”

Time will tell if Jensen Huang’s crystal vase can be glued back together or if this affair will, as it has with so many others, prove to be his undoing.

Nvidia shares plunged more than eight per cent as Wall Street opened on Monday after a spying scandal involving chief executive Jensen Huang threatened to derail the chipmaker’s recovery from last week’s brutal tech sell-off.

Shares in the AI giant fell 8.04 per cent to $171.64 in early trading, wiping billions from its market value as investors reacted to Nvidia’s announcement of an independent investigation into reports that Huang had been targeted by Chinese intelligence.

Mandating salary transparency is another burden for employers to bear, and is no silver bullet for fair pay, writes Jay Bhayani

Should every job advert come with a salary attached? The Prime Minister thinks so, but I’m not convinced.

This question comes after Andy Burnham urged businesses to publish pay details now, ahead of upcoming legislation to make disclosure compulsory. 

The government argues that greater pay transparency would help jobseekers, particularly young people entering the workforce for the first time, make informed decisions about employment opportunities and reduce the risk of pay discrimination.

Those are worthwhile goals. Candidates understandably want to know the salary before committing to an often lengthy application and interview process. But encouraging good practice is different from legislating for it. Compulsory disclosure risks adding to employers’ growing compliance burden while overlooking how recruitment works in practice.

My own experiences of recruiting have shown me that overly prescriptive adverts can often mean missing out on strong candidates. By keeping the advert more open, I’ve attracted people who might not have fitted my original brief but have ultimately turned out to be better suited to the business.

A couple of years ago, an applicant to the HR consultancy team I lead illustrated the value of this approach. She was earning considerably more than our budget could stretch to, so publishing a salary might have deterred her. However, in conversation, she was open to lower pay in return for greater flexibility, more interesting work, less travel and fewer overnight stays.

That conversation would never have happened had the advertised salary put her off. Requiring employers to set pay upfront risks closing down opportunities before either side can explore them.

Salary only tells part of the story

There is also the question of what employers will actually be required to disclose. Salary is only one element of remuneration. Overtime, bonuses, pension contributions, sick pay and other benefits can all form part of an employee’s overall package. 

For the manufacturers that Make UK represents, shift arrangements, working patterns and additional responsibilities can vary significantly, these elements are particularly important. Some may also depend on length of service or individual circumstances. 

The government needs to be clear about the scope of any requirement and avoid creating an administrative exercise that becomes increasingly difficult to manage.

Publishing starting salaries can also expose differences between new recruits and existing colleagues, creating difficult conversations about pay and retention. But those differences are not necessarily evidence of unfair treatment but rather driven by market forces. 

For example, manufacturing wages already average eight per cent above those in the wider economy but acute skills shortages and a shallow pool from which to recruit often means employers within the sector are required to offer even higher salaries to secure the people they need ahead of their competitors.

The sheer variety of roles in manufacturing alone – more than 100 covered by Make UK’s annual pay research – further illustrates why setting salaries is far from straightforward. Add differences in location and business circumstances, and a published figure can only tell part of the story.

Disclosure is therefore no silver bullet for fair pay. Any legal requirement must preserve employers’ ability to respond to changing skills needs and labour market conditions.

Encourage good practice, not more paperwork

The wider context cannot be ignored either. Employers have already implemented significant employment law reforms because of the Employment Rights Act and are preparing for more. Make UK and PwC UK’s Executive Survey 2026 found that 86 per cent of manufacturers identified employment costs as a major business pressure. 

Our research has also found that 32 per cent want employment rules made simpler and less costly, while only 11 per cent believe the Employment Rights Act should continue as planned.

Against this backdrop, another statutory requirement needs careful consideration. Businesses are not opposed to fairness or transparency, but they do need a stable and proportionate regulatory environment in which they can recruit effectively and invest in their workforce.

Pay discrimination must be taken seriously, but we should not assume that mandating salary information in every job advert is automatically the most effective way to tackle it. 

Employers should be encouraged to be transparent, and many already choose to publish salary ranges voluntarily. There are clear benefits to doing so, including managing expectations and attracting suitable candidates.

But there is a difference between encouraging sensible recruitment practices and prescribing how businesses must operate through law.

Not every good idea should be a law

If the government proceeds, it must at the very least allow meaningful salary ranges rather than forcing employers to advertise a single figure. It must also recognise the complexity of total remuneration and ensure the requirements are workable for businesses of all sizes.

The objective should be to make recruitment fairer and more effective, not to create another compliance headache for employers already navigating substantial changes to employment law in an already turbulent and expensive operating environment.

Good employment practice is something to encourage. But not every good idea needs to become a legal requirement.

Jay Bhayani is executive director for legal at UK manufacturing trade body Make UK

Independent, revenue-driven contracts between London councils and e-bike operators fragment cross-borough travel and inflate costs for riders without resolving pavement clutter. So will TfL’s cross-London licensing scheme solve the problem? Asks Myra Stok

Everywhere you look, there are e- bikes, littering pavements, stopping people in their tracks – sometimes literally. Councils have taken on a central role in the battle between public disgust at e-bike behaviour by cutting deals with operators themselves. Yet, the problems persist.

This might be because councils aren’t incentivised to make your journeys better, or to reduce the burden dockless e-bikes pose to residents. A big claim, I know, beloved as they are. 

Virtually all 33 councils in London take independent approaches to dealing with dockless e-bikes. Nine councils have no e-bike schemes whatsoever, with Waltham Forest currently operating under an eight year ban. Of the remaining 24, there are a mixture of agreements, ranging from Memorandums of Understanding (MOU) all the way to multi-year exclusive contracts. 

Councils have no power to licence operators, but they can use other levers, the most powerful being contracts between themselves and operators. These can come in the form of tendered exclusive contracts or individually negotiated agreements. Beyond direct agreements, council enforcement powers mean they can remove road and  pavement obstructions under the Highways Act, and they can issue Fixed Penalty Notices and Penalty Charge Notices directly to operators.

Yet, these arrangements don’t tend to improve journeys because councils don’t have to consider inter-borough commuting needs, and because councils have discovered these contracts create new revenue streams. 

Exclusive contracts, where councils tender for operators, are the most formal and lucrative of them all. Councils often include pricing as a consideration in the tender, meaning that operators can increase their chance of winning contracts with higher ‘concession payments’ (yearly lump sums paid to councils) and greater revenue sharing commitments. Frustratingly, excluding operators and encouraging unsustainable bids leads to worse service, exacerbating differences between boroughs, rather than facilitating travel between them.

A council-negotiated £1.75 fee for half an hour rides within Hackney, will be charged at the normal rate if you travel into another borough

Journeys are split across borough lines. Cross Hammersmith Bridge on a Lime into Richmond, and you’ll find yourself unable to park. Bikes completely power down upon entering no-go boroughs. Prices can depend on borough boundaries. A council-negotiated £1.75 fee for half an hour rides within Hackney, will be charged at the normal rate if you travel into another borough. 

While it might leave riders frustrated, councils benefit. Richmond is reportedly receiving over £3m for its contract with Forest over three years. The Council’s scoring gave a quarter of all points to the size of the ‘concession payment’. Camden awarded Lime and Forest two contracts after a tender between four bidders, receiving a “commercially confidential” amount. Their scoring process was equally transparent. Lime received the highest score because of “quality and demonstrated added value”. On closer inspection, this does not translate to prices of the service. Out of 40 points awarded for price, revenue sharing makes up 22.5 points of the total score, the concession payment 10 points, and price a measly 7.5 points. 

Costs get passed on to riders, while simultaneously removing their discernment as consumers. In Hounslow, this anti-market spirit had a demonstrable effect. After a switch from Lime to Forest and Voi, trips fell from 128,000 in July 2025 under Lime, to just over 73,000 in the five weeks after switching. Voi later admitted it had supplied only around half the bikes it promised. 

Should we be surprised by this underperformance? Considering that Lime came 10 points ahead of Forest on quality, before being reportedly outbid by “about five times the council’s initial financial expectations”, I think not.

Councils may balk at suggestions that revenue is a deciding factor, pointing to their comprehensive evaluations. In Richmond, scoring criteria covered service quality, safety, parking, customer experience, pricing and value for money. But, shouldn’t service quality, customer experience, pricing and value be evaluated by riders themselves? Aren’t all of these things maintained and improved when users have choices in a market with multiple operators?

The range of other revenue generating fees, from flat access fees, to bay fees and tiered fees, aren’t much better. Most councils insist these are to cover operational costs, yet, increasingly, they are used to fund other commitments. Hackney Council stated that “any additional income” would be “considered within the budget setting process”, while Sutton Council reported they would use potential e-bike income as a help “to bridge the Council’s anticipated budget gap”.

Meanwhile, fees have been shooting up. City AM reported that one unnamed borough raised operator fees by 403.6 per cent between 2024 and 2026, while its parking bays grew by only 46 per cent. Another raised fees by 277.2 per cent, while bays grew by just 6.3 per cent. Even when operators pay more, infrastructure that addresses the problems that residents and pedestrians face does not necessarily follow. In fact, the cost of some bays still falls on the public, including £1.7m from the Mayor this year. Although Lambeth charges operators £700 a year per bay, its bays have been funded by TfL grants, receiving £94,000 in 2025/26.

TfL is in the process of cooking up its new policy, which will see all operators licensed for the whole of London. The new regulations should limit council-operator deals. They are bad news for riders, pedestrians, and residents. 

Myra Stok is a research associate at Looking for Growth, the political movement to end decline and save Britain

To talk of Tamdhu is to talk sherry, and for those who love the rich, raisin-like flavours of sherried whisky, Tamdhu is the ‘Real McCoy’. But it swims in a sea of single malts that have somewhat diluted the sherry category, reports Tom Bruce-Gardyne.

In 1975, the country’s top-selling wine was Harvey’s Bristol Cream, according to Jancis Robinson, who began her career as a wine writer at the same time. In her Weekend FT column this September, she wrote of how the syrupy sweet sherry enjoyed annual sales of 12m bottles, though the UK’s moment of ‘peak sherry’ was only four years away.

She went on to write that “unfortunately, sherry today has become a niche wine beloved, like Alsace wine and Riesling, by professionals but spurned by the mass market.” Thinking of crisp, salty Manzanillas and nutty, savoury Amontillados that are a million miles from Bristol Cream, she makes a good point.   

But in the world of single malt Scotch, the word ‘sherry’ is anything but niche, as it appears on countless labels as the go-to extension for brands. The industry rather blithely assumes that consumers naturally understand what it means.

The sherry cask finish 

In practice, the word is essentially a short-hand for a whisky that has been matured in a Bourbon barrel before spending a final year, or perhaps just a few months, in a sherry cask – a process known in the trade as ‘finishing’. 

If we are talking of an active, first-fill cask and the whisky spends sufficient time there, it will help shape its character. If not, it is more just a marketing wheeze. In either case, distillers often add a dollop of spirit caramel, or ‘fake tan’, to give its sherry veneer a nice amber glow. 

Whiskies that are fully matured in sherry casks are much rarer. The Macallan was the classic example until it strayed into Bourbon with its Fine Oak range, now discontinued, and today talks of ‘sherry seasoned’ casks. 

A 2025 bottling, released to support The Atlantic Salmon Trust

There are distilleries that release great examples like Arran with its Bodega Cask, and others that lean heavily into sherried whiskies like Dalmore, Glenfarclas and Glenallachie. But, according to Iain Weir, marketing director of Ian Macleod Distillers, there is only one that is 100 per cent sherry – namely Tamdhu.

Tamdhu’s unique sherry nature 

This makes the Speyside distillery unique, in his view. Tamdhu was in the same stable as The Macallan as part of the Edrington Group. It was mothballed in 2010, sold to Macleod’s a year later and fired back to life in 2012. 

“The stocks we inherited were pretty good, though predominantly ex-Bourbon,” says Iain. “When we tried them, it was a no-brainer. It was good in Bourbon, but exceptional in sherry, and Leonard (Russell – the MD) said; ‘Right, from now on, everything that goes into a bottle of Tamdhu single malt must be matured in sherry’.” 

For Iain, it reconnects the distillery with its roots. “I’ve got some old, quill pen-written ledgers from 1898, a few months after the distillery opened, with mention of Spanish oak sherry casks coming in by train,” he says. “The founders thought sherry-maturation was best for Tamdhu and we’ve brought that back.”

The distillery dates from the late Victorian whisky boom on Speyside. “Its founders were entrepreneurs – sixteen businessmen, one of whom was Tommy Dewar and another Alexander Walker,” he says of two of the most eminent whisky barons. “They raised about £20,000 and hired Charles Doig to build it with his signature pagoda roof. He was tasked to build the most efficient distillery of its time and create the best whisky.”

Within a few years Tamdhu became part of Highland Distillers – a forerunner of Edrington – and for the next century its role was to supply its well-regarded malt for blends, especially after the 1970’s when it trebled in size to a capacity of 4m lpa (litres of pure alcohol).

A token Tamdhu single malt without an age statement did appear, but it would have been mainly from ex-Bourbon barrels. 

Better than Macallan?

What was in sherry casks was better than Macallan, reckons Iain, not that he’s biased. He wonders if it partly explains why Tamdhu was sold with Edrington’s directors thinking, ‘what’s the point of having two Macallans in the portfolio’. 

But maybe it was just Edrington selling off the family silver once again. The company had already shed Glengoyne and Bunnahabhain, the former to Macleod’s, and has since disposed of Cutty Sark and Famous Grouse, seemingly to focus on its beloved Macallan.

What is sometimes unkindly dubbed ‘the Man United of single malts’ is being challenged, at least on substance, by Tamdhu. 

As well as the quality of its liquid and the strength of its sherry story, Tamdhu is also rather more accessible. In Royal Mile Whiskies, its 12 YO is currently around £40, compared to £74 for the equivalent Macallan. While Tamdhu 18 YO at £174 is half the price of its Big Mac rival.

But in style and brand recognition there’s a way to go. “I think people are beginning to talk about us,” says Iain. “We haven’t got anywhere near the awareness of a Dalmore or Macallan, but we’re beginning to get more of the conversation.” 

Meanwhile there are all those malts that have been to finishing school to compete with. “It’s something that frustrates me somewhat,” he says. “The word sherry does get bandied around.” It certainly does. 

Getting the message across is challenging however. Obsessing about sherry might delight an aficionado, but be less compelling for your average malt whisky drinker. It also gets more complicated because you have to explain the differences between European and American oak.

Tamdhu is determined to try and enthuse drinkers about the benefits of being fully matured in Oloroso casks. Iain talks of the “richness” and “integrated character you get from having your whisky in a sherry cask from day one right through to bottling.”

Next year is the distillery’s 160th birthday, and it will see the release of a 63 YO Tamdhu, its oldest expression yet. To widen its appeal, Iain and his team hope to connect with consumers on a more emotional level as they tell their ‘Spain to Speyside’ story.

Award-winning drinks columnist and author Tom Bruce-Gardyne began his career in the wine trade, managing exports for a major Sicilian producer. Now freelance for 20 years, Tom has been a weekly columnist for The Herald and his books include The Scotch Whisky Book and most recently Scotch Whisky Treasures. Consultancy firms have pumped a lot of money into frontier AI tools that have fundamentally changed tasks traditionally done by juniors. But the return on investment question lingers, writes Maria Ward-Brennan.

Model ML’s platform for the consultancy market has automated manual steps such as supporting research, presentation and Excel model creation, and reviewing client-facing materials.

They are the kind of roles traditionally done by a junior. But a growing number of consultants, known for their ranks of graduate staff are leaning on the platform, upending a strategy that has lasted decades.

In a recent case study with one of its clients, BDO, over the first eight weeks, the accounting firm’s deal teams asked more than 10,000 questions, analysed over 25,000 documents, and generated more than 14,000 AI review comments.

Raghav Sehgal, a former Bain executive and now Model ML’s head of consulting go-to-market, explained that because consulting carries massive reputational risk once a client logo is attached, the role shifts, particularly for juniors, to rigorous double-checking, insight creation, and managing the AI’s output.

However, the biggest question in the industry, and in others, is the real ROI of these expensive technology tools. The Big Four giants, Deloitte, KPMG, EY, and PwC, alone, have collectively committed several million pounds towards AI investment.

“ROI ultimately is a function of two inputs,” he said. “One is the tool itself … Does it fundamentally deliver and do what it’s supposed to do … and two, it’s change management: how do you reorganise yourself as a company around these tools?”

Milan Malik, former McKinsey and head of consulting engagement at Model ML, added: “ROI [return on investment] is a function of capability and adoption. If the platform performs at the frontier, the only thing left to solve is adoption, and that’s a change management question.”

Former consultant-turned-AI specialist Sehgal said “it is an exciting time” for the sector as “the way you work with your clients internally is changing”.

We’re seeing some creative approaches to this with our clients,” Malik continued, adding that one firm has placed its AI model on an internal learning platform, rewarding staff with learning credits if they upskill and share wins with colleagues. Another publishes a weekly leaderboard of its top users across every region, which turns them “into AI champions and creates a competitive spirit that drives adoption and, ultimately, ROI.”

From finance to the Big Four

Model ML, founded by brothers Chaz Englander and Arnie Englander, started in the financial sector but has since evolved to the world of professional services. Among its roster of clients are PwC, Deloitte for specialist M&A agents, and, most recently, a partnership with BDO.

The AI platform, co-headquartered in London and New York, crossed the $1bn (£748m) valuation mark and raised more than $100m in its first 18 months.

Like the consultancy sector, the platform takes a page from their book and goes into clients’ offices to ‘understand the business as a whole’.

“We’re not just a vendor, but we’re really an extension of their team,” Sehgal said. He also noted that, for such a risk-averse industry as consultancy, “like in any relationship, whether that’s personal or professional, trust is earned over time.”

    Burnham should be praised for his longer-term thinking, but how much use is a 10-year plan with only 2½ years to execute it, asks Eliot Wilson

    From the time of his election as Leader of the Labour Party, Andy Burnham has shown himself comfortable in thinking about public policy in broad terms and over a long time frame. When he accepted the leadership, he referred to “four decades of the neoliberalism that began in the 1980s”; as a lifelong politician, unlike his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, he can reach back to his teens to place himself in the Labour tribe.

    When he made his first speech as Prime Minister in July, outside 10 Downing Street, it reflected this sense of the longue durée, a desire to think strategically rather than a Starmerite desperation to reach the weekend unscathed: “Later this year, I will bring forward a new plan for Britain, a 10-year plan, laying out a path from where we are now to where I believe we all want Britain to be, wherever we’re coming from, whatever party we support.”

    It reeked, of course, of the genially authoritarian assumption that there is a place “we all want Britain to be”, a certainty that his vision is so universal and benevolent that it must be the ambition of every voter. The Prime Minister might want to reflect on whether “we all” want the United Kingdom to be a member of the European Union, for example. Still, politicians are often criticised for short-termism, so there is something refreshing about a leader crafting a “10-year plan”, even if it does invoke the language of tractor production and grain harvests.

    A 10-year plan already delayed

    Last week, however, talking to The New Statesman, Burnham admitted the plan was behind schedule: “We may go into the new year, to be honest … December or January, I think we will need to leave that open.”

    You might question why a 10-year plan could take six months merely to draft, and roll your eyes at Burnham’s casual “we will need to leave that open”. Just as Starmer’s administration seemed incapable of producing any major policy document on time – the Industrial Strategy, the National Security Strategy, the Defence Investment Plan – so too the Burnham government seems to have staked out a position for long-term residence on the back foot.

    With the 10-year plan, though, there are additional factors of timing. Let us assume, for the purposes of argument, that it is published at the very beginning of 2027. The next general election must be held on or before 15 August 2029. So what Burnham will be offering is not so much a 10-year plan as a 2½-year plan with IOUs. It is a constitutional maxim that Parliament cannot bind its successors: no law can be made which is irrevocable. One of the elements of parliamentary sovereignty is that parliament may do as it wishes – it could legislate tomorrow to say that fair is foul, and foul is fair – but the next parliament could enshrine the opposite in statute.

    Burnham’s boldness should be praised

    It would be absurdly restrictive to say that no politician could talk about his or her intentions or objectives beyond the last theoretical date for the next general election. But anything after that is contingent, and when three-quarters of Burnham’s 10-year plan could fall within that category of contingency, it prompts questions about the usefulness of the whole affair.

    It is not as if Burnham lacks ambition. Like Sir Keir Starmer, he wants to “rewire” the British state. He promised to “make this moment a circuit breaker for Britain, bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years” and spoke of “a new political model and a new economic model”. This includes “put[ting] life’s essentials back under stronger public control to make them affordable”, which seems to be a slightly milquetoast formulation for “nationalisation”, and “re-industrialising Britain, using public procurement to back British industry”.

    These are major changes in policy and, while they may horrify anyone with any attachment to free markets and the dynamism and innovation of the private sector, voters are entitled to know more about the government’s plans. With so much of its strategy likely to be in effect a promissory note, and facing an electorate which now no longer just suspects but assumes that politicians are lying, the government runs the risk of its plan echoing St Augustine’s plea for chastity: re-industralise me, o Lord, but not yet.

    How a 10-year plan could work

    One of (at least) two courses of action could have ameliorated this problem. The first would have been an early general election: there is absolutely no constitutional requirement for a new prime minister to go to the polls immediately, there is no personal mandate, and in post-War history only Sir Anthony Eden in 1955 and Boris Johnson in 2019 have done so. But the option was there, if Burnham had wanted a sense of public endorsement for a change of direction. He seems to have chosen not to, and choices have consequences.

    The alternative would have been producing perhaps a shorter, higher level document in a much shorter timeframe. Burnham became Prime Minister on 20 July; if some kind of plan or mission statement had been ready for Parliament returning from the summer adjournment on 1 September, that could have bought him some breathing space and a sense of engagement. It would not have given him much time to prepare, but no-one imagines he had not considered the premiership for some time before. The American Declaration of Independence was drafted over about 17 days, while the modern Constitution of Japan took nine.

    Trust is a vital part of the political process and currently in very short supply. Burnham’s leisurely amble towards a 10-year plan risks making a potentially pointless document misleading or malign. It is good that politicians think over the longer term to produce more coherent policy, but that should not expand the thinking time in proportion. Across the board, the government needs to speed up.

    Eliot Wilson is a writer and historian. He is a senior fellow for national security at the Coalition for Global Prosperity and a contributing editor at Defence on the Brink

    We are the world’s leading financial centre, our workforce has grown by 25 per cent to almost 700,000 jobs, and EU banks are doing 60 per cent more business with UK institutions than they did prior to the referendum.

    Now, it will be for the politicians to determine what form this new relationship takes. What the City wants to see is a new relationship that unlocks more investment, supports innovation, strengthens sustainability and delivers prosperity.

    Both sides recently ratified the Kensington Treaty, the first ever legally binding bilateral treaty between the UK and Germany, with the aim of promoting prosperity, growth and innovation in both countries. The City of London strongly welcomes this important agreement and we encourage both sides to use it to further deepen our ambitious cooperation.

    The UK-EU Summit on 20 November provides an opportunity to turn political goodwill into practical economic gains between the UK and all of the EU. Financial and related professional services belong high up on the agenda. 

    Mutual recognition of professional qualifications would make it easier for businesses to access talent. Greater certainty around data arrangements would support digital trade and innovation. And closer regulatory cooperation could reduce unnecessary duplication and make cross-border investment easier, while maintaining high standards and ensuring financial stability.

    London can provide the capital Europe needs. Our financial markets give European companies access to international investors, while our expertise in areas such as insurance, technology and sustainable finance can support projects across the continent.

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

]]> Agility’s 284-pound Digit 5 runs for 90 minutes and recharges in nine, a 10-to-1 work-to-charge ratio the company says can deliver more than 20 productive hours a day, with early customer access planned for the first half of 2027 https://siliconcanals.com/n-agilitys-284-pound-digit-5-runs-for-90-minutes-and-recharges-in-nine-a-10-to-1-work-to-charge-ratio-the-company-says-can-deliver-more-than-20-productive-hours-a-day-with-early-customer-access/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 19:00:38 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109721

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

What a 20-hour day actually means

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. Agility has not published an independent customer-floor validation of a Digit 5 working day yet.

Independent reporting on the launch has generally repeated the 20-hour figure as Agility’s claim rather than as a verified outcome. IEEE Spectrum’s Evan Ackerman, reviewing Digit 5, raised a broader doubt about Agility’s underlying assumption that the robot can function as what he called “a more or less effortless drop-in replacement for human labor,” noting he was not sure that had happened yet with any robot, anywhere. The one field metric that has been independently reported involves the previous generation, not Digit 5: at a GXO logistics facility, Digit 4 reportedly 98% accuracy sorting totes over more than 100,000 units, a real operational number — though it speaks to picking accuracy, a separate metric from hours worked per day.

Heavier lifts, taller reach than the last generation

Alongside the battery changes, Agility increased what Digit 5 can physically do. The robot can repeatedly lift loads of up to 50 pounds, which the company describes as a 40 percent jump over Digit 4’s payload, and it can reach items up to 7.2 feet high, up from about 5.5 feet on the previous version, according to Forbes’ coverage of the launch. Both changes target the same use case Agility has pursued since the original Digit: moving totes, boxes and cases between conveyors, shelving and pallets in warehouses and distribution centers, work currently done by human “pickers” and “stockers.”

How Digit 5 compares with Boston Dynamics’ Atlas

Agility is not the only company chasing this category, and the comparison is not entirely favorable to Digit 5 on paper. Boston Dynamics’ electric Atlas, per the same Forbes report, is rated to carry up to 66 pounds, reach 7.5 feet and run for about four hours on a hot-swappable battery pack that can be physically pulled and replaced rather than recharged in place. On payload and reach, Atlas currently claims an edge. Digit 5’s advantage is charging speed and, by extension, uptime: a fixed nine-minute recharge cycle is a different operational model than swapping battery packs, and it is the piece Agility is betting its productivity math on.

Orders, a SPAC, and a company still losing money

The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. Agility disclosed more than $300 million in multi-year customer orders for Digit 5, a figure the company itself qualifies as subject to unspecified contractual milestones being met, and it disclosed the number days after filing paperwork for a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a deal valued at roughly $2.5 billion. Regulatory filings tied to that merger show a company still far from commercial scale: Agility net sales and losses came to $1.78 million in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, against an operating loss of $140.2 million that roughly doubled year over year, and an auditor’s note flagging “substantial doubt” about its ability to continue as a going concern absent further financing.

That financial picture is the backdrop against which the hardware claims should be read; it doesn’t make them false. A company preparing to go public via SPAC has a direct financial incentive to publish its most favorable operating math right before that listing, and the $300 million order figure and 20-hour productivity claim are doing real work in that narrative, alongside more grounded facts, like Amazon’s $1.05 million purchase of five Digit units — a completed transaction, not a pipeline projection.

What 2027 actually promises customers

Agility says early customer access to Digit 5 is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability, aimed at manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators, following by the end of that year. The company also plans to extend sales into the European Union and United Kingdom alongside its existing North American base, pending regulatory approval in those markets. Those dates put Digit 5’s actual commercial debut several months out from this week’s unveiling, and every performance figure attached to the robot right now, from its 90-minute runtime to its 20-hour workday, is a specification and a projection. Still, this has not yet been measured on a customer floor.

]]> At 19, an Estonian borrowed €5,000 from his family and recruited Tallinn taxi drivers face-to-face for an app he had built because the city’s taxis were unreliable; twelve years later the company took €2.27 billion in revenue in more than 50 countries and posted its first annual profit — €920,000, a margin of four hundredths of one percent https://siliconcanals.com/n-at-19-an-estonian-borrowed-e5000-from-his-family-and-recruited-tallinn-taxi-drivers-face-to-face-for-an-app-he-had-built-because-the-citys-taxis-were-unreliable-twelve-years-later-the-company-took/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 14:00:26 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109712

An Estonian founder’s company posted its first annual net profit in 2025: €920,000 on €2.27 billion in revenue.]]>

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. The company launched as Taxify and rebranded as Bolt in March 2019, taking the name from the electric scooter service it had just launched, a signal, as the company put it at the time, that it saw the future of urban transport as electric and intended to be far more than a taxi app. Existing users didn’t have to do anything; the new name and logo simply appeared the next time they opened the app.

From a taxi app to a five-line business

What Bolt actually is today looks very different from what Villig built in 2013. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. Micromobility came earlier, e-scooters in Paris from September 2018 and e-bikes from mid-2020, and by early 2023 had grown into roughly 250,000 shared vehicles across 260 cities in 25 countries. Bolt Drive, a car-sharing service, launched in Tallinn in May 2021 and has since spread to Latvia, Lithuania, Germany, Poland, Czechia and Portugal. Bolt Market, a grocery-delivery arm launched the same year, has partnered with the robotics company Starship Technologies on autonomous sidewalk delivery in parts of the Baltics.

A decade of growth without a profit

None of that expansion was cheap, and for most of Bolt’s history it wasn’t profitable either. The company pushed early and aggressively into markets Uber had mostly ignored or arrived in late, establishing itself in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria as early as 2016, and it now operates in more than 850 cities across over 50 countries spanning Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America, with more recent entries into Dubai (December 2024) and the Toronto area (February 2025).

Investors funded that land grab at increasing valuations: Bolt crossed $1 billion, and unicorn status, in May 2018 after a $175 million round led by Daimler, according to TechCrunch’s coverage, then climbed to $2 billion by March 2021, $4.75 billion five months later, and $8.4 billion by January 2022.

Revenue kept climbing through all of it. Profit didn’t.

As recently as 2024, the company’s operating loss was €87.7 million even as revenue grew, a pattern common among ride-hailing and delivery platforms still spending to win market share rather than to defend one already won.

Who was willing to fund a decade of losses

Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. The largest of those rounds closed in January 2022: $709 million, co-led by Sequoia Capital and Fidelity Management and Research, with Whale Rock, D1, G Squared and several other funds also participating, valuing the company at $8.4 billion, according to TechCrunch’s coverage of the round.

That changed with the 2025 financial year. Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

That per-capita figure is a calculation built on CB Insights’ data, not a ranking CB Insights itself publishes, and it is worth reading as a proxy for the ecosystem’s density rather than a formal league table.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. Two decades later, in 2014, the government extended the same instinct outward with e-Residency, a digital identity scheme that lets people anywhere in the world register and run an Estonian company online, without granting them any right to actually live there. Neither programme produced a unicorn by itself. What they produced was a population that treated computers as ordinary tools a generation before most of Europe did, and a legal and administrative system built to let a small number of people start companies with very little friction.

The first of the ten billion-dollar companies was Skype, built in Tallinn in 2003. Its founders, the Swede Niklas Zennström and the Dane Janus Friis, co-founded the company with three Estonian engineers, Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu and Jaan Tallinn, who built the software behind what was then an unusually good way to make free voice calls over the internet. eBay bought the company two years later for a reported $2.6 billion in upfront cash and stock (total consideration including later earn-outs was reported as high as $4.1 billion).

Skype itself has since been folded into Microsoft and no longer exists as a standalone business, but it left something behind in Tallinn that the other nine companies on the list arguably needed first: a generation of engineers and early employees who had already helped build something that scaled to hundreds of millions of users, and who knew, from direct experience, that it could be done from Estonia rather than London or Silicon Valley.

The clearest example of that inheritance is Wise. Its co-founder Taavet Hinrikus was Skype’s first employee; his eventual co-founder, Kristo Käärmann, worked at Deloitte in London. Both were Estonians living abroad with an ordinary, irritating problem: Hinrikus was paid in euros but lived in the UK, and Käärmann was paid in pounds but had a mortgage back in Estonia in euros. That pattern, alumni from one successful company seeding the next, is common in tech clusters generally, but it is unusually visible in a country as small as Estonia, where the total pool of experienced software engineers was never large to begin with, and where a handful of Skype veterans and their networks touch a disproportionate share of what came after. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. Annus died in 2020, but the firm he helped start is still one of the more active early-stage investors operating out of Tallinn, another channel through which Skype’s original payout kept funding whatever came next.

The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. What the density figure doesn’t tell you

A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. What the figure does capture, reliably, is how much outsized technology output a small population has produced relative to its size, whatever has happened to any individual company since, and how much of that output traces back to a single, now-defunct voice-calling app and the state’s own earlier bet on wiring its classrooms. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

The part of Vinted’s model that isn’t obvious from the outside is that listing and selling on the platform costs a seller nothing. An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Where the tiredness comes from

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.

A pair of speakers, two years old, is up for sale online. When no music is playing, they give off an annoying static noise, and the listing does not say so.

A buyer’s message ends with a pointed question: “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” In one of the experiments built around that exact question, 85 percent of sellers mentioned the noise, and fewer buyers than that expected their seller to mention a problem.

Shira Garber and three colleagues staged a string of these secondhand sales online across five main studies and a pilot, added a second pilot that surveyed people about what drives negotiators, and reported the results in an open-access paper in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin this July. Buyers, they found, often underestimated how honest sellers would be. Sellers also reported more concern with being honest, fair and kind, and less concern with the money, than buyers credited them with.

How often did sellers come clean?

In each of the five main studies, some participants played sellers of a secondhand device with a defect they had been told about: an iPod whose battery drained fast, an electric scooter with a faulty battery, the speakers with the static. The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

In the first four studies, a seller counted as honest only if a reply named the defect. Staying quiet counted as dishonest, and so did a dodge like a battery that “isn’t brand new.”

The first pilot set the pattern. Of 76 online workers playing sellers, 63.2 percent picked a truthful opening message over one describing the iPod as being in excellent condition. Of 85 observers given the same information, 43.5 percent predicted the truthful one.

In Study 1, the 176 sellers wrote their own replies to “What can you tell me about it?” and “Anything else?” Of those sellers, 51.7 percent disclosed the battery problem, while the 270 buyers guessed, on average, that 43.2 percent would. With the scooter and a direct question in Study 2, three quarters of sellers disclosed the fault.

The rate swung with the setup. One cause, a direct question, got its own test; other swings the researchers could not fully explain. Until the last study, the exchanges were also largely scripted, with sellers answering pre-written buyer messages rather than a live counterpart.

The way the question is asked

Study 3, with 483 participants, gave half the sellers the pointed “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” and half the open “What can you tell me about them?” Buyers here were not told about the static, which is closer to how a real listing works.

The direct question made sellers more likely to mention the noise. Buyers’ predictions did not move with it.

The gap between expected and actual honesty was statistically significant under the direct question and not under the open one, so even inside this paper it did not show up everywhere. Of several possible reasons Study 1 still found a gap with open questions, the authors single out one: sellers there had two chances to come clean, and concealing twice may weigh more on a seller’s conscience than concealing once.

A few minutes of small talk

Study 5 was the only one that paired people live. It matched 422 participants into 211 buyer-seller pairs on an online platform, and some pairs first spent three minutes chatting about something they had enjoyed recently or how they unwind after a busy day.

Across the study, buyers rated their seller’s likely honesty at 6.56 on a ten-point scale, while coders scored the sellers’ actual replies at 7.51. Among pairs who chatted first, that difference was no longer statistically significant. Sellers’ scores did not differ significantly between the two conditions. The chat raised buyers’ expectations of honesty instead.

Study 4 tried a different nudge on 358 participants. Some buyers were asked about the seller’s moral concerns before predicting, others afterward. Thinking about the seller’s conscience first raised buyers’ expectations, and the gap was nearly halved.

It did not close. The authors suggest one reason: 85 percent of sellers in that study disclosed, a rate higher than in the matching condition of Study 3 for reasons they say are not readily apparent.
