The post OPINION: Long sales cycles could be FinTech’s biggest competitive advantage appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Any FinTech founder raising in the UK this year will have seen the numbers – according to KPMG’s Pulse of FinTech, investment fell to €2.1 billion (£1.8 billion) in the first half of 2026, down around two-thirds on the same period last year and the lowest since the report began in 2016. Deal count hit a ten-year low. The capital that is still moving is going to AI, and within AI it is going to where the results can be seen fastest. 

Alongside the numbers runs a story: AI has collapsed the sales cycle. Products that used to take a year to sell now close much more quickly, and founders who can’t match the pace should question whether they are building the right thing, or building it in the right country.

For anyone selling into regulated financial services, the story is a little different. Worse, believing the first version of the story is one of the fastest ways to put a good company out of business. Rather than being an issue, the long sales cycle is one of the few things in this market that is a strength and cannot be copied in other industries. 

What a sale actually looks like

Here is what selling AI to a mortgage network, a wealth manager or an advice firm actually involves. It means integrations into systems that were not built with an innovative AI provider in mind. It means lengthy security reviews, several boards and committees, each on its own calendar. It takes several internal sponsors, who need to be won over separately and who do not all agree with each other. You also need trust in the system, trust in the output, and the certifications to prove it, from the usual ISOs through to the new AI equivalent, ISO/IEC 42001.

In the UK at least, the procurement cycle has not sped up. Regulated financial services firms are accountable to the FCA for what their systems decide, a point the regulator’s own Mills Review made quite plainly this summer, and in compliance much of the work is straight-through: a file review or a financial promotions check is either right or it is a regulatory problem. A highly regulated product, with many integrations, that has to pass several boards and several sponsors, moves as slowly as it always has. The sales cycle is long, and that is fine and normal.

Founders arriving with consumer expectations miss this. They hear about the fastest sales cycle in AI without noticing that the companies telling that story are B2C, or B2B businesses that behave like B2C. The lesson travels but the conditions do not.

Surprise is what kills a startup, not the cycle

A long cycle only becomes dangerous when it is a surprise. If a founder expects deals to close in weeks and sizes their future round, their hiring plan and their investor conversations around that timeline, the business can find itself in real trouble by month nine, with nothing closed and no fault in the product. If the cycle is a known quantity from day one, it is simply a parameter to design around.

Designing around it means a few unglamorous things. Size rounds so the money lasts through more than one full cycle. Hire people who have sold into regulated institutions before and know that a fourth meeting with the risk committee is normal rather than a warning sign. Set investor expectations before the term sheet, not after the first missed quarter – and get the certifications done early, because the security review will ask for them either way.

Our investors describe the length of our sales cycle as a moat, and they are right. The entrants it protects against are the naive ones, and in this market they are usually people from inside the industry – they have very good product knowledge, a real understanding of the problem yet no experience of how running a startup works. They build something credible, start selling, and run out of money before the first contract lands. The technology can be copied and the domain knowledge is widely held. Being set up to wait is the hardest thing to copy, because it has to be built into the funding, the hiring and the expectations from the beginning.

Build in the slow lane, and build it here

The other conclusion founders are drawing from the funding numbers is that conditions will be better in the US and while for some companies it is, for others it would be wise to question what they are actually aiming to build before making that move. The most compliance in the world is in Europe, not America: the most demanding regulators, the most complex rulebooks, and the customers with the strongest reason to buy. Leaving the market where your problem is most prominent, because the deals there take longer, is a strange trade. The US may not be the answer for everyone.

The slow lane has three things going for it. There are fewer competitors, because most cannot afford to wait and many of those that do try, fail. The customers you win stay, because a firm that has just spent a year taking you through three committees has no appetite to repeat the exercise with someone else. And the market rewards the one thing that is hard to fake: a company designed, from its first round, to survive the wait.

FinTech is not dying. Parts of it are, but companies using AI to do work that firms could not do before are growing quickly but selling slowly. The nine-month deal is not a flaw in regulated FinTech. It is the entry fee, and the founders still standing in two years will have paid this on purpose. 

The post OPINION: Long sales cycles could be FinTech’s biggest competitive advantage appeared first on EU-Startups.

The post SWISSto12 and UNIVITY work together to build sovereign 5G infrastructure in space appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Swiss SpaceTech startup SWISSto12 and French startup UNIVITY are advancing Europe’s ambitions for sovereign satellite communications after successfully completing a Critical Design Review (CDR) for two active antenna systems designed to deliver 5G connectivity from space.

The milestone brings the companies closer to demonstrating broadband and direct-to-device connectivity through a single satellite architecture, combining European satellite manufacturing expertise with a homegrown approach to space-based telecommunications infrastructure.

The collaboration brings together two startups that have attracted significant investment in 2026.

Switzerland-based SWISSto12 secured €73 million in January from European Space Agency member states for its HummingSat programme, and then closed a €61 million Series C in July. While Paris-based UNIVITY raised €27 million in April from Blast, Expansion, the Deeptech 2030 fund managed by Bpifrance on behalf of the French State, and two family offices.

Emile de Rijk, CEO and founder of SWISSto12, says: “UNIVITY set us an ambitious schedule; reaching Critical Design Review in less than one year was possible due to SWISSto12’s proprietary and differentiated payload and antenna technology and a vertically integrated delivery model. It’s a significant milestone for the program and the start of the next phase as we move into hardware production and an extensive verification and acceptance campaign.”

Founded in 2011 by Emile de Rijk as a spin-off from his doctoral research at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne (EPFL), SWISSto12 specialises in satellite payloads, antenna systems and compact geostationary satellites, using proprietary manufacturing technologies including 3D printing. UNIVITY, founded in 2022 by Charles Delfieux and previously known as Constellation Technologies & Operations, is developing a Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) satellite constellation designed to enable telecom operators to extend their existing 5G services into space.

At the centre of their collaboration are two active phased-array antennas being developed by SWISSto12 for UNIVITY’s 5G non-terrestrial network (NTN) demonstration satellites. The first, an S-band direct radiating array, is designed to connect standard 5G smartphones directly to satellites. The second, a Ka-band antenna operating at 26 GHz, will support broadband services and feeder links connecting satellites with terrestrial infrastructure.

By integrating both capabilities into a single satellite, UNIVITY aims to enable telecom operators to provide broadband and direct-to-device services under their own brands, complementing existing terrestrial networks rather than replacing them.

The development forms part of UNIVITY’s uniShape programme, supported by France 2030 and the French Space Agency (CNES). The programme aims to demonstrate high-throughput, low-latency 5G connectivity using VLEO satellites, with the longer-term objective of developing a shared, neutral space infrastructure that enables European and international telecom operators to maintain greater control over their connectivity services.

For SWISSto12, the partnership puts its HummingLink antenna and payload technologies to work on a European connectivity project. The company manufactures passive radiating antenna components through 3D printing, integrating miniaturised, low-loss filters with beamforming electronics and digital controls. Design and manufacturing are carried out at its Swiss facilities, providing a vertically integrated process from technical specifications through to finished hardware.

Completing the Critical Design Review means the antenna designs can now progress towards hardware production, verification and acceptance testing. While the milestone does not yet demonstrate operational connectivity in orbit, it represents a step towards validating a satellite architecture capable of supporting two different 5G services simultaneously.

Charles Delfieux, Chief Executive Officer of UNIVITY, adds: “Active antennas are central to our 5G payload architecture: they will enable a single satellite to deliver both broadband and direct-to-device connectivity. This dual capability is essential to our ambition of providing telecom operators with a shared space-based infrastructure that complements their terrestrial networks. By reaching this milestone in less than a year, SWISSto12 has demonstrated its ability to support our ambitious roadmap for the uniShape program.”

Their collaboration comes amid broader investment activity across Europe’s SpaceTech sector. In October 2026, EU-Startups highlighted financing announcements exceeding €1.3 billion across a selected group of European companies, including €450 million in primary financing for Finland’s ICEYE and €387 million for Germany’s The Exploration Company.

Investment has also reached smaller startups developing technologies essential to future space operations. Switzerland’s Stellar Alpina raised €3.8 million to develop propulsion systems for in-space mobility, while France’s ArcSpace secured more than €2 million to advance technologies for satellite servicing and repair.

Against this backdrop, the SWISSto12–UNIVITY collaboration illustrates how European startups can combine specialised technologies to develop more independent space infrastructure. Rather than relying on a single company to manufacture satellites, develop payloads and operate connectivity services, their partnership brings together complementary capabilities across borders.

Their progress could help establish whether Europe can turn its growing investment in SpaceTech into infrastructure that provides greater technological and commercial autonomy.

The post SWISSto12 and UNIVITY work together to build sovereign 5G infrastructure in space appeared first on EU-Startups.

The post Jülich-based SRTD Biotech secures €31.5 million to develop precision mRNA therapies targeting diseased cells appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> SRTD Biotech, a Jülich-based BioTech startup focused on developing next-generation precision mRNA therapeutics, has completed an oversubscribed €31.5 million Seed financing round.

The funding was led by Mérieux Equity Partners, with NRW.BANK and Boehringer Ingelheim Venture Fund joining the syndicate as co-leads. Lilly Ventures, HTGF, and the Freiburg-based family Office Anobis Asset also participated in the Seed round.

“We believe SRTD Biotech has the potential to redefine what is possible with mRNA therapeutics. Its highly differentiated technology addresses one of the key challenges facing the field today: achieving precise, selective therapeutic activity while limiting effects on healthy cells. 

“Having worked closely with the company to strengthen its strategy, build its leadership team and establish a scalable platform, we are delighted to lead this financing with our Mérieux Innovation 2 fund (MI2) alongside an exceptional group of investors,” said Kristin Thompson, Director at Mérieux Equity Partners. 

Founded in 2019 in Jülich by Dr. Bernd Hoffmann and Dr Heribert Bohlen, SRTD has developed an approach to cell-specific messenger RNA (mRNA) expression using intracellular RNA disease markers that activate the mRNA expression exclusively within target cells.

The company notes that these selectively expressed RNA (seRNA) constructs enable the controlled expression of therapeutic payloads within diseased cells, while minimising exposure in healthy tissue.

With this novel approach, SRTD plans to create safer, more effective, and differentiated RNA therapies that overcome limitations of non-selective mRNA expression and the constraints of targeting cell-surface proteins. 

SRTD is an integrated RNA therapeutics company combining three technology platforms: proprietary seRNA technology; a novel fusogenic LNP delivery platform to access the liver, lung, brain, and other organs; and a synthetic biology platform with bioinformatics and AI-driven RNA design capabilities. This integrated technology platform provides an end-to-end solution for generating differentiated RNA therapies across a wide range of therapeutic areas and indications.

After the financing round, Matthias Alder was appointed SRTD’s Chief Executive Officer. He has held senior C-suite roles (including CEO, COO and CBO) at publicly traded BioTech companies in the US and Europe. 

“The proceeds will enable SRTD to advance Bernd’s vision of delivering safe, effective, and differentiated RNA therapeutics to patients whose diseases remain inadequately addressed by current therapies,” said Alder.

Along with Matthias Alder, Dr. Heinz Koeppl has joined SRTD’s leadership team as the company’s Chief Technology Officer and the founder of SRTD’s synthetic biology platform. He is also a professor at the Technische Universität Darmstadt and the director of its Centre for Synthetic Biology. 

Together with Dr. Hoffmann, Dr. Koeppl will lead the scientific strategy of SRTD, with a particular focus on RNA marker identification and AI-based construct optimisation to ensure the selective and efficient activation of seRNA constructs.

Most recently, Dr. Jens Hennecke joined the executive leadership team of SRTD as its Chief Business Officer. He is responsible for driving business development and strategy, seeking to leverage the company’s platform through R&D collaborations in therapeutic areas and indications beyond SRTD’s own product pipeline.

“SRTD Biotech shows how cutting-edge research from North Rhine-Westphalia can open up new ways to treat many diseases with significant unmet medical needs. Bringing innovations like these from research into medical practice takes capital. With our investment in SRTD Biotech, we are helping a highly innovative company develop a promising new technology in NRW and scale it internationally from here,” Johanna Antonie Tjaden-Schulte, Member of NRW.BANK’s Managing Board. 

NRW.BANK is participating in SRTD Biotech’s financing round through its NRW.Venture EU Tech&Scale fund. Under its InvestEU partnership, a guarantee agreement with the European Commission enables the Düsseldorf-based bank to invest a total of up to €200 million in additional funding in young scale-ups through the fund.

]]> Every startup faces the same squeeze: big ambitions, small team and limited budget. Free open-source software, which can be used, modified, and redistributed under its license, can help founders ease the squeeze. It lets a small startup build products that once required a large engineering department.

But a shortcut is not a strategy. To make good use of open source, founders must decide what they should build themselves, what to borrow, and which skills their team needs to retain. Here is what to consider, from saving time and standing out to staying secure and talking to investors.

Saving time

Microsoft’s Edge browser shows how this can work. I co-authored a study of its move to Chromium, the open-source engine also behind Google’s Chrome, found faster releases and closer alignment with Chrome’s supported web features. Edge remained Microsoft’s own product, on a shared foundation. For founders, the question is how much development work a shared foundation can save, and what trade-offs come with it.

Artificial intelligence offers a similar shortcut. Free toolkits such as TensorFlow and PyTorch help developers build AI applications. “Open-weight” models, such as Meta’s Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen, let teams download an AI system that has already been trained and adapt it, rather than start from scratch.

But open-weight does not necessarily mean open source. Founders should read the license carefully: downloading a model does not necessarily provide access to its training data or unrestricted rights to sell products built on it.

Before committing, startups should build a small prototype around a real customer task. A polished demo can hide missing features, thin documentation or fiddly integration work. Founders should also factor in the costs of computing power and upkeep. Access to the code lets teams tailor software or run it in a customer’s own systems, provided they have the skills and resources to manage it.

Standing out

If competitors can use the same technology, a startup needs to give customers a reason to choose its product. That might mean specialist features, smoother links with the systems customers already use, or reliable support. Founders can use the development time saved to find out what customers value enough to pay for.

Take an AI tool for manufacturers. It could pair a widely available model with a factory’s equipment records and tests designed around how engineers work. Tying the technology to a real job can make a product useful even when the model underneath is available to everyone.

Some companies make money from their own open code. Strapi, a French startup, offers a free content management system and charges for extra features and support. Founders who publish their code need to be equally clear about what customers pay for. They also need to allow time for users’ questions, documentation and outside contributions.

Keeping expertise in-house

Startups need staff who understand how the product works and can change it. In research I led on German firms, I found that product innovation was strongest among companies that outsourced a moderate amount of IT work. In related research I co-authored, we found that excessive reliance on outsourcing raises the risk of intellectual-property infringement.

The practical question for founders is which skills they need to retain as they draw on outside work. Early choices can become expensive to reverse. A team learns one framework; data takes on its format, and other parts of the product grow around it.

Before the business relies on a critical component, the team should test how easily it could be replaced. Design decisions and the ability to investigate failures should stay within the team. When working with outside developers, founders should agree who owns the work and what stays confidential.

Engineers also need time to experiment. If all their effort goes into stitching together other people’s software, they may struggle to build the know-how needed for the startup’s next product.

Maintenance and security

Joining an open-source community can help a startup’s developers learn. Research on larger companies found that contributors got more value from using open source, partly through feedback from other developers.

An active community can help spot and fix problems, but security still needs an owner inside the startup. 

The Open-Source Security Foundation advises tracking outside components, checking their origins and maintenance, and monitoring newly discovered vulnerabilities. Someone within the startup should be responsible for testing and installing updates.

Some popular projects rely on a single volunteer. Paid support may be worthwhile for critical components, while startups publishing their own code also need time for handling security reports and maintaining new versions.

Making the case to investors

Founders should show what the head start delivered, whether they have a working product, paying customers, or evidence of demand. They should explain what they didn’t have to build because they used open source, and what they developed themselves.

Our study found that US startups that engaged with outside projects on GitHub, a popular code-sharing site, were more likely to have raised their first funding round. The link was stronger for novel technologies and weaker in crowded markets. However, the research does not imply that publishing open source code alone will win over investors.

Founders should be ready to explain their own contribution to the product, the cost of maintaining it and how they would manage problems with a critical dependency. The test is whether open source helps them build something customers value while leaving the team able to maintain and improve it.

]]> Calogena, a French nuclear startup developing a small modular reactor (SMR) designed to supply low-carbon heat to district heating networks, has secured €40 million.

The funding came in the form of a grant from the European Commission’s Innovation Fund ,and it marks the first time that European funding has been given to an SMR earmarked for the direct construction of a commercial facility.

“This funding marks a major milestone for Calogena. Having developed our technology and brought it to industrial scale, we are now entering the construction phase of our first commercial reactor,” said Julien Dereux, Executive Chairman of Calogena.

Calogena was founded in 2021 as a subsidiary of Groupe Gorgé, a Paris-based high-tech industrial group with approximately 3,500 employees and €600 million in revenue. The company is developing a 30-thermal-megawatt, water-cooled SMR specifically designed to decarbonise district heating networks.

Its reactor is based on pool-type research reactor technology, a design proven in hundreds of installations worldwide. It operates at low temperature (100°C) and low pressure (6 bar), less than a bicycle tyre, making it simpler and safer to operate than conventional power reactors.

Another strength of Calogena’s SMR is its compact footprint, requiring just 3,000 square metres of land and under 1,000 square metres of building. The design also does not require major water or electricity supply, and refuelling requires only one lorry delivery every two years. Each module can supply heat to around 20,000 households and produces less than 80ml of nuclear water over a lifetime of use.

The grant follows more than €50 million already secured under France’s national industrial strategy programme, France 2030, which helped the company develop its technology and bring it to industrial readiness. 

The €40 million grant will be used to fund the construction of Calogena’s first commercial reactor in Pierrelatte, which would serve as the company’s inaugural commercial reference project. The company says the town will receive locally produced, low-carbon heat, an alternative to the carbon-intensive and largely imported energy sources that currently account for nearly one-third of Europe’s total energy demand. 

“The European Commission’s support confirms the maturity of our project and its potential to address one of Europe’s major energy challenges: producing local, low-carbon, cost-competitive heat at scale while strengthening energy sovereignty. Pierrelatte would be our first commercial reference and should pave the way for wider deployment across Europe,” added Dereux.

In addition to the Pierrelatte project, the company is also pursuing projects across Europe and is in contention to supply more than fifteen reactors in Finland, where it opened a subsidiary in 2025. In June, Calogena signed a cooperation agreement with Veolia, a European leader in district heating, to explore the deployment of its SMRs across Central and Eastern Europe.

As the European district heating market is projected to reach around 1,000 TWh by 2050, Calogena argues that its technology can provide a price-stable, long-term solution for energy sovereignty. It is targeting initial deployments from 2030, with its first commercial reactor in Pierrelatte scheduled to go live in 2032.

Marble highlighted that although VHR imagery is a core input for security and commercial intelligence, Europe and many of its partners rely on non-European providers. “This makes them vulnerable to being cut off from coverage over key areas of interest, as materialised in Ukraine or the Strait of Hormuz, creating massive economic as well as security knowledge gaps,” it stated. 

Marble is therefore setting up Germany’s first commercial constellation of very-high-resolution (VHR) satellites. The German startup is also building an AI-powered analytics platform that converts multi-source data into insights. ]]> Airbus has claimed the world record for the longest flight by a commercial airliner, snatching the accolade from competitor Boeing after two decades.

The record was set by the Airbus A350-1000ULR, a specific variant of its flagship widebody aircraft developed for Qantas, to allow the Aussie airline to fly directly from Sydney to London and New York. To make such ultra-long flights possible, Airbus added an extra fuel tank, giving it a published range of around 10,000 nautical miles (nm).

But the world record-setting flight substantially exceeded this range, clocking in at over 12,500 nm and unseating Boeing’s 777-200LR ‘Worldliner’ as the longest flight by distance by a commercial airliner.

Airbus A350-1000ULR goes the long way round to set a new record

The record-breaking flight took place between 27 and 28 July this year, and saw the A350-1000ULR depart Melbourne and fly to Toulouse. A direct flight would cover around 9,100 nm – a long flight indeed, but not enough to break any records.

In order to go the distance, Airbus opted to travel the long way round, crossing two oceans in the process.

Leaving Melbourne on the afternoon of 27 July, the aircraft flew over Sydney and headed across the Pacific, crossing the international date line. It passed by Los Angeles and crossed the American continent before heading across its second ocean: the Atlantic.

From there, the flight headed south, crossing the UK and landing in Toulouse in the morning of 28 July. Airbus added that the 13 people onboard got to witness two sunrises and two sunsets during the journey.

The flight took a total of 24 hours and 24 minutes, and covered a distance of 12,503 nm. Airbus said the flight was part of the test campaign for the A350-1000ULR, which Qantas had requested be tested with a block time of 23 hours to simulate the very longest commercial operations it could face.

The official Guinness World Record for the longest flight by distance by a commercial airliner was announced on 9 November, and is based on aircraft data independently validated by the International Aeronautical Federation and Flightradar24.

Airbus A350 unseats the mighty Boeing 777

The previous record for the longest flight by distance by a commercial airliner was set 21 years ago, in November 2005.

Between 9 and 10 November 2005, Boeing flew its 777-200LR ‘Worldliner’ from Hong Kong to London. Like Airbus, it went the long way round the globe to give it the space for the demonstration. In all, the aircraft covered 11,664 NM nonstop before landing at Heathrow.

The flight took 22 hours and 42 minutes, and had a representative of the US National Aeronautic Association on board to monitor the attempt. Guinness representatives met the aircraft in London.

Boeing has previously held the record with the 747 and its 777-200ER. Airbus, too, had the crown for a while with its A340-200.

Why Airbus has made a plane that can fly for 24 hours

Located a long way from most of the populated world, Qantas is no stranger to long flights. But nonstop flights from Sydney to Europe and the East Coast of the US remained out of reach.

Qantas asked Airbus to develop a widebody aircraft that would be capable of routes like Sydney to London and New York.

Airbus answered that challenge with the A350-1000ULR. It had already developed a longer-range version of the smaller A350-900 for Singapore Airlines, which currently operates the world’s longest scheduled flights from Singapore to the New York area. It’s also stretched the range of its popular narrowbody A321neo into the XLR, and was well placed to do this again with its biggest aircraft.

The A350-1000ULR has an additional rear centre fuel tank which provides around 20,000 litres of extra capacity. Coupled with that is an upgraded maximum takeoff weight (MTOW), allowing it to carry the extra fuel. Airbus says this adds around 1,000 nm to the A350-1000’s range.

Alongside changes to the fuelling, the aircraft has a new lighter galley cooling system, which has saved around 300 kg of carried weight. Although this was developed for the ULR specifically, Airbus plans to make it standard across the A350 family.

The manufacturer thought of the humans on board too, with revised crew rest facilities for the pilots and cabin crew who will operate these mega flights. The passenger cabin is premium-heavy and includes a wellbeing zone for stretching and standing.

]]> The four-engine transport aircraft touched down at 13,629 feet in Ladakh, demonstrating the capabilities of a newly upgraded airbase and a Soviet-era aircraft that remains central to India’s military airlift operations.

An Indian Air Force (IAF) IL-76 MD heavy transport aircraft has landed at 13,629 feet at Nyoma airbase in eastern Ladakh, setting what the service says is a world altitude record for the aircraft type and demonstrating its ability to operate from a newly upgraded runway near the Chinese border.

The landing, carried out on Friday and announced by the IAF on Saturday, marks a significant development for India’s military airlift operations in the Himalayas. Nyoma lies approximately 25 kilometres from the Line of Actual Control (LAC) with China, where maintaining reliable supplies to troops deployed in difficult mountain terrain remains a major logistical challenge.

The IAF described the landing as “a remarkable demonstration of the aircraft’s enduring capability, backed by the exceptional skill, precision, and professionalism /f its crew”.

It called the achievement “a milestone that reinforces India’s strategic airlift capability”.

The flight also demonstrated the continuing relevance of the Russian-origin IL-76, an aircraft India began operating more than four decades ago.

From a basic airstrip to a strategic airbase

Nyoma’s transformation is central to the significance of the landing.

The airstrip was reactivated in September 2009 when an IAF Antonov An-32 transport aircraft landed there. Until recently, its facilities were better suited to smaller tactical transports and helicopters than large military freighters.

Following the military confrontation with China that began in 2020, India accelerated infrastructure development across Ladakh, including roads, bridges, tunnels and airfields.

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh laid the foundation stone for Nyoma’s redevelopment in September 2023.

The Border Roads Organisation subsequently constructed a 2.7-kilometre paved runway under a project costing approximately INR 2.18 billion (approximately $23.2 million). The development included aircraft parking areas, hangars and air traffic control facilities.

The upgraded airbase was inaugurated in November 2025 when then IAF chief Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh landed a C-130J Super Hercules there.

Its runway is designed to accommodate transport aircraft, helicopters and fighter operations, considerably expanding the military’s options in eastern Ladakh.

The arrival of the IL-76 provides evidence that the upgraded facilities can handle a substantially heavier aircraft than those previously operating from the old landing ground.

Why landing at 13,629 feet is difficult

High-altitude operations present challenges even for aircraft designed to use relatively austere airfields.

At Nyoma’s elevation, the air is considerably less dense than at sea level. Aircraft wings must move through the thinner air at a higher true airspeed to generate the lift needed for flight.

That means a transport aircraft can approach the runway at a higher ground speed for the same indicated airspeed, potentially increasing the distance required to stop.

Reduced air density also affects engine performance, particularly during take-off and climb.

Crews must account for aircraft weight, temperature, wind, runway conditions and the performance margins available at the airfield.

The IL-76’s high-mounted wings, four turbofan engines and robust undercarriage were designed to support military transport operations, including from relatively demanding runways.

However, the aircraft’s published payload capability cannot automatically be assumed at Nyoma. High elevation and operating conditions can impose substantial restrictions on the weight an aircraft can safely carry.

The IAF has not disclosed the aircraft’s landing weight or cargo load during the record flight.

An earlier milestone at Daulat Beg Oldie

India has previously demonstrated high-altitude airlift capability using the American-built C-130J Super Hercules.

On 20 August 2013, an IAF C-130J landed at Daulat Beg Oldie in northern Ladakh, at an elevation of approximately 16,614 feet.

The aircraft operated from a compacted-earth landing strip near the Karakoram Pass, demonstrating the ability to deliver personnel and supplies to one of India’s most remote military outposts.

The C-130J was developed for tactical airlift operations and is equipped to operate from short, relatively austere runways.

Its four turboprop engines, high-lift wing configuration and specialised landing gear make it particularly suitable for such missions.

The distinction between the two achievements is important.

The C-130J’s landing at Daulat Beg Oldie demonstrated its ability to operate at extreme altitudes using a relatively basic airstrip. The IL-76’s landing at Nyoma is a different achievement. Unlike the smaller C-130J, the IL-76 is a heavy transport aircraft designed to carry substantially larger loads, including armoured vehicles and bulky military equipment. Operating such a large aircraft at 13,629 feet presents its own challenges because the thin mountain air affects aircraft performance.

Why India’s ageing IL-76 still matters

Known as Gajraj (King Elephant) in IAF service, the IL-76 entered India’s transport fleet in 1985, initially equipping No. 44 Squadron.

India acquired 17 aircraft between 1985 and 1989, establishing a heavy-lift capability that had previously been beyond the reach of its smaller transport fleet.

The four-engine aircraft can carry approximately 40–45 tonnes under suitable operating conditions, including military vehicles, equipment and other bulky loads.

Its rear loading ramp allows heavy cargo to be moved into the aircraft without the specialised loading arrangements required by conventional passenger aircraft.

The IL-76 has been used to transport troops, armoured vehicles and equipment to forward military areas, including Ladakh. It has also supported humanitarian assistance, disaster relief and overseas operations.

The IAF subsequently acquired Boeing C-17 Globemaster III transports, which offer greater payload capacity and modern avionics.

Nevertheless, the IL-76 remains an important part of India’s available heavy-lift capacity, particularly when multiple aircraft are required to sustain large military deployments.

Its continued service also presents growing maintenance challenges.

The ageing airframes require structural inspections, engine maintenance and a reliable supply of replacement components. Obtaining Russian-origin spares has become more difficult, with supply problems aggravated by the war in Ukraine.

India has examined extending the technical life of some IL-76 aircraft while expanding domestic maintenance and repair capabilities. Russian technical support remains important, particularly for engines and specialised systems.

Proposals to keep the fleet operational into the 2030s or beyond depend on the condition of individual aircraft, the availability of spares and the viability of further upgrades. No confirmed fleet-wide service extension into the 2040s has been established.

India is also pursuing a Medium Transport Aircraft programme as part of its longer-term effort to modernise military airlift.

]]> A Russian military transport aircraft has landed at Ben Gurion International Airport (TLV) in Israel amid growing regional tensions and concerns over the possibility of major US military strikes against Iran.

The aircraft, identified as a Tupolev Tu-154M with registration RA-85042, arrived from Chkalovsk Air Base (CKL), near Moscow, at 19:10 local time on November 8. Its arrival has attracted considerable attention, particularly given the deteriorating security environment in the Middle East and the potential risks facing foreign diplomatic missions in the region.

One possibility being discussed across social media is that the aircraft was dispatched to Israel to evacuate Russian diplomats and members of their families ahead of a possible escalation involving the United States and Iran.

However, this explanation has not been independently confirmed, and neither Moscow nor Israeli authorities have publicly established the exact purpose of the flight.

Russian military aircraft arrives from Moscow

Flight-tracking information identified the aircraft as RA-85042, a Tupolev Tu-154M operated by the Russian Ministry of Defence.

The aircraft departed Chkalovsky Air Base, a military installation in the Moscow region that serves as an important centre for Russian government and military aviation operations.

The base is regularly associated with flights transporting senior military personnel, government officials and official delegations.

Unlike conventional commercial passenger aircraft, the Tu-154M involved in the flight is associated with Russia’s government aviation infrastructure. Its appearance at one of Israel’s busiest international airports is therefore particularly noteworthy.

According to flight-tracking reports, the aircraft arrived at Ben Gurion on Sunday evening, with its landing reported at approximately 19:01 local time.

The flight was also notable because of the aircraft’s ownership and sanctions status. RA-85042 is associated with the Russian Defence Ministry’s 223rd Flight Unit, which has previously been targeted by US sanctions.

Possible evacuation of Russian diplomatic personnel

The timing of the aircraft’s arrival has prompted questions about whether Russia is preparing contingency measures for its diplomatic presence in Israel.

With the possibility of further military confrontation between Washington and Tehran dominating regional security calculations, foreign governments may be reviewing the safety of their diplomatic personnel and their families.

Russian government plane arrives at Ben Gurion and evacuates Russian diplomats and their families. https://t.co/JH8tF14Mjx

— Sprinter Report (@SprinterReport) November 9, 2026

An escalation involving large-scale US strikes against Iranian military infrastructure could potentially trigger retaliatory action across the region. Israel, given its central role in the confrontation with Iran, could face additional security risks, including missile attacks and other forms of retaliation. For Russia, maintaining the safety of its diplomatic personnel would be an important consideration.

The arrival of a dedicated government aircraft capable of transporting officials and other personnel could be consistent with an evacuation or precautionary relocation operation. However, there is currently no publicly verified passenger information confirming that Russian diplomats or their relatives were aboard.

It is also unclear whether the aircraft arrived specifically to collect passengers, whether it was transporting Russian officials to Israel, or whether the mission involved another form of diplomatic or government activity.

Aircraft involved already under US sanctions

Another interesting aspect of the flight concerns the aircraft’s sanctions history. The United States included RA-85042 among aircraft identified in its May 19, 2023, sanctions action targeting Russia’s 223rd Flight Unit.

The US Department of State accused the unit of transporting personnel and equipment associated with the Wagner Group to countries where the organisation operated.

The sanctions formed part of Washington’s broader efforts to restrict Russian government and military networks following the invasion of Ukraine.

The 223rd Flight Unit operates within the Russian Defence Ministry’s aviation structure and has been associated with transporting government representatives, military personnel and other official passengers.

The appearance of an aircraft linked to a sanctioned Russian military aviation unit at Ben Gurion Airport adds another unusual dimension to an already closely watched arrival.

Israel and Russia yet to explain the flight

Israeli authorities have so far provided little information about the aircraft’s arrival. According to reporting by The Jerusalem Post, the Israeli Defence Forces had been approached for comment, alongside the Russian Embassy and several US government bodies.

At the time of publication, no official explanation had been provided establishing the purpose of the mission. The identities of the passengers, if any, also remain unknown.

The absence of an official explanation means that the suggested diplomatic evacuation scenario must be treated cautiously. Flight-tracking data can establish an aircraft’s movement, registration and departure airport, but it cannot independently reveal the identities of those on board or the operational purpose of a government flight.

A potentially significant development

The arrival of RA-85042 comes at a particularly sensitive moment for the Middle East. Washington’s posture towards Iran, Israel’s security concerns and the possibility of a wider regional confrontation have created an increasingly uncertain environment for governments operating diplomatic missions across the region.

Russia also maintains important strategic interests in the Middle East, including its relationship with Tehran and its diplomatic channels with Israel.

Any decision by Moscow to relocate diplomatic personnel would therefore be significant, particularly if it reflected an assessment that the regional security situation was approaching a dangerous turning point.

In the meantime, the Russian Tu-154M’s arrival at Ben Gurion remains an unusual and potentially important development. Whether RA-85042 was dispatched as part of a planned evacuation of Russian diplomats and their families, a precautionary government mission, or an entirely different operation remains unconfirmed.

]]> US investigators say they have recovered parts of both engines, wings and flight control systems from the Learjet 60 that crashed in Florida on 1 November, killing all nine people on board.

Posting on X, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) shared its latest update today (8 November), confirming that parts of the wreckage have now been sent to its laboratories in Washington for further examination.

The development comes as investigators continue to try and establish why the jet, operated by Aurora Aviation under the Upper Jets name, crashed in Palm Beach County.

Which parts of the crashed Learjet 60 have been found?

The NTSB says it has found components from both wings, both engines, the flight deck, vertical stabilizer, left elevator, aileron sections and multiple flap track assemblies.

It said it had also recovered the jet’s horizontal stabilizer – this had appeared to be missing in harrowing video footage of the crash that was shared on social media. 

Last week, experts from the NTSB found part of the engine as they excavated the crash crater.

And NTSB board member Tom Chapman also confirmed at a press conference last week that three sections of the Learjet’s left elevator had been found between 1.3-3.8 miles from the crash site.

Speaking at the briefing, he said investigators are examining whether the aircraft began to break up in-flight before impact.

And he said: “Certainly it tells us that at least some components, some pieces of the aircraft, important pieces of the aircraft, separated before the impact. 

“What that means exactly in terms of what caused the aircraft to lose control, or whether the loss of this piece was a result of the forces on the aircraft, we don’t know yet.” 

The elevator moves up or down to change the aircraft’s pitch.

What investigators know so far

  • The Learjet 60 crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida, on 1 November.
  • All nine people onboard were killed.
  • Wreckage from both engines, wings and flight control systems has been recovered.
  • Parts of the aircraft were found several miles from the impact site.
  • Investigators are examining weather conditions and possible in-flight breakup.
  • No cause has been determined.

Investigation continues at crash site

In its update, the NTSB confirmed that it is still excavating the impact site.

Excavation work at the crash site began on 4 November. The NTSB revealed debris has been found away from the impact location and also on the roofs of homes and buildings near the crash site.

An unstable utility pole had to be removed before experts could access the impact crater.

Speaking at an earlier press conference, Chapman said: “I feel confident that they’re going to find the evidence that they need within that crater despite the challenges.

“I feel confident they’re going to find what they need to help put together what happened here and why it happened.”

How will investigators establish what happened to the Learjet?

Tom Chapman told the press conference on Wednesday: “What we often do is we try to lay out the aircraft in such a way that we can try to identify as much as possible the shape, the form and the location of various components that we’ve found.

“Sometimes that helps us identify something that may have occurred which may not be obvious. The force of this impact very severely damaged the remnants of this wreckage so I don’t know how realistic it is that we’re going to be able to do that, but that is a possibility in terms of the investigation as it goes forward.”

What caused the Florida Learjet 60 crash?

The Learjet was travelling from Austin, Texas to the Bahamas when the crew reported encountering icing, turbulence and precipitation before the aircraft entered a rapid descent.

The NTSB said weather conditions and evidence of an in-flight breakup are both being investigated. It has not confirmed a cause of the crash, and the investigation is ongoing.

They are also asking people to get in touch if they find parts of the jet, saying: “Recovering all available wreckage is critical to the investigation and helping to determine the cause of the crash.”

The seven passengers have been named as entrepreneur Adam Robinson, 44, his wife Helen Sharp, 40, their two children Emma, four, and Charlie, two. Also onboard was the family’s nanny Anita Maria Cetina and two family friends Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr.

The pilot has been identified as Jeff Gregory, 55, from Pennsylvania and the co-pilot as Nathalia Gadelha, 20.

]]>
Athens International Airport (AIA) is putting growth in US and other long-haul services at the forefront of its plans to strengthen the Greek capital’s position as a key European hub, with the airport expecting 2026 to be its busiest year on record. 

Passenger numbers rose 4.4% in the first nine months of the year after a record 34 million in 2025, said Ioanna Papadopoulou, the airport’s director of communications and marketing.

Speaking to Aerospace Global News at the Routes World 2026 event in Frankfurt, she said AIA was “focusing on long haul in general, but in the US in specific”, citing an increase in weekly US frequencies from 46 in 2019 to 103 in the summer of 2026. 

The airport expects Alaska Airlines to add Seattle and Delta to add Detroit in 2027, with further growth to follow. 

Terminal expansion to address capacity pressures

The expansion of the terminal is another key strand to the airport’s plans to accommodate further growth, with a phased development programme scheduled to begin in 2027 and run until 2030-31.

The first stage will concentrate on the southern, non-Schengen section of the terminal, before work moves to the northern, Schengen area. 

The investment is intended to increase capacity and improve passenger flows, particularly during the busiest periods of the day.

Papadopoulou said the airport did not currently anticipate the need for additional runway infrastructure, with its two parallel runways capable of handling traffic equivalent to more than 50 million annual passengers.

“The terminals need to grow,” she said, noting that additional aircraft gates, security screening facilities and passport-control booths were priorities.

Managing the impact of the EES system

The introduction of the European Union’s Entry/Exit System (EES), which requires biometric registration of non-EU nationals entering and leaving the Schengen area, has added to the pressure on border-control facilities.

Papadopoulou said airports across Europe had experienced bottlenecks during the summer of 2026 as the EES system was introduced, and that Athens was looking at ways to minimise any further disruption from the new checks.

“There is technology which has been introduced because of the EES, but this needs to roll out much more efficiently,” she said. “We will try as much as we can to alleviate the impact on the passenger flows.”

Several associated infrastructure projects are also under way, ahead of the main terminal expansion.

These include a multi-storey car park, scheduled for completion by early 2028, and the Northwest Apron project, which will provide additional aircraft parking positions. A new 600m² VIP terminal, intended for heads of state and other senior officials, is also due to be completed within two years.

Using technology to improve the passenger experience

Alongside physical infrastructure, Athens is looking to make greater use of technology to improve the passenger experience and understand how travellers interact with the airport.

One recent initiative involved a pilot project using artificial intelligence to assess passengers’ emotional engagement at different stages of their journey.

The trial was conducted in partnership with Canadian technology company PathosAI and was intended to provide insight into passenger perceptions.

Papadopoulou said AIA conducts surveys involving more than 40,000 passengers annually, helping the airport make informed decisions about which areas needed focusing on first.

Net-zero target achieved ahead of schedule

Papadopoulou said the achievement had been delivered despite the disruption caused by the pandemic, and put the airport significantly ahead of the aviation industry’s broader 2050 net-zero ambitions.

“We are now self-producers and self-consumers of clean energy for all the airport needs, by 100% through solar parks,” she said.

The airport is also seeking to influence emissions beyond its direct operations, particularly those generated by airlines using its facilities.

Scope 3 emissions, which include aircraft operations and other activities outside the airport operator’s direct control, are a challenge for any airport.

However, AIA has introduced a sustainability incentive scheme that offers airlines greater discounts when they use newer-generation aircraft. 

The financial benefits increase according to the age of the aircraft, with the intention of encouraging carriers to introduce more efficient fleets on services to Athens, she said.

Financial incentives to support route development

Financial incentives and direct support for airline marketing are also key to AIA’s strategy of attracting new airline, including those serving long-haul extra-European markets.

Papadopoulou said AIA’s incentive programme covered a range of operators, including new long-haul carriers, driving additional frequencies with existing airlines, and encouraging low-cost flights. 

The airport also provides marketing support to carriers, particularly those launching new operations in Athens or seeking to build their presence in the Greek market.

She said AIA works with airlines to develop and implement locally focused promotional campaigns, with the marketing budgets funded by the airport.

The incident is the latest in a series of reported departure deviations involving aircraft departing from LAX’s runway 24L.

Air France aircraft turns towards parallel departure route

Air France flight AF28, operated by A350-900 F-HUVK, took off from runway 24L at approximately 12:15 am local time, bound for Papeete in French Polynesia. American Airlines flight AA1660, operated by A321-200 N191UW, departed from runway 25R about a minute later for Dallas/Fort Worth.

A potential mid-air collision was narrowly avoided at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) on Saturday, thanks to excellent work by ATC. Air France AF028 (A350-900 F-HUVK), departing runway 24L for Papeete, began turning left. At the same time, American Airlines AA1660 (A321-200), departing runway 25R for Dallas–Fort Worth, also turned left, putting the two aircraft on conflicting flight paths as they climbed out. ATC immediately intervened, issuing instructions to both crews to turn away from each other. The aircraft reportedly came within just 400 feet vertically of one another. You can hear the pressure in the Air France crew’s voice as the controller gives them time to collect themselves and correctly read back the instructions before addressing the possible pilot deviation and providing a number to call. Excellent situational awareness from the controller.

— Turbine Traveller (@Turbinetraveler) November 8, 2026

The two runways are the inner runways of LAX’s northern and southern parallel runway pairs. Both aircraft initially departed west over the Pacific.

AF28 reportedly had the SUMMR2 standard instrument departure assigned. The FAA’s SUMMR2 departure procedure at LAX requires aircraft departing from Runways 24L/R and 25L/R to climb on a heading of 251° to 640 feet before proceeding direct to their initial assigned waypoints.

After takeoff, however, the A350 turned left towards the American Airlines aircraft’s departure path rather than continuing along its expected routing.

The American Airlines crew checked in with Southern California departure control at 2,000ft while climbing towards 5,000ft. Controllers then issued immediate instructions to both aircraft to avoid a collision.

Controller orders heading change and halts climb

In recorded ATC exchanges, the controller instructed the Air France crew to “fly heading 270 immediately”, directing the A350 westwards. Seconds later, the controller warned the American Airlines pilots of traffic at their 12 o’clock position, less than one mile away, and told them to maintain 2,000ft.

The American Airlines crew acknowledged the instruction, saying it would return to 2,000ft. The controller later cleared AA1660 to climb to 17,000ft, with a 250-knot speed restriction.

One published reconstruction of ADS-B tracking data estimated the closest horizontal separation at about 0.76 nautical miles (1.4km). According to ADS-B data published by flight-tracking company Wingbits, the aircraft were approximately 300ft apart vertically when separated by 1.6 nautical miles horizontally.

Close call at LAX on Saturday. AF028 and AA1660 took off seconds apart and both turned left on climb-out. Our ADS-B shows them about 300 ft apart vertically at 1.6 nm, with the closest pass at 0.76 nm. ATC turned them apart. Here’s what our network saw https://t.co/Myj0eKRSyt

— wingbits (@wingbits) November 8, 2026

Other flight-tracking reports estimated vertical separation at around 400ft.

These figures are preliminary and do not establish whether either aircraft received a traffic collision avoidance system resolution advisory.

Air France crew questioned about departure clearance

After the immediate conflict had passed, the controller told the Air France pilots that they had been instructed to climb via the standard instrument departure rather than turn to a heading. When asked why the aircraft had turned, the crew initially replied, “Standby.”

The controller asked the Air France pilots to confirm the departure procedure they had been instructed to fly. The pilots ultimately confirmed the SUMMR2 departure. The controller directed the aircraft towards the DART waypoint and said there was “a possible pilot deviation,” providing a telephone number for the crew to report.

Afterwards, the controller apologised to the American Airlines crew, explaining that the other aircraft had turned in front of it. The American crew responded: “Great job, thank you.”

Both AF28 and AA1660 continued safely. Neither Air France nor American Airlines had issued statements on the incident at the time of writing.

The latest close call follows two other reported departure deviations involving aircraft taking off from runway 24L at LAX. 

On 20 October 2026, a TAP Air Portugal A330-900 made an unexpected left turn shortly after departure. 

On 31 October 2025, an ITA Airways A330-900 turned towards an American Airlines A321 departing from parallel runway 25R. ADS-B data showed that the ITA Airways A330-900 and American Airlines A321 came within 0.6 nautical miles horizontally while flying at the same altitude.

]]> SpaceX is about to attempt its first Starship ‘double catch’: Here’s how it works https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/spacex-starship-double-catch-how-it-works/ Mon, 09 Nov 2026 13:16:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56105 SpaceX is preparing to catch both Starship stages on Flight 15, with the booster returning within minutes and the spacecraft more than 22 hours later.

The post SpaceX is about to attempt its first Starship ‘double catch’: Here’s how it works appeared first on AGN.

]]> SpaceX is preparing to attempt something it has never done before: return both stages of its giant Starship rocket to the launch site and catch them using mechanical arms on launch towers.

The company has set Friday, 13 November, as the earliest date for Flight 15 from Starbase, Texas, subject to regulatory approval. The 75-minute launch window opens at 16:45 Central Time.

The mission will build on SpaceX’s earlier success in catching Super Heavy boosters, but the bigger challenge will come more than 22 hours after liftoff, when the Starship upper stage returns from orbit for its first attempted tower catch.

SpaceX has previously recovered boosters using the launch tower’s giant mechanical arms, nicknamed chopsticks. Catching Starship itself would bring the company closer to its goal of making the entire rocket reusable.

Flight 15 will also carry 26 Starlink V3 satellites into orbit, combining a commercial satellite deployment with the most ambitious recovery test yet attempted under the programme.

How SpaceX plans to catch both stages

Starship consists of two stages: the Super Heavy booster, which provides the thrust needed to leave the launch pad, and the Starship spacecraft, which continues towards space after separation.

Super Heavy uses 33 Raptor engines, while Starship has six.

About two minutes and 21 seconds after launch, the upper stage will ignite its engines and separate from the booster in a manoeuvre known as hot-staging.

Super Heavy will then turn around and fire its engines to head back towards Starbase. As it descends, four grid fins near its top will help steer it towards the tower.

A final engine burn will slow the booster enough for the tower’s two large mechanical arms to support it at specially designed attachment points.

The manoeuvre requires the booster to approach the tower at the correct position and speed. SpaceX’s flight computers control the engines and steering surfaces, while automated checks determine whether the vehicle can safely proceed with the catch.

If the required conditions are not met, the booster can be directed away from the tower.

SpaceX’s published timeline places the Super Heavy catch approximately six minutes and 35 seconds after liftoff.

The upper stage faces a much longer journey.

Starship is expected to reach an orbit approximately 275km above Earth and complete about 14 orbits during a flight lasting more than 22 hours.

Before attempting its return, the flight control team will confirm that the spacecraft’s critical systems, including those needed for re-entry and its final landing burn, are working properly.

Starship will then fire an engine to leave orbit, descend through the atmosphere and use its four flaps to control its approach.

Near the ground, its engines will restart to slow the spacecraft and rotate it from a horizontal descent into a vertical position. The tower arms will then attempt to catch it.

SpaceX’s schedule places the planned Starship catch at about 22 hours and 32 minutes after launch.

The first catch in October 2024

SpaceX first demonstrated its tower-catching technique on 13 October 2024, during Starship’s fifth flight test.

The Super Heavy booster returned to Starbase approximately seven minutes after liftoff, fired its engines to slow its descent and was caught by the tower arms on the first attempt.

The success showed that a large rocket booster could be recovered without conventional landing legs.

SpaceX subsequently caught boosters during Flights 7 and 8 in January and March 2025. It has also reflown previously caught boosters.

Flight 15 will be the first attempt to catch a Super Heavy V3 booster, the newer version equipped with Raptor 3 engines.

Unlike SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rockets, which land vertically on legs at landing pads or offshore platforms, Super Heavy is designed to be recovered directly by the launch tower.

Removing landing legs reduces the hardware carried by the rocket. Catching it at the launch site also avoids transporting the booster back from a separate landing area.

The longer-term aim is to inspect, refuel and reuse rockets more quickly, although the ability to catch both stages does not by itself establish that they can be relaunched immediately.

Starlink satellites and heatshield tests

Flight 15 follows Starship’s first orbital mission on 28 September, when Flight 14 delivered 26 Starlink V3 satellites into orbit.

The next mission will carry another 26. SpaceX says each satellite can add one terabit per second of network capacity, with the combined payload providing capacity equivalent to approximately ten Falcon 9 launches carrying Starlink V2 Mini satellites.

After deployment, the satellites will unfold their antennas and solar arrays, establish communications and use onboard thrusters to raise their orbits. SpaceX expects them to begin serving customers within weeks, subject to successful checks.

Three satellites will also carry cameras to inspect Starship’s heatshield during flight and transmit images to engineers.

The heatshield is particularly important because Starship must survive the extreme temperatures generated during atmospheric re-entry before it can attempt a catch.

SpaceX says Flight 15 incorporates additional mechanisms to retain heatshield tiles, improvements to prevent hot plasma from entering gaps behind them and a curved tile design intended to reduce heating between tiles.

Safety checks before the return

SpaceX has designed the mission with alternative flight paths and predetermined ocean disposal areas if the spacecraft cannot safely continue towards a tower catch.

The company says Starship will return to Starbase only after engineers have confirmed that the systems needed for re-entry, descent and the final approach are healthy.

A live webcast is scheduled to begin approximately 30 minutes before liftoff, with coverage planned through the Starship catch attempt.

The launch remains dependent on regulatory approval, and SpaceX has cautioned that the schedule could change.

]]> Russia is building missile launchers for Iran, leaked documents suggest https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/russia-iran-missile-launcher-deal/ Mon, 09 Nov 2026 12:34:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55876 Leaked Russian documents reveal plans to supply Iran with guided-missile launchers, while analysts question whether a new ground-launched variant could threaten shipping.

The post Russia is building missile launchers for Iran, leaked documents suggest appeared first on AGN.

]]> The Russian defence industry arranged to manufacture missile-launch equipment for Iran under an export order covering 90 helicopter-mounted launchers, according to leaked documents published by Ukrainian intelligence organisation Dallas Analytics.

The records concern launchers for Russia’s LMUR precision-guided missile, also known as Izdeliye 305 or Kh-39, and offer further evidence of military cooperation between Moscow and Tehran.

However, the documents do not establish whether the launchers were ultimately delivered.

Russian documents identify order for 90 missile launchers

A Financial Times investigation drew on the records obtained by Dallas Analytics, which subsequently published the underlying documents.

The paperwork includes a May 2024 letter from Russian missile and launcher manufacturer Vympel, part of the state-controlled Tactical Missiles Corporation (KTRV).

An accompanying production schedule identifies an export customer under the code “K-10.” Dallas Analytics links that designation to Iran through separate supplier paperwork explicitly naming the country.

🇮🇷🇷🇺 Despite Washington’s recent assertions that Moscow is not backing Tehran, confidential Russian defence records tell a different story. Dallas Analytics publishes primary industrial documents proving conclusively what the export code "K-10" designates: Iran. 🕵️ State plants built specialised missile-launch hardware – arming the forces now strangling global energy transit in the Strait of Hormuz – alongside a wider pipeline spanning Yak-130 trainers and helicopter upgrades. Read our investigation and examine the original schedules: https://t.co/uzHDyssDzr

— Dallas Analytics (@dallas_analytic) November 5, 2026

According to the organisation, the schedule allocates power units for 90 APU-L twin-rail launchers, with component shipments scheduled between late 2024 and December 2025. Those industrial delivery dates do not establish when finished equipment reached Iran.

What are the missile launchers designed to carry?

The APU-L launch system carries two LMUR missiles and is associated with Russia’s attack helicopters, including the Mi-28.

The missile weighs around 105 kg and carries a 25 kg warhead. Its electro-optical guidance system incorporates thermal imaging and a two-way data link, allowing an operator to guide it during flight.

The equipment could therefore strengthen the precision-strike capabilities of helicopters equipped to use it, rather than representing a standalone ground-based missile system.

Russia’s wider military cooperation with Iran

In 2023, Iran announced plans to acquire Russian Mi-28 attack helicopters, Su-35 fighters and Yak-130 advanced trainers.

The launcher paperwork adds another element to that relationship: the equipment needed to carry and deploy guided weapons.

Dallas Analytics also published records concerning Yak-130 aircraft destined for the customer designated K-10. Iran publicly received its first Yak-130s in 2023.

An Iranian Yak-130 was subsequently shot down by an Israeli F-35.

Russia’s Rostec leaks reveal Su-34, Su-35, Su-57 fighter jet sales to Iran, Algeria Russia’s Rostec leaks reveal Su-34, Su-35, Su-57 fighter jet sales to Iran, Algeria

Russia’s new ground-launched missile raises questions over Iran

Dallas Analytics links the K-10 export contracts to Iran through supplier paperwork that explicitly identifies the recipient as “«K10» Iran.”

The organisation also examines Russia’s recently unveiled ground-launched missile system, known as Izdeliye 347 or Product 347, which adapts the LMUR missile for launch from a mobile ground platform.

Mounted on a truck, the system provides a surface-to-surface capability without requiring a helicopter. Dallas Analytics estimates that ground launch would reduce the original missile’s range to around 10 km, while citing a Russian claim of 20 km for an upgraded version.

The organisation suggests that mobile launchers could threaten vessels in the confined waters of the Strait of Hormuz. However, its suggestion that the system may have been developed with Iran in mind remains speculative.

Dallas Analytics explicitly acknowledges that it has seen no operational or photographic evidence of ground-launched LMURs in Iranian hands. The documents concerning helicopter-mounted launchers do not establish that Iran ordered or received the truck-mounted system.

]]> C-17s and C-130s could soon launch large numbers of cheap cruise missiles https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/usaf-c17-c130-cruise-missiles/ Mon, 09 Nov 2026 11:48:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56070 Starting next year, USAF C-17s and C-130s may be able to start firing low-cost, long-range cruise missiles from pallets.

The post C-17s and C-130s could soon launch large numbers of cheap cruise missiles appeared first on AGN.

]]> The US Air Force has outlined more of its plans to employ its C-17 Globemaster III and C-130 transport aircraft as cruise missile platforms, with service leaders saying the capability could arrive in the “very near future.”

These aircraft have the potential to deploy large numbers of long-range cruise missiles, significantly increasing the number of platforms available to launch strikes.

C-17s and C-130s move toward affordable cruise missile role

At the recent Airlift/Tanker Association’s annual symposium in Kissimmee, Florida, the Air Force outlined its plans to launch cruise missiles from its cargo airlifters.

Lt. Gen. Dan Tulley, commander of Air Mobility Command (AMC), underscored the warfighting imperative to defend airmen, aircraft, networks and bases, while making every mobility aircraft a potential threat.

This is being explored through experimentation with palletised payloads designed for use across different aircraft, including the Family of Affordable Mass Missiles-Palletized.

The approach could allow C-130 Hercules and C-17 Globemaster III aircraft to deliver massed missile strikes against enemy threats, supplementing their traditional transport missions.

Builds on earlier reporting on giving transports strike capability

The comments build on May 2026 AGN reporting that the Air Force was working to turn cargo aircraft into strike platforms, with anticipated fielding in 2027.

Aviation Week now reports that airlifters will be able to start deploying cruise missiles in the “very near future.” The development will require a mindset change among aircrews, although that description does not establish a firm operational date. aviationweek.com

The Family of Affordable Mass Missiles (FAMM) is the broader Air Force effort to develop low-cost, mass-producible cruise missiles.

A midyear request for information outlined separate palletised and lug-mounted requirements under its Beyond Adversary’s Reach effort.

The lug-mounted FAMM-L version is intended for carriage by fighters and bombers, while the palletised FAMM-P version is intended for deployment from cargo aircraft.

In July 2026, Anduril, CoAspire and Zone 5 secured framework agreements with the Pentagon to advance FAMM development.

However, a September acquisition notice confirmed that the FAMM-P BAR risk-reduction effort had been cancelled. That notice concerned a specific acquisition effort and should not be read as cancellation of the Air Force’s wider ambition to deploy palletised missiles.

Zone 5 Technologies’ AGM-188A Rusty Dagger is among the low-cost missile designs feeding into the Air Force’s wider affordable weapons plans, alongside designs from Anduril and CoAspire.

Rusty Dagger is being developed for multiple service branches and for launch from land, sea and air.

Zone 5’s president, Kyle Maxhimer, told The War Zone that the team had taken less than three months to progress from design to demonstration of its surface-launch configuration, expanding beyond aircraft pylons and pallets to ground launchers and shipping containers.

Ukraine narrows long-range strike gap with new missiles and drones Ukraine narrows long-range strike gap with new missiles and drones

Rapid Dragon testing dates back to 2019

The effort to transform cargo aircraft into weapon delivery systems has been ongoing since 2019 under the Rapid Dragon program.

In December 2021, an Air Force Special Operations Command MC-130J Commando II conducted a live-fire demonstration using a four-cell deployment system containing one live cruise missile and three mass simulants.

After leaving the aircraft, the deployment system stabilised under parachutes before releasing its payloads sequentially. The live missile then transitioned to powered flight and struck its target. The test did not involve launching nine live missiles.

While earlier Rapid Dragon demonstrations involved JASSM-ER cruise missiles, the newer affordable weapons effort aims to provide lower-cost options that can be produced in much larger quantities.

The Air Force has outlined a five-year plan to spend approximately $12.6 billion procuring almost 28,000 missiles under FAMM. The planned purchases cover both lug-mounted and palletised weapons, rather than missiles exclusively for cargo aircraft.

Those figures imply an average of roughly $450,000 per weapon across the proposed spending plan, but that calculation should not be treated as the production price of an individual missile design. Actual costs will depend on the weapons purchased and what the funding includes.

.sie-field-hero{position: relative; 
 left: 50%;
 right: 50%;
 margin-left: -50vw;
 margin-right: -50vw;
 width: 100vw; 
 min-height: 480px;
 max-height: 560px;
 background-size: cover;
 background-position: center 40%;
 background-repeat: no-repeat; 
 background-color: #003B73;
 overflow: hidden;
 margin-bottom: 0;}
.sie-field-hero--no-image{background: linear-gradient(
 135deg,
 var(--field-color, #003B73) 0%,
 color-mix(in srgb, var(--field-color, #003B73) 65%, #000) 100%
 );}
.sie-field-hero__bg-img{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center 40%;
 z-index: 0;
 display: block;}
.sie-field-hero__overlay{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 1;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.90) 0%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.60) 38%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.25) 65%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.12) 100%
 );
 display: flex;
 align-items: flex-end;
 padding-bottom: 52px;}
.sie-field-hero__inner{width: 100%;
 max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-field-hero__label{display: block;

 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}

 margin-bottom: 14px;

 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-category-badge i{font-size: 11px;

.sie-field-hero__title{font-size: clamp(30px, 5vw, 54px);

 never set flex-direction on an inherited flex container without checking

 .lh-hero .lh-hero-text{flex:0 0 auto}

 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat{padding:clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) clamp(14px,2vw,28px) clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) 0;border-right:1px solid #E4E0D8;text-align:left;background:none;border-radius:0;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat:last-child{border-right:0}

 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat-label{margin-top:8px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:1.3px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#4F5967}

 /* ── Institutional pass, part 2 (2026-11-08, evening) ──────────────────

 /* The page itself: the site-wide body is cold pale blue (#E8F1FA), which

 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title,.lh-wrap .lh-hero h2.lh-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif !important;font-weight:600 !important;font-size:clamp(34px,4.4vw,58px) !important;line-height:1.08 !important;letter-spacing:-.6px !important;color:#12233D !important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#12233D !important}
